en: Commentary on the Mind: A Rhapsody, Scroll One.
Composed by Chan Master Zhijue Yan-shou of Huiri Yongming Temple in Hangzhou during the Song Dynasty.
The Awakened Kings received this teaching in common.
The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its core principle; it has no gate, yet this absence of gates constitutes its dharma-gate. Furthermore, a verse from the sutra says:
"Just as there is a skilled physician in the world who cures illness with wondrous medicines, so too do the Buddhas teach 'Mind-Only' for the sake of sentient beings. Question:
The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence; having no gate is the Dharma-gate. Since this is titled "A Rhapsody on the Mind," it is already a manifestation of its essential principle.
Why rely on the extensive use of literary language or further elaborate commentaries?

Moreover, when discussing the fundamental principle, one addresses only those of sudden capacity—like the rising sun illuminating the high mountains, or a swift horse seeing the shadow of the whip. Thus, Master Danxia said: "When we meet..."
It is not brought out; as soon as the intention arises, one knows it exists. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Perfect and luminous awareness does not depend on mental thought.
Even raising an eyebrow or moving an eye is already a circumlocution. As a former master’s verse says: "This is still a redundant phrase; moving the eyes is already a deviation.
If you ask for the purport of Caoxi, do not wait for an eyebrow to be raised. [The Master] replied: "I shall now explain for you..."
For those who delight in the Buddha Vehicle but have not yet realized it, these words and phrases are provisionally employed to assist in manifesting the true mind.

Although they are suspended within the realm of literary expression, the wondrous intent resides therein. Bending down to gather in those of middling and inferior capacities, they encompass all types of spiritual potential. Let each person simply rely upon them to benefit themselves accordingly.
Though the hundred rivers provide moisture, how can this hinder the vast containment of the great ocean? Though the Five Peaks are naturally lofty, they do not obstruct the sky.
The sun shines universally, yet the capacities of beings are not equal; their inclinations and desires are not the same.

Although they differ in the four gateways through which they enter, there is no distinction when they perceive the One True Reality. It is like a bird-catcher who uses a net with many meshes—one mesh alone cannot constitute a net;
or a ruler whose success depends on a single person—one person alone cannot constitute a state. This is as with inner virtue.
The treatise says: Now, a single kind of water cannot harmonize a soup; a single type of wood cannot construct a house; a single garment does not suit all bodies;
a single medicine cannot cure diverse ailments; a single color cannot form embroidery; a single note cannot harmonize the lute and zither; a single word cannot encourage many virtues;
and a single precept cannot prevent manifold transgressions. How, then, could [a single thing suffice]?
To eliminate the distinctions between the strange and the sudden, and to ensure that the Dharma-gate remains singular, it is said: "As it is for one person, so it is for many;
as it is for many, so it is for one. How could this be the same as the limited views produced by the inferior understanding of ordinary minds?
This unimpeded and vast Dharma-gate of mine is like space, which is without characteristics, yet does not reject the manifestation of all phenomena.
It is manifested as if the Dharma-nature were formless, yet it is not obstructed by the simultaneous appearance of all forms. Thus, Master Zang said:

"Since the beginning of sentient beings, those who seek the teachings attain the truth; having realized the principle, they are unobstructed. They constantly contemplate the principle without hindering their upholding of the teachings."
If one constantly recites and studies without hindering the contemplation of emptiness, then principle and teaching will both be harmonized, merging into a single contemplation;

only then can one be said to possess ultimate and comprehensive mastery. This is what is meant by the identity of teaching and contemplation, where the expression and its underlying meaning share a common source.
The ancestral lineage was transmitted directly.
The Great Master Bodhidharma, the first patriarch in this land, said: "Transmit the mind by means of the mind; do not establish written words. He also said:

"Directly point to the human mind; see one's nature and become a Buddha. Furthermore, he spoke of the silent transmission of the seal of the mind, which has been inherited from generation to generation until the present.
Up to the present day, the fundamental nature of the ultimate and the conventional has been fully revealed.
As stated in the *Mahāyāna-śraddhotpāda-śāstra*: "There is the Mahāyāna, which is able to give rise to the great [mind] of all sentient beings."
Riding upon the faculty of faith. That which is called Mahāyāna is here translated as "Great Vehicle" (Dàchéng). Furthermore, the Great Vehicle is the mind of sentient beings;
because the essence of the mind is all-pervasive, it is called "Great. Because the mind can transport [beings], it is called a "Vehicle.
This establishes the Gate of the True Suchness of Mind and the Gate of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind. The Treatise states: "The Mahāyāna, when explained in general, is of two kinds."
First is the Dharma; second is its meaning. What is called the Dharma refers to the mind of sentient beings.
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Based upon this mind, the meaning of Mahāyāna is revealed. Why is this?
Because the aspect of the true suchness (*tathatā*) of this mind reveals the essence of Mahāyāna. Furthermore, it is the cause and condition for the arising and ceasing of this mind.

[The term] "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to its ability to demonstrate the essential nature, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna. As for what is called "meaning" (*artha*), there are three kinds:
first, the greatness of essence (*tattva-mahat*), which means that the *tathatā* (suchness) of all phenomena is equal, neither increasing nor decreasing;

second, the greatness of characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-mahat*), which means that the *tathāgatagarbha* is fully endowed with the qualities of untainted nature; third, the greatness of function (*vṛtti-mahat*), which is able to produce...
Because it is the cause and fruit of all mundane and supramundane virtues; because it is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted;
and because all Bodhisattvas mount this Dharma to reach the stage of a Tathāgata—therefore, one should know that this single mind is that which all Buddhas have fundamentally mounted.
It is because Bodhisattvas rely on this mental dharma as their vehicle that they all reach the stage of a Tathāgata. Apart from this...
Apart from the single mind, there is nothing else particularly superior; therefore, my present poetic composition is directed toward this. Master Zang said:

"When both the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously extinguished, the two truths eternally persist; when both emptiness and existence are equally lost, the single flavor constantly manifests. Thus, the *Huayan* commentary states:
"Although the ultimate and the conventional are mutually identical, each does not destroy its own characteristics; this is called the emptiness that is inherent in existence."
Only then is it true emptiness; only then is existence within emptiness wondrous existence. Emptiness and existence are non-dual, yet their two aspects remain distinct.
It is like waves being water while constantly moving: the conventional is the ultimate while conventional characteristics arise.

It is like water being waves while remaining ever-moist: the ultimate is the conventional while the ultimate essence persists. All of the above are metaphors for the essence and function of the mind; they are not...

They are neither identical nor different. Furthermore, it is said: "The gate of birth-and-death is not destroyed to speak of the gate of True Suchness (tathatā), nor is the gate of True Suchness concealed to speak of the gate of birth-and-death.
This is because these two gates are but the one mind. Therefore, the Buddhas of the ten directions always rely upon the two truths to preach the Dharma;
for if one does not attain the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one cannot attain the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). By means of the conventional truth...
It has no self-nature, for it is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It alone stands prior to heaven and earth.
As Master Fatu’s verse says: "There is a thing prior to heaven and earth; formless, it is fundamentally quiescent and solitary. It is able to give rise to the myriad phenomena."
The Lord does not wither with the four seasons. Laozi said: "There is a thing, a chaotic perfection, born before heaven and earth.

It is silent and vast; it stands alone and does not change. It moves through all things without exhaustion; it may be regarded as the mother of the world. I do not know its name; I designate it as 'the Way' (Dào). Forcedly, I call it 'Great.'* The *Pao-tsang lun* says: 'Emptiness can be emptied. *Note:

The term "forcedly" (qiǎng) implies that "Great" is merely a provisional designation for that which transcends all categories. The asterisk indicates a reference to the preceding citation from the *Laozi*. The final sentence refers to the realization that even the concept of emptiness is ultimately empty.
It is not the empty void; form is that which can be formed. It is not true form; true form is formless.

The empty void is nameless. The nameless is the father of names; the formless is the mother of forms. It acts as the root-source of the myriad dharmas and serves as the primordial ancestor of heaven and earth.

Above, it bestows the profound celestial phenomena; below, it arranges the dark courts of the netherworld. Primordial qi is contained within the Great Image, and the Great Image is hidden within [the Nameless].

It is formless, yet it constitutes the spirit of things. Within this spirit there is the divine, and within the divine there is the body. Through non-action they undergo transformation, each receiving its nature from spontaneity.
It is eternally the teacher of all Buddhas and can contain all wonders.
All Buddhas take the Dharma as their teacher. The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called the Dharma is the mind of sentient beings.
Furthermore, the single word "knowledge" (*zhi*) is the gateway to all wonders. The *Chan Yuan Ji* states: "Now, that which is called 'mind' is the mind's..."
As for the term "knowing," it refers to the essence of the mind. Regarding its ability to contain all wonders:
within the profound and dark depths of the single mind, all wonders reside. The pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), vast and obscure, serves as that which contains;

the infinite, wondrous virtues and the subtle, marvelous marks of greatness serve as that which is contained. These qualities depend upon the nature (*prakṛti*); since this nature encompasses everything without exception, it is so called.

[The Master] said: "Furthermore, it is said: 'Delusive thoughts are fundamentally quiescent; sensory objects are fundamentally empty. This mind of emptiness and quiescence possesses a numinous awareness that is never obscured.
This very awareness within emptiness and quiescence is the pure mind transmitted previously by Bodhidharma.

Whether one is deluded or awakened, the mind inherently knows itself; it does not depend on conditions to arise, nor does it originate because of objects. When deluded, there are afflictions; [yet this] knowing..."

It is not affliction; it is a spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*) at the moment of awakening, yet one knows it is not a spiritual transformation. Nevertheless, by being deluded regarding this knowing, the mark of a self (*ātman*) immediately arises.
If one realizes this knowing, one attains Buddhahood in a single instant (*kṣaṇa*). Thus, the *Xinyao jian* states: "The dharma of mind is fundamentally based on non-abiding.
The essence of the non-abiding mind is a numinous knowing that is never obscured. Furthermore, it is like a single mani jewel—a single, numinous mind."
It is simply perfect, luminous, and pure—the empty, quiescent awareness. It is entirely devoid of all differentiated forms and appearances;
yet, because its essence is luminous, when it encounters external objects, it can manifest all differentiated forms and appearances.

While the forms and appearances themselves possess their own distinctions, the bright pearl never undergoes change. For instance, when the pearl manifests blackness, one simply says that the blackness and so forth are the pearl.

As the Great Master Mazu of Hongzhou said: "The arising of thought, the movement of a念 (nian), the snapping of fingers, the twinkling of eyes—whatever is done and whatever is enacted is all Buddha-nature.
This is to clarify the true within the deluded; it is not like attempting to seek a pearl apart from the blackness [of the water].

As the Great Master Xiu of the Northern School said: "Sentient beings inherently possess the nature of awakening, just as a mirror possesses the nature of luminosity, yet it is shrouded by afflictions."
It is not seen. Just as a mirror may be covered by dust and darkness, when deluded thoughts are exhausted, the mind becomes luminous; when the turbid dust is extinguished, the mirror becomes bright.
This is the departure from delusion and the illumination of the true. As for those who say that both light and darkness are utterly non-existent, it is as the Great Master Niu-t’ou Jung said:
"All phenomena are like dreams; fundamentally there is no affair. The mind and its objects are originally quiescent; they have not become empty only now. One should thus relinquish [all attachments].
When one has forgotten emotions, and emotions are forgotten, they are severed. This is the state where both the real and the false are absent. The first [of the three stages] is entirely real;
the second is entirely false; the last is entirely non-existent. All of these represent not yet having seen the pearl.

It is like Master Heze, who, within the state of empty non-characteristics, pointed out knowing-seeing: "Clear and constant knowing does not obscure the nature and mind"—this is seeing the blackness of the pearl.
At that time, one sees only the bright and pure essence of the jewel, without observing its black color or its various hues such as blue and yellow.
It is neither identical to black, nor is it separate from black; nor does it exclude both black and white. This is when one clearly perceives the nature of the mind.
Neither identical nor separate; without abiding and without attachment; neither one nor different; neither grasping nor abandoning.

Furthermore, the fundamental substance of the true mind has two kinds of function: first, its self-nature which is inherently present; second, its responsive application according to conditions. It is like a bronze mirror:
the substance of the bronze is the self-nature body, and the clarity of the bronze is the self-nature function. As for the clarity...
The manifestation of reflections is the function that accords with conditions. A reflection only appears in response to conditions and thus manifests in a thousand variations;

clarity, however, is simply luminosity, and luminosity is of a single flavor. This serves as a metaphor for the fact that the mind’s constant stillness is its essential nature (*svabhāva-kāya*), while the mind’s constant awareness is its functional activity (*svabhāva-vṛtti*).
Now, when Master Hongzhou points to the capacity for speech, discrimination, and so forth, he is indicating only the function that accords with conditions; [the essence] is absent.

This refers to the function of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, in the Exoteric Teachings, there is manifestation through inference (*anumāna*) and manifestation through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Hongzhou said: "The mind cannot be pointed out; one only knows that Buddha-nature exists by inferring it from such things as the capacity for speech.
This is manifestation through inference. Heze, however, stated directly: "The essence of the mind is capable of knowing; knowing itself is the mind. He did not rely on knowing to manifest the mind.
This is manifested through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); Hongzhou lacks this. Furthermore, non-changing is the essence (*tattva*), while following conditions is its function (*vṛtti*).
Moreover, regarding the "empty stillness and knowing" (*śūnyatā-śānti-jñāna*) that Heze takes as his primary tenet: empty stillness is precisely the absence of marks (*animitta*).

Although the nature of spiritual understanding has no form or appearance, its numinous knowing is not obscured; therefore, it is called "still knowing. It is also called "still illumination," and also called "non-... [the text here is fragmentary].
The wisdom of characteristics is also called "knowledge of non-knowledge. As the *Zhao lun* says, and as the *Prajñāpāramitā of the Radiant Light* states:
"Prajñā has no characteristic of existence; it has no characteristic of arising or ceasing. The *Prajñāpāramitā of the Path of Practice* says: "Prajñā has nothing known and nothing seen.
Why is it that, while this explains the function of the illumination of wisdom, it is described as being "without characteristics" and "without knowledge"? Indeed.
It is clear that there is knowledge of both existence and non-existence, and an illumination that does not know. Why is this so? For where there is something known, there is something unknown.
Because the Sage’s mind is without knowing, it knows all things. This knowledge through non-knowing is called "omniscience. Thus, the Sūtra says:
"The Sage’s mind is without knowing, yet there is nothing it does not know. This is indeed true. Emptiness and stillness are—
This is signlessness (*animitta*). It is precisely non-cognition. The *Śāstra* says there is nothing that is not known; it also says, "He is called the All-Knower. This knowing is true knowing.
It is the essence of the self-mind of all sentient beings, the numinous knowing of true nature, which is profoundly still and constantly illuminating.
It is also called "knowing without thought. If one knows with thought, one is an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).
Therefore, it is said that perception and cognition belong to sentient beings. If there is neither thought nor cognition, this is the realm of the Two Vehicles.
If there is cognition without thought, this is the realm of the Buddhas. Emptiness and stillness are precisely non-thought; they are also called non-abiding cognition.
If there is anything upon which one dwells, it is like a person entering darkness and seeing nothing. If there is no place of dwelling, it is like the sun.
The moonlight shines, illuminating various forms. The *Huayan jin guan* (Brocade Crown of the Flower Ornament) states:
"To contain all wonders with abundance" refers to the fact that all phenomena do not alter their fundamental characteristics and do not depart from their original positions.
Every dharma is capable of being large or small, one or many, the principal or the attendant; it is this very thing and yet that, it is hidden and yet manifest.
The long and the short immediately extend into and encompass one another, layer upon layer without end, like the Indra-net or celestial jewels. To state the essential point:
in accordance with each and every phenomenon, every moment of thought is fully endowed with the ten mysteries; they are simultaneously complete, without before or after.
Just as a single drop of ocean water contains all the hundred rivers, so it is with every drop; therefore, it is called "wondrous."
To be eternally the mother of the multitude of sages may be called profound and mysterious.
Now, Prajñā is the mother of all Buddhas; thus, a verse in the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says: "Prajñāpāramitā is the mother of Bodhisattvas;
she can give birth to all Teachers. What is called Prajñā is precisely the self-mind of all sentient beings.

It is simply the nature of numinous awareness. As the *Treasury of Jewels* (*Baocang lun*) says: "Within heaven and earth, amidst the universe, there is a single treasure hidden within the mountain of form.
It is the numinous illumination that cognizes things; internally and externally it is empty and still.

It is so silent and tranquil that it is difficult to perceive, and is thus called 'profound beyond the profound. Its skillful manifestation lies beyond the Purple Microcosm (*Ziwēi*), and its function resides within the realm of non-being (*xūwú*)."
Its transformation is upright and unmoving; solitary and without peer. From its voice issues a wondrous resonance; from its form exudes a radiant countenance.

To the utmost, one gazes but finds nothing; it lends its name to the "emptiness of emptiness. Who retains its sound? One does not see its form. Only its merit remains; one does not see its appearance.

It illuminates clearly both the hidden and the manifest; the principles of things are empty and pervasive. The myriad phenomena are the seal of the jewels; the ten thousand images are the true source. Its...

In its manifestation, it takes form; in its stillness, it is profound darkness. Its fundamental purity is not merely polished clarity; it is spontaneously perfected by the nature of reality (*dharmatā*). Its radiance transcends the sun and moon; its virtue surpasses the Great Clarity (*Taiqing*).
The myriad things are without action; all things are without name. It can transform heaven and earth, moving with sovereign ease in every direction.

Myriad subtle functions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, are formed from the primordial chaos (*hundun*). Who would hear this and not rejoice? Who would hear this and not be struck with wonder? It is like...
Why is this priceless treasure hidden within the pit of the sense-bases (*āyatana*)? Alas, alas! To say it is self-depreciation; how tragic, how tragic!
How can that which is obscured become luminous? That treasure is resplendent and brilliant, shining brightly throughout the ten directions.
It is profoundly still and devoid of things, yet its perfect response is majestic. It responds to sound and form, responding to both the Yin and the Yang—how extraordinary!
It has no root; its wondrous function is ever-present. One does not see it when closing one’s eyes, nor hear it when tilting one’s ear.
Its essence is dark and profound; its transformation takes form. Its being is sagely; its function is numinous. It may be called the true quintessence of the Great Way.
This quintessence is exceedingly numinous—the cause of all that exists. It remains eternally concentrated and abiding, sharing the same category as the Way. Thus, the Sutra says: "Following..."
When the mind is pure, the Buddha-field is pure; all that is manifested therein is called "sacred. Furthermore, if one realizes this single mind, one understands all dharma-gates.
As it says in the *Zhiguan*: "It is like a skilled physician who possesses a secret prescription that encompasses all other prescriptions.
The Agada medicine combines the efficacy of all other medicines. It is like eating milk gruel; after which nothing else is needed."
Whatever is required is fully provided, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.

Even this single mind is the greatest among the great, the highest among the high, the most perfect among the perfect, the most complete among the complete, the most real among the real, the most true among the true, the most definitive among the definitive, the most profound among the profound, and the most wondrous among the wondrous; it is the inconceivable among the inconceivable. If one can thus...
This excludes what is not [the true cause] and reveals what is. One who generates the mind of awakening by realizing the identity of the provisional and the real is the seed of all Buddhas;
it is like a diamond produced from the nature of gold. The Buddha’s bodhicitta arises from great compassion and is the precursor to all practices.
Just as when taking the *apāmārga* herb, one first uses pure water; just as among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is supreme;
just as among all faculties, the life-faculty is supreme; so too, among the Buddha’s true Dharma and right practice, this mind is supreme.

It is like the birth of a crown prince, who possesses the marks of royalty, is honored by great ministers, and has a great reputation; it is like the kalaviṅka bird, which sings even within its shell.
Its voice already surpasses that of all birds. This bodhicitta possesses great power, like a lute string made of lion sinew, like lion’s milk, like a vajra hammer, and like Nārāyaṇa’s arrow.
Endowed with all manner of jewels, it can eliminate the suffering of poverty, like a wish-fulfilling gem.
Even if one is slightly indolent or slightly lapses in dignified conduct, it still surpasses the merits of the two vehicles.
To state the essentials: this mind itself possesses all the merits of a bodhisattva and is capable of accomplishing the unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment of the three periods of time.
Its numinous nature is like a pearl, encompassing and penetrating all things beyond measure.
This nature of the mind’s inner citadel is the most intelligent and most wondrous; it acts as the sovereign of all phenomena and serves as the substance of all existence.
Vertically, it penetrates the three periods of time; horizontally, it spans the ten directions. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Within the category of sentient beings, it is Buddha-nature; within the category of insentient things, it is Dharma-nature. Thus, a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) pervades all places; all sentient beings and lands throughout the three periods of time are entirely contained within it without exception, yet it possesses no form or characteristic that can be apprehended.
As stated in the "Chapter on the Purity of the Essence Beyond Subtlety" in Sengzhao’s *Treatise on Emptiness*:
"Now, that which is the essence beyond subtlety is neither grasped nor discarded; it is neither cultivated nor studied; it is not something originally non-existent that now exists."
Originally existent and now non-existent; even down to a single dharma, there is neither arising nor ceasing. It is not subsumed within the three realms, nor transformed by the six destinies.
It is not altered by the ignorant or the wise, nor shifted by the real or the false. It is equal and all-pervasive.

All things are perfectly complete, collectively constituting a single great Dharma-realm, a wondrous mansion of illusory transformation. Those who are deluded wander through kalpas in vain cultivation;
those who awaken realize that its very substance is still and quiescent.
The thousand paths all arise from that; the myriad phenomena all emerge from this. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"All dharmas take non-abiding as their root. This "non-abiding" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) of all sentient beings.
Because this mind has no abiding and no root, it is said to "establish all things from the root of non-abiding."
Regarding the Dharma, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "That which is perceived is pure, being not separate from the mind. It further states:
"Not separate from the mind, it has no location. Thus we know that the mind gives rise to all phenomena, just as water emerges from the earth or as wind is contained within a valley.
It is like clouds arising from stone or fire emerging from wood; thus we know that apart from the mind there are no phenomena, and apart from phenomena there is no mind.

As the *Kāśyapaparivarta* states: "If one were to speak directly of the eighth seed-consciousness as the Tathāgatagarbha, then the seeds of karma would be eternally real, which would cause fear and be difficult to believe. By the power of such a Dharma, what sentient being would not [attain liberation]?"

Possessing supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), they rely on the merit of the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-bodhi*). How could even a single speck of dust not contain the traces of the Way?

Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* speaks of "the power of the suchness of phenomena" (*dharmatā-tathatva-bala*), meaning that it is inherently and naturally so. It further speaks of "the Buddha’s spiritual power" (*buddha-adhiṣṭhāna-bala*).
The Arhat replied, "It is the divine. Thus, the ancient masters said: "One's own power and the Buddha’s power are no different; one's own wisdom and the Buddha’s wisdom are without distinction.
They further said: "A single body takes the Dharma-realm as its measure; the boundaries of self and other are entirely extinguished.
The Dharma-realm is itself the pervasive totality of one's own body; the dualistic sentiments of subject and object are severed. It is like a drop in the great ocean."
Within every single drop, one attains the great ocean; comparing this to the minds of sentient beings, every thought-moment contains the Buddha-wisdom.
The phenomena are as vast as the sands of the Ganges, yet the principle is marked by its essential reality. To swallow the vast blue sea within a single pore is solely due to one's own causes;
to roll the entire dharma-realm into a speck of dust requires no other method.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are bewildered and distressed; turning their backs on awakening and uniting with the sensory dust, they give rise to worldly toil and manifest the signs of the mundane world.
I, however, unite my wondrous clarity—neither arising nor ceasing—with the Tathāgata-garbha.
And this Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm. Therefore, within it, one becomes infinite, and the infinite becomes one."
The small manifests the large within; the large manifests the small within. Without moving from the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), one manifests the worlds of the ten directions;
the body contains the infinite space of the ten directions. Within the tip of a single hair, one manifests jewel-king lands; seated within a mote of dust, one turns the Great Dharma Wheel.
Thus we know that by turning one's back on objects and contemplating the mind, the great luminosity naturally interpenetrates, and one is no longer turned by external things. Furthermore...
As in the case of a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru and so forth, the *Yibaimen yihai* (The Ocean of Meaning of the Hundred Gates) states:

"For instance, when one perceives a mountain as high and vast, it is the self-mind manifesting as large; now, when one perceives a speck of dust as small, this too is the self-mind manifesting as small.
Since the perception of the speck of dust now occurs entirely by means of the same mind that previously perceived the mountain's height, the small [dust] contains the large."
It is like clouds [enveloping] the myriad phenomena, while the pure mind is like a mustard seed. Thus it is said:
"The forested peaks and the myriad phenomena are all sealed by a single dharma. This means that the myriad dharmas are the one mind, and the one mind is the myriad dharmas;

hence, it is called "a hair swallowing the vast ocean" or "a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru. This does not depend on the power of supernatural transformations, for the true mind is inherently endowed with these qualities.
The nature is thus. As the *Huayan ji* (Record of the Avataṃsaka) states:
"Regarding the differentiated nature of all worlds within a single hair-tip, this means that the nature of one hair-tip is itself the differentiated nature of all worlds.
Now, all worlds are the phenomena (*dharma*), and according to their *dharmatā*, they are a single hair-tip. Because the nature is identical to the hair-tip, [all things are so].
Because the realm (*dhātu*) is itself the nature (*prakṛti*), names are inaugurated according to the capacities of beings, and titles are established in response to phenomena.
All dharmas are fundamentally nameless; it is only the mind that creates names. Thus, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "The six sense objects are dull..."

Therefore, names are not established by themselves, nor are they established by their own accord; all are established through the mind. Thus it is said: "The myriad dharmas are fundamentally at rest, yet people themselves create turmoil.
It is further said that the names of the three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas are all but different designations for the mind.
As the *Tiantai Jingming shu* states: "Regarding one dharma having various names, the various sūtras employ different names to speak of true nature and reality."

The marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Some call it the single ultimate truth (*ekābhisamaya-satya*); some call it the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*); some call it the *tathāgatagarbha*; some call it suchness (*tathatā*);
some call it the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); some call it the prajñā of true marks (*bhūtalakṣaṇa-prajñā*); some call it the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*); some call it the Śūraṅgama;
some call it the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*); some call it the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); or some call it the Middle Way (*madhyamā pratipad*). Or they call it...

Ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*), or what is called the causal Buddha-nature (*hetu-buddhadhātu*), or nature-pure nirvana (*prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa*)—these various different names are all alternative designations for the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Thus, a verse in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says:
"Prajñā is a single dharma, yet the Buddha speaks of it by various names; according to the types of sentient beings, he establishes different terms for it. — *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
The Sūtra states: "Just as Śakra, Lord of the Devas, has a thousand names, so too does liberation have many names.
It further states that because the Buddha-nature has five names, these are all established as distinct appellations to accord with the capacities of sentient beings and to benefit them;
yet the essence of the Dharma is one and has never been otherwise. It is like the thousand names of Śakra: although the names differ, [the deity remains the same].
In the end, one must look to the Lord of Heaven (*devendra*). How could one, upon hearing a different name, claim that it is not the true principle of reality?
It would be like someone who makes offerings to Śakra while disparaging Kauśika, or who makes offerings to Kauśika while disparaging Śakra;
such offerings do not necessarily yield merit. Those who cling to their own doctrines in the final age are likewise: they may either place their trust in *ālaya* itself...

Some disparage the intrinsically pure mind while [asserting] ultimate emptiness; others, believing that ultimate emptiness is non-existent, disparage the *ālayavijñāna* and the intrinsically pure mind.
Still others claim that the *Prajñāpāramitā* clarifies the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*) while the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* clarifies the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
None of these constitute Buddha-nature. In seeking such blessings, how can one fail to consider the potential for calamity?
If one understands that while names differ, their substance is one, then the merit of sympathetic joy (anumodana) pervades the entire Dharma-realm; what, then, is there to dispute?

Furthermore, within the various sutras, [the Buddha] adapts to conditions and accords with capacities, establishing many different names in various contexts. From the perspective of its vast and expansive meaning, it is designated as a "sea. By means of...
The principle of perfect luminosity is manifest; thus it is called a "jewel. Because it is the source of all phenomena, it is designated as the "king.
Because it can give birth to all things, it is named the "mother. It is the true meaning within the absence of meaning; though manifold, it is not many.

It is the true mind within the absence of mind; though singular, it is not one. Therefore, the *Huayan siji* (Private Record on the Avataṃsaka) states that it is determined by taking the sense of decisive resolution.
Speaking in terms of wisdom, it takes that which can cause growth; speaking in terms of earth, it takes that which is lofty and prominent;
speaking in terms of mountains, it takes that which is deep and vast; speaking in terms of oceans, it takes that which is round and pure;
speaking in terms of jewels, these aforementioned named things are already innumerable, let alone those without names—how could they ever be measured? It is like the *Dafahujie* (Great Dharma Torch).
The *Dhāraṇī-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas, saying, "You should not say that gods are fixed as gods, humans are fixed as humans, or hungry ghosts are fixed as hungry ghosts.
Just as a single thing may have various names, or as a single person may have various names, so too do the gods, and even the hungry ghosts and animals, have various names."
It is likewise so. There are also many hungry ghosts who have no names at all; in the space of a single finger-snap, they transform their bodies into various forms.
In this way, these sentient beings manifest immeasurable physical bodies in a single moment.

How could one possibly call them by name? If beings such as hungry ghosts have names for their place of birth, names for the food they receive, and names for their lifespan, then as for hell-beings who have no name for a place of birth, [how could they be named]?
Thus, their forms are also not fixed. Because the causal conditions for their evil karma within that state have not yet been exhausted, they manifest various bodies in a single moment of thought.
The commentary states: For example, in the hells, one undergoes ten thousand births and ten thousand deaths within a single day and night;
how could one possibly name them? Furthermore, in the Avīci Hell, each body arises without interval, each [undergoing the same].
Each [hell] extends throughout eighty-four thousand *yojanas*, yet the dimensions of these hells do not obstruct one another.
Thus we know that the fruits of karma are inconceivable; it is not only the fruit of the sages. As it is said: "The pure and wondrous *dharmakāya* is serenely responsive to all.
People of the present age assume that the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas can be divided and can pervade [all things], yet they do not believe in the multitude [of karmic results].
Birth is both a single body and infinite bodies, because the karmic fruits of sentient beings are inconceivable.
Therefore, a sutra says: "The Buddha-realm is inconceivable; the realm of sentient beings is also inconceivable."
The Great Being cultivates these and brings them to fulfillment.
The ten pāramitās, the four means of integration, and the myriad practices performed by a bodhisattva all arise from the mind of true compassion.
Therefore, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "The empty mind is unmoving; it fully possesses the six pāramitās. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"With a single mind, one fully possesses the myriad practices and the ten pāramitās. Regarding *dāna* (generosity), it is the relinquishing [of things] by means of the mind.
The sūtra says: "That which has nothing to give is called giving; this is termed true giving. If there were dharmas outside of the mind, then...

This is called "giving while abiding in characteristics. It is like a person entering darkness who sees nothing at all. Precepts are maintained by means of the mind. As a sutra says: "The nature of precepts is like empty space;
those who maintain them are deluded and inverted. How could the law of self-nature cling to formal characteristics and falsely distinguish between maintaining and violating?
Patience is received by means of the mind. As a sutra says: "How does a bodhisattva practice patience? The Buddha [said:]...
He said: "One observes that the characteristics of the mind perish moment by moment. How could one take this mind to confront external objects as a means of endurance?
Diligence (*vīrya*) is produced because of the mind; as a sutra says: 'If the mind does not arise, diligence is boundless.

Why then cling to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and vainly give rise to weary deliberations? Meditation (*dhyāna*) is triggered by the mind; as a sutra says: 'To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called supreme.'"
As for meditative concentration (*samādhi*), how could one avoid clamor and confusion only to cling to stillness as a defilement? Prajñā arises from the mind. As a sutra says:
"Not seeking the nature, characteristics, causes, or conditions of all dharmas is called right wisdom. How could one instead pursue external words and forcefully generate intellectual understanding?
Expedient means (*upāya*) arise from the mind. As a sutra says: "The Bodhisattva takes non-attainment as expedient means. Thus...
There are no phenomena outside the mind; only then can one practice the path of a bodhisattva. Power is mobilized from the mind;
the power of the four great elements is all inferior to that of the mind. Because the mind has no form, its power is supreme.
Its supernatural transformations enter the inconceivable—all this is the power of the mind. Aspiration is spread from the mind; all intentions and wishes arise entirely from the mind. All...
The gates of practice all arise from vows; wisdom is realized through the mind. The numinous wisdom of the Tathāgata is the very mind of sentient beings.
This mind, in every thought-moment, is fully endowed with the ten pāramitās, even unto the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, all of which issue forth from the mind.
Just as there is the "great essence" within the minds of sentient beings, today’s cultivation draws forth the Dharmakāya from the mind. The mind...
Within it is the Great Aspect; by practicing today, one brings forth the Reward Body (*saṃbhogakāya*). Within the mind is the Great Function;
by practicing today, one brings forth the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Thus, one should know that the three bodies and four wisdoms all emerge from within the mind.

Outside the mind, there is not a single thing or a single dharma that can be established. As the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) says: "The One Substance gives rise to the two."
Regarding its functions: first is the eternally abiding function of the ocean-seal array. "Ocean-seal" refers to the original enlightenment of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

When delusion is exhausted and the mind is clarified, the myriad phenomena appear simultaneously, just like a great ocean; when the wind arises, waves are stirred, but if the wind ceases, [the water remains still].
The waters of the sea are clear and limpid; there is no form that does not appear within them. Thus it is said:
"The myriad phenomena and the ten thousand images are all sealed by a single dharma. This "single dharma" refers to the one mind. This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas;
it is the Great Universal Characteristic Dharma-gate of the Single Dharma-realm. Its essence is solely one, yet it depends upon deluded thought.
Yet there is a distinction: if one is free from deluded thoughts, there is only True Suchness (tathatā); therefore, it is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgarāmudrā-samādhi*).

Second is the sovereign function of the perfectly luminous Dharma-realm; this is the Flower Ornament Samādhi (*avaivartika-vaipulya-samādhi*). It refers to the extensive cultivation of the myriad practices.

Accordant with principle, one accomplishes virtue; universally identical with the Dharma-realm, one realizes Bodhi. This is because there are no practices flowing from the True that can accord with the True;
how could there be any practices adorning the True that do not arise from the True? Thus, the True encompasses the extremities of delusion, such that there is no practice that is not cultivated;
delusion penetrates to the source of the True, such that there is no characteristic that is not quiescent.
The Awakening Emperor realized this body and attained perfect fulfillment.
All Buddhas understand that all phenomena are the true mind, the perfected-real nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Sentient beings are deluded regarding their own minds;

these are merely the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which exists in the realm of emotion but is non-existent in reality. As the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) says: "Precisely because..."

The Dharma has no divisions or limits; when it arises, it necessarily does so simultaneously. True reality does not obstruct the myriad differences, and its manifest responsiveness is nothing other than the single boundary.
Its function is like surging waves and boiling oceans, operating entirely through the movement of the true essence. Its essence is like a clear mirror and limpid water.
Arising in accordance with conditions, it converges upon stillness; like the radiance of sunlight streaming forth, it illuminates the ten directions without conscious intent.
Like a clear mirror reflecting forms, it manifests the myriad phenomena without movement.
The Śrāvakas realize these as the Four Noble Truths.

Not understanding that they are their own minds, they perceive only the emptiness of persons and realize them as the truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of cessation, and the truth of the path—the four truths of arising and ceasing—which result in the fruit of extinction through ashes. They do not reach the non-conditioned four truths of the One Mind Perfect Teaching.

Truly so. He possessed vast and great supernormal powers. This is why Śāriputra, within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, was able to realize the nature of the mind and personally receive the Buddha’s prediction;
it was only later that he offered this repentance, saying: "While sharing in the same Dharma, I failed to attain this matter."
The Pratyekabuddhas awaken to this and designate it as "dependent origination.
Within the scope of their own mental objects, the Pratyekabuddhas perceive the nature of causes and conditions as being detached;

they realize the dharma-gate of the twelve links of dependent origination and likewise achieve the fruit of cessation (nirvāṇa). None of them, however, are able to single-mindedly and perfectly embody the ten dharma-realms.
Regarding essence and function:
in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, when the heavenly maidens scattered flowers upon the bodies of the bodhisattvas, they did not adhere to them; however, [the flowers] did adhere to the śrāvakas.
The flowers on his body immediately adhered to him. Generally speaking, all the activities of Bodhisattvas are the functioning of their own minds.

Because the mind is free from attachment, the flowers likewise do not adhere. For this reason, the Śrāvakas grasped at them as flowers existing outside the mind and falsely gave rise to aversion and detachment, saying they were "not in accordance with the Dharma.
Yet, as soon as they were brushed away, the flowers arose again. Thus one knows that the myriad dharmas follow [the mind].
They arise from one's own mind and perish along with one's own mind.

When the waters of the ocean of Sagaramati became clear and still, as described in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*, when the Bodhisattva Sagaramati first arrived, he did not see the fourfold assembly; he saw them all as...
Water. Because there is no dharma outside of the Dharma, one clings to erroneous interpretations and the gates of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) open; their nets of extreme heterodoxy are dense.
Among the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhists in India, none have realized their own minds; they merely torment their bodies and practice [asceticism].

Climbing cliffs or leaping into fire is useless asceticism. To perceive phenomena as external to the mind, or to seek something apart from principle, constitutes being a non-Buddhist and results entirely in false views.
Like being entangled in a dense net, one cannot escape the three realms.
By employing deluded thoughts, the karma of the mundane path arises; thus, the waves of birth and death surge across.
All karmas arise from the presence of a mind; where there is no mind, there is no karma. Therefore, a verse in a sutra says: "All phenomena are not solid;
they exist only in dependence upon thought. One who skillfully understands and perceives emptiness has no conceptualizations whatsoever."
It is further said: "Within a single thought-moment (citta-kṣaṇa) there are ninety kṣaṇas; within a single kṣaṇa there are nine hundred births and cessations.

Therefore, one knows that birth-and-death is precisely the thought-moment, and the thought-moment is precisely birth-and-death. Thus, a verse in the Sūtra says: 'Where there is thought, there is birth-and-death;
where there is no thought, there is nirvāṇa.'"

Encompassing the past and searching through the present, it profoundly contains and uniquely possesses this Dharma of the One Mind, which all teachings equally elucidate; there are none that do not point toward and transmit it through this.
As the "Contemplation of the Mind" chapter of the *Mahāyāna-mūla-jātaka-citta-bhūmi-darśana-sūtra* states: At that time, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī...

The Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, as the Buddha has said when instructing the five hundred elders, such as Mañjuśrī, ‘I shall expound for you the subtle and wondrous Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground,’ I now inquire of the Tathāgata regarding this:
what is the mind? What is the ground? ... [and so on] ... until the Bhagavat spoke to the Mothers of all Buddhas.
The Great Holy One, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, addressed him, saying:
"O Great Son of Good Family, this Dharma is called the 'Dharma-gate of the Most Supreme Secret Mind-Ground of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions.
This Dharma is called the 'Dharma-gate of Sudden Enlightenment for All Ordinary Beings to Enter the Ground of the Tathāgata. This Dharma is called [the Dharma-gate] of all Bodhisattvas..."

This is the true and correct path leading to great bodhi. This Dharma is called the subtle and wondrous jeweled palace where the Buddhas of the three periods of time enjoy the bliss of the Dharma for themselves.
This Dharma is called the inexhaustible jewel treasury that benefits all sentient beings.
This Dharma can lead the assembly of Bodhisattvas to the realm of sovereign wisdom at the pinnacle of form (*akaniṣṭha*).
This Dharma can lead the true guides, those Bodhisattvas in their final birth before reaching the Bodhi tree.

This Dharma can rain down mundane and supramundane wealth, like a *maṇi* jewel that fulfills the aspirations of sentient beings. This Dharma can give rise to [the realization of] the oneness of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
This is the fundamental source of all Buddhas' merits. This Dharma can eliminate the fruits of all evil karma of all sentient beings.
This Dharma can bestow the seal of fulfillment upon all that is sought by all sentient beings.
This Dharma can deliver all sentient beings from the perilous difficulties of birth and death. This Dharma can still the waves of the ocean of suffering for all sentient beings. This Dharma...
It is able to rescue sentient beings from suffering and distress, acting as their refuge in times of urgent peril.
This Dharma can exhaust the ocean of old age, sickness, and death for all sentient beings. This Dharma is well able to produce the seeds of the causal conditions for all Buddhas.
This Dharma can serve as a great torch of wisdom for the long night of birth and death. This Dharma can destroy the armies of the four Māras and act as armor.
This Dharma is the banner of victory for the army of true valor. This Dharma is the unsurpassed Wheel of the Dharma of all Buddhas.
This Dharma is the most supreme Banner of the Dharma. This Dharma is the beating of the Great Dharma Drum.
This Dharma is the blowing of the Great Dharma Conch. This Dharma is the Great Lion King.
This Dharma is the great lion’s roar. This Dharma is like a great holy king of a nation who is well-versed in the True Dharma.
If one accords with the king’s transformation, one will obtain great peace and happiness; if one opposes the king’s transformation, one will soon be executed and destroyed.
Good son, within the three realms, the mind is sovereign. Those who can contemplate the mind will ultimately attain liberation; those who cannot...
As for the observer, they ultimately sink into delusion. The minds of sentient beings are like the great earth;

just as the five grains and five fruits grow from the great earth, so too do these mental phenomena give rise to the mundane and supramundane, the good and evil, the five destinies, those in training (śaikṣa), and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
For Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, by virtue of these causes and conditions, the three realms are mind-only. Mind is called the ground.

All ordinary beings who associate with virtuous friends, hear the Dharma of the Ground of Mind, investigate it according to principle, and practice as taught—benefiting themselves, instructing others, and encouraging, exhorting, and rejoicing with them—such persons are able to sever the two obstacles and swiftly [attain liberation].
Completing all practices, one swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The path of the five vehicles is refined within the profound breast.

As for the five vehicles: first, by upholding the five precepts, one attains the human vehicle; second, by practicing the ten wholesome deeds, one attains the celestial vehicle; third, by cultivating...
The four truths lead to the attainment of the Śrāvaka vehicle. The fourfold awakening to the law of the twelve links of dependent origination leads to the attainment of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

The fifth is the practice of the six perfections, which leads to the attainment of the Bodhisattva vehicle. These five vehicles all emerge from the cultivation and refinement of a single thought of goodness.
The ten dharma realms are conceived and formed in the first thought-moment.
As for the ten dharma realms: first, the realm of devas, which cultivates the ten wholesome karmas; second, the realm of humans, which maintains the karma of the five precepts;
third, the realm of asuras, which practices the karma of arrogance; and fourth, the realm of hell-beings, which commits the ten unwholesome karmas.
Fifth is the realm of hungry ghosts, who create karma through stinginess and greed. Sixth is the realm of animals, who create karma through ignorance.
Seventh is the realm of śrāvakas, who realize the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths. Eighth is the realm of pratyekabuddhas, who awaken to the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination.
Ninth is the Dharma-realm of Bodhisattvas, which practices the gateway of the six perfections. Tenth is the Dharma-realm of Buddhas, which practices the single vehicle of equality.
Altogether, these constitute the ten dharma-realms of both ordinary beings and sages. Although their ascent and descent differ, they all originate from the first thought-moment.

Thereafter, they continue in succession from moment to moment to accomplish their respective tasks: virtuous causes lead to pleasant fruits, while evil causes lead to suffering fruits. As stated before...
Later they repaid one another, never failing to do so. Thus the Sūtra says: "The mind can create heaven; the mind can create hell.
To take the realm of hell as an example, the *Ten Suchnesses* (daśatathatā) in the *Lotus Sūtra* are solely of the mind. This is likewise true for the nine higher realms.

As the *Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sūtra* (Fahua xuanyi) states: "The realm of hell possesses the ten suchnesses: nature, characteristics, substance, power, activity, cause, condition, effect, retribution, and the fundamental."
"Ultimately and perfectly equal. First, regarding this nature of hell: "nature" means that which is unchanging. It is like the nature of fire within bamboo;
if it were not present, one could not seek fire from the bamboo, water from the earth, or wind from a fan.
That the mind possesses the nature of the hell realm is likewise so. Second, as for the characteristics of hell: they can be grasped...

They are distinct; this is what is called "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*). One who skillfully observes the mind immediately recognizes the characteristics of the hells, just as a skilled physiognomist discerns features without error.
As for the substance of the three hells, they take the mind as their substance. Because the mind perceives suffering and pleasure, it constitutes their very essence.
It is like the pearls in hairpins, cauldrons, rings, and bracelets, which ultimately have silver as their substance. This applies to the six realms of existence as well.
Although the forms (rūpa) differ, they are merely based on the mind; therefore, the mind is their essence. As for the power of the four hells, "power" refers to the capacity for movement and control;
that one encounters the mountain of blades and enters the mass of fire is entirely due to the power of the mind. Fifth, regarding the creator of the hells:
To initiate [an action] is called "karma" (*karman*). Since there is already power, there is that which is performed; whether one performs good or performs evil, all are created by the mind.
Sixth, regarding the causes of the hells: karma is the cause of the mind. Seventh, regarding the conditions of the hells:
"conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to that which is borrowed as a supporting factor. For example, when craving moistens karma, this is the convergence of cause and condition. Eighth, the ground...
The "fruit of hell" refers to the fruit of habitual practice (*abhyāsa-phala*). For example, a person in hell who was excessively lustful in a previous life is born within the hells;
because his habits remain predominant, when he encounters a desirable object, he immediately goes to seek intimacy with it, such as seeing a beautiful woman and approaching her to embrace her.

This refers to the copper pillar; it is called the "fruit of habituation. Regarding the retribution of the nine hells: "retribution" means the fruit. In the past, there was the offense of sexual misconduct;
now one falls into hell and undergoes the suffering of being scorched and roasted. The past commission of the offense of sexual misconduct is termed the "fire of desire."
Later, one receives its retribution, immediately undergoing the suffering of the iron chariot and the iron bed;

the beginning and the end are identical, and as there is no goodness in the response, it is called the "retributive fruit" (*vipāka-phala*). Regarding the ten aspects of "root and branch": the root of hell is the dharma of inherent virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*);
the branch of hell is the dharma of cultivated virtue (*bhāvanā-guṇa*). As for "ultimate equality," this means that upon examining cultivated virtue, one finds it is equal to inherent virtue.

Upon examining the nature of the virtues (*dharmatā-guṇa*), one finds that they inherently possess the virtues of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*); because the initial and the final are mutually present, they are said to be "equal.
This is likewise true for the other nine dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*). Although the characteristics and activities of each realm differ, none of them transcend the single mind (*ekacitta*).

Just as with nature and appearance, essence and function, cause and condition, and fruit and retribution—from beginning to end—the ten realms and the ten suchnesses (*daśatathatā*) all arise from the substance of the mind.

First, one creates the causal conditions of good, evil, and other karmas through the mind; subsequently, one receives the retributions of suffering, pleasure, and so forth for ordinary beings and sages.
Since the beginning and the end are both the mind, and the root and the branch are entirely equal, it is said that "the root and the branch are ultimately equal."
The illusory sounds suddenly ceased, and the correct faith in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*) immediately arose.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states: "When Chan Master Fakong first dwelt in a forest hermitage (*araṇya*), every midnight there was often a clear voice outside his hut calling out, 'Fakong! It called repeatedly, yet when he opened the door, no trace remained. Later..."
Wu said, "This is indeed the realm of one's own mind. Thereafter, the sound ceased forever and the fierce flames suddenly vanished.
Thus, the sincerity of Lingrun was truly and immediately verified.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*) states: Shi Lingrun was once traveling through mountain valleys with four other monks when they were suddenly surrounded by a wildfire on all sides.
Three of the monks fled in panic, but Lingrun alone did not move. He said, "Outside the mind there is no fire; the fire is one's own mind.
If one flees from the fire, how can one escape the fire? As soon as he finished speaking, the flames reached his body and spontaneously subsided.
Rising and sinking are its functional manifestations; its essence is endowed with spiritual awareness (*jñāna*).
This awareness is the fundamental substance of the minds of all sentient beings. It is not like empty space; its nature is inherently intelligent and liberated.

It does not involve deliberate mental effort, but knows spontaneously and effortlessly. The *Canyuan ji* (Anthology on the Source of Chan) states: "This so-called 'knowing' is not a cognition attained through realization. The meaning is...

It is said that true nature is not like wood or stone; therefore, it is called "knowing. It is not like the consciousness that discriminates objects through conditions, nor is it like the wisdom that clearly realizes ritual propriety.
Rather, it is simply the nature of *tathatā* (suchness) which possesses natural, eternal knowing. Furthermore, it is not the same as empty space, for it is a luminous and conscious awareness.
This "conscious awareness" carries the meaning of spiritual understanding (*shenjie*), which cannot be fathomed by the principles of yin and yang.
This is called "spirit" (shen). Understanding is itself wisdom; wisdom is itself knowledge; and knowledge is the single mind. Therefore, the Patriarch said:
"Upon the body of emptiness and stillness, there is inherently the fundamental wisdom that knows.
Amidst all defiled and pure phenomena, there is a true essence that clearly reflects and awakens; this is designated as 'mind. Such is the seed of outflow-free ignorance."
The various karmic seeds and illusions are all identical in their nature and characteristics to True Suchness (*tathatā*).

This is because True Suchness, following conditions, manifests as all things, yet all things do not depart from True Suchness. When integrated through principle, they are of a single flavor; this is the universal characteristic.

This characteristic is itself without characteristic. If explained according to specific manifestations, the activities and formations of defilement and purity are precisely the true mind not abiding [in a fixed state].
The self-nature, with its manifestations and functions that follow conditions, is neither fixed in its concealment nor its revelation.

Should there be even a slight discrepancy in its ascent or descent, it remains alert and unclouded; how could such clarity be diminished? It is profoundly still, without dependence and without abiding.
All phenomena rely upon space, yet space has nothing upon which it relies. All phenomena rely upon true wisdom, yet true wisdom has nothing upon which it relies.
It is serene, neither conjoined nor separated.
The Patriarch’s verse says: "What you say accords with the mind; even one's parents cannot be compared to it. Your practice accords with the Way;
the minds of all Buddhas are precisely this. To seek outwardly for a Buddha with form is not like you.
If you wish to know your original mind, it is neither joined nor separate."
The Single-Syllable Jewel King expounds an inconceivable ocean of Dharma.
The mind is the sovereign within this single syllable. As a sutra says: "A single phrase can instruct eighty-four thousand kingdoms and towns.
Furthermore, among all phenomena, the mind is the most supreme. The myriad phenomena are contained within a single syllable, and a thousand teachings are fully prepared therein.

Regarding the single statement, it is as follows: based on the five categories of object, teaching, principle, practice, and fruit, within the context of Consciousness-Only (Vijñaptimātra), there are first, the clarification of the *object-as-consciousness-only*, which involves abandoning the notion that objects exist outside the mind, because all objects are not separate from the mind;

second, the *teaching-as-consciousness-only*, which refers to the fundamental teachings of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* that explain that very consciousness-only; and third, the *principle-as-consciousness-only*, which establishes what is taught in those fundamental teachings.

1. The *Vijñaptimātratā* of Principle, because it distinguishes the meaning of the nature and characteristics of consciousness-only; 2. The *Vijñaptimātratā* of Practice, because it clarifies the practice of consciousness-only throughout the five stages; 3. The *Vijñaptimātratā* of the Path, because it demonstrates that the path is established through the cultivation of the three natures;

4. The *Vijñaptimātratā* of Action, because it elucidates the practice of consciousness-only during the five stages; and 5. The *Vijñaptimātratā* of the Fruit, because in seeking the great fruit, one also realizes the nature of consciousness-only.
The compassionate father of all sentient beings, his teachings that bring about accomplishment are those of an unfathomable master.
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra-verse* states: "Skillful means serve as the father;

all sages enter through the gateway of skillful means within the single mind, thereby attaining the state of the ancestral Buddha and becoming teachers of gods and humans. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "By means of a small..."
Through skillful means, one swiftly attains Bodhi because the mind itself is it; thus, one realizes it quickly. Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"Taking non-attainment as the skillful means, since there are no phenomena apart from the mind, how could there be anything to be attained?
Therefore, only when a Bodhisattva personally realizes their own mind can they enter the web of worldly illusions to benefit both themselves and others. There is no...
There is a definitive conclusion: it is known that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions all attained Buddhahood by awakening to the mind. Thus, a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm:
all things are created solely by the mind. Therefore, the various Buddhas such as Amitābha of the West mentioned in the sutras are all [manifestations of] Śākyamuni.

Ka. As the ancient commentators have said: when one infers this through reasoning, it establishes the correct principle that all [manifestations] are suddenly revealed by my original teacher, the Sea-Seal (Sāgarāmudrā).
Furthermore, since the *Lotus Sūtra* mentions many pure lands for the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), why does the Tathāgata not point to his own pure land?
Reflect on this: it causes one to go separately to Amitābha’s Land of Utmost Bliss. Thus, we know that Buddhas such as Bhadraśrī and Amitābha were all his original teachers.

What cause for wonder is there? As for the one called Bhadraśrī, he is the Tathāgata of the final world, the Supreme Lotus, located beyond hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya lands within the "Life Span" chapter. A verse in the sutra says:
Or one may see a supreme and wondrous lotus realm where the Tathāgata Bhadraśrī dwells.
If this were not a praise of one's own original teacher (the Buddha), what would be the purpose of speaking of another Tathāgata residing in another land?
Furthermore, as in the teachings of the *Dhāraṇī*, it is also said that the thirty-seven honored ones are all manifestations of the single Buddha Vairocana. That is to say, [they are] Vairocana...
That Tathāgata internally realizes self-enjoyment and accomplishes the five wisdoms (*pañca-jñāna*). From four of these wisdoms, the four Tathāgatas of the four directions flow forth:
from the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) flows forth Akṣobhya Tathāgata of the east;

from the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*) flows forth Ratnasambhava Tathāgata of the south; from the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*) flows forth Amitābha Tathāgata of the west...
From the Tathāgata Amitāyus comes the Wisdom of Accomplishing What is to be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which flows forth as the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the North.
The Wisdom of the Purity of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu-viśuddhi-jñāna*) is himself Vairocana Tathāgata.
Regarding the "thirty-seven," each of the Tathāgatas of the five directions has four great Bodhisattvas at his left and right, totaling twenty; these are [the ones] in the center...
As for the four great bodhisattvas of Vairocana Tathāgata: first, the Bodhisattva Vajrapāramitā; second, the Bodhisattva Ratnapāramitā;
third, the Bodhisattva Dharmapāramitā; and fourth, the Bodhisattva Karmapāramitā.
As for the four bodhisattvas of Akṣobhya Tathāgata in the eastern direction: first, the [Bodhisattva] Vajrasattva.
The Bodhisattvas: first, Vajrarāja; second, Vajrarāga; third, Vajrasādhu; fourth, Vajrāśaya.
These are the four Bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Ratnasambhava in the south: first, Vajraratna; second, Vajratejas; third, Vajraketu; fourth, Vajrahāsa. In the west...
As for the Tathāgata Amitāyus, he is also named the Tathāgata Avalokiteśvararāja.
His four bodhisattvas are: first, Vajradharma; second, Vajrakhadga; third, Vajrahetu; and fourth, Vajratīkṣṇa.
As for the four bodhisattvas of the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the northern direction, the first is Vajra...
The Bodhisattva Karma, secondly the Bodhisattva Vajradharma, thirdly the Bodhisattva Vajrayakṣa, and fourthly the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi—these complete the twenty-five.
Together with the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the eight offerings, they constitute thirty-seven.

Regarding the "four means of integration" (*catvāri saṃgrahavastūni*), these are the hook, the noose, the chain, and the bell. Regarding the "eight offerings," these are burning incense, scattering flowers, lamps, unguents, garlands, song, dance, and music.
Above each of these is a *vajra*, and below each is a bodhisattva. Furthermore, these thirty-seven deities each have their own seed-syllable (*bīja*);
they all flow forth from the wisdom-activity of the Original Teacher, appearing instantaneously like a reflection in the ocean-seal (*sāgaramudrā*) as described in this present sutra.
The general meaning is the same. Question: If one relies on this interpretation, does it not contradict the intention of equality?
For the intention of equality states that "the Tathāgata is precisely the self. Answer: This is spoken based on the intention of equality; it does not mean that he is my own physical body.
How can it be said that all are the Original Teacher? In the answer, the samādhi of equality is the single underlying meaning.
Even in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, it is stated that among all sentient beings, there are those who belong to many Buddhas;
that many Buddhas may collectively manifest as a single Buddha, and a Buddha can manifest as many bodies. This is true for every one of the Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions. Now, precisely...
A single Buddha can manifest as many bodies; it is based on this that one praises the Original Teacher. Furthermore, the Original Teacher is none other than my own mind.
When I gather and return all things to my own mind, there is no dharma that is not complete therein—how could it be limited to others alone?

It unfolds and rolls up according to its own nature; it appears and disappears in accordance with conditions. It manifests the primordial beginning of the single truth and synthesizes the structural framework of all phenomena.
From the origin to the end, there is only the Way of the One Mind. The ultimate principles of the Great Teaching are all explained in common with this.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha, when the Bodhisattvas first dwell in the stages, they should skillfully observe everything that exists."

Regarding all dharma-gates, they thoroughly observe them according to their respective profound wisdoms, their respective cultivated causes, their respective attained fruits, their respective spheres of activity, their respective functional powers, their respective manifestations, their respective conceptual distinctions, and their respective attainments;
knowing that all dharmas are but one's own mind, they remain free from all attachment. As it is said:
Having known this, one enters the stages of a bodhisattva and is able to dwell securely within the great tree of the twelve links of dependent origination, which grows from a profound root.
This dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination is established entirely from within the minds of sentient beings. Why is it called a "tree"? If...

Within the realm of sentient beings, ignorance serves as the root; watered by the moisture of craving, it sprouts the shoot of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), blooms with the flowers of outflows (*sāsrava*), and bears the fruit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The four characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing are in constant flux, never ceasing for a moment.

If, within the realm of all sages, the sprouts of right enlightenment are produced, the flowers of the myriad practices are opened, and the fruit of bodhi is realized, such that one serves the Buddhas and benefits sentient beings without ceasing until the end of the future—this all arises from the great tree of the single mind and the twelve links of dependent origination.
Therefore, it is said that the twelve links of dependent origination are themselves Buddha-nature. Furthermore, the single mind and the twelve links of dependent origination...

Regarding "condition" (*pratyaya*): when the eye sees a form, the mind’s lack of comprehension is called ignorance (*avidyā*). The mind’s arising of attachment or aversion toward that form is called volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
Within this process, the mental faculty is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Form together with consciousness and the formations is called name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

The arising of craving through the six bases, such as the eye and forms, is called the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). The encounter between form and the eye is called contact (*sparśa*). When the mind perceives a form, its experiencing [of it]...

Accepting a name is "reception" (*upādāna*). When the mind is entangled with form without interruption, it is called "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). When the mind conceives of the characteristics of form, it is called "grasping" (*upādāna*).

When the mind arises in mindfulness of form, it is called "existence" (*bhava*). The arising of a single thought-moment is called "birth" (*jāti*); the ceasing of a single thought-moment is called "extinction" (*nirodha*).
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "All that exists within the three realms is but this one mind. The Tathāgata has analyzed and expounded upon this.
The exposition of the twelve links of existence is established entirely upon this single mind. Furthermore, a verse states:
"Thoroughly understand that the three realms depend on the mind; The twelve links of dependent origination are likewise so. Birth and death are all produced by the mind;
If the mind is extinguished, birth and death are exhausted."
The perfect exposition of the five thousand scriptures ultimately returns to the cave of principle.
All Buddhas, in accordance with the minds of all sentient beings, proclaim all dharmas. A verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The Buddhas do not preach the Dharma;
how could there be any preaching by the Buddha? It is only in accordance with their own minds that they preach such a Dharma. As it is said:
The *Commentary on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra* states: "To point to its source: the dust of the emotions has its scripture, yet the ocean of wisdom has no exterior.
Delusive confusion is not something to be grasped; the double mystery is not empty. The fire of the four propositions cannot burn it; the gates of the myriad dharmas all enter therein."
The two ultimate limits merge yet remain not one; movement undergoes a thousand transformations yet remains not many. Phenomena and principle penetrate each other so that both vanish;
nature and appearance are interfused without end. It is like the mutual reflection in the mirror of Qin, or the interpenetration of the Emperor’s pearls.

Layer upon layer of intermingling lights manifest clearly and simultaneously; thus, one attains perfect realization in an instant and perceives the realm of the Buddhas within every speck of dust and hair.
Within the minds of all Buddhas dwell sentient beings who newly and continuously attain Buddhahood, and within the minds of sentient beings dwell all the Buddhas.
In every thought-moment he realizes the Truth;
solitary and serene, he stands alone with majestic dignity.

He is like a miraculous and auspicious flower that blooms but once every three thousand years, appearing when a Buddha enters the world to manifest the Dharma-gate of the One Mind of the Perfect Teaching.
At that time, it is difficult to hear and difficult to encounter, like the divine light within that illuminates from the inside.
Among all lights, the divine light is supreme. The Patriarch said: "Among all forms of clarity, the clarity of the mind is foremost."
To sever the branches of jade, every inch is treasure; to split the sandalwood, every slice is fragrant.
This clarifies that every dharma is this mind, and every dust mote accords with the Way.
In an instant, one may ascend to the stage of enlightenment from the body of an ordinary person; while still in the state of a layman, one may sit directly upon the Dragon Throne.
If one believes in and enters the inexhaustible principle of the single mind of the *Avataṃsaka*, as the *Jang-che lun* (Treatise on the Elder) says: "It is like [bestowing] a precious throne."

To directly bestow [the teaching] upon the ordinary and mundane is like a dream of a thousand years at night; once awakened, it vanishes along with the dream. The *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states:
"For one of the Sudden Teaching, the non-arising of a single thought is itself Buddhahood. This refers to the mind of all sentient beings, which is not yet the essence of Buddhahood.
