Because deluded thoughts arise, one is a sentient being. When the deluded thought of even a single moment does not arise, why could it not be called [Buddhahood]?
Therefore, a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally empty and quiescent;

there is neither grasping nor seeing. This very emptiness of nature is the Buddha; it cannot be conceived or measured. Another verse states: "The nature of phenomena is like space; all Buddhas dwell therein.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says: "One takes the emptiness of intrinsic nature as the Buddha-eye. If one discusses this emptiness of nature, all...

This is the essence of both ordinary beings and sages; it is merely because of non-awakening that deluded thoughts suddenly arise, causing one to drift and transmigrate according to external conditions.
Therefore, it is said that the *dharmakāya* transmigrates through the five paths and is called a "sentient being. Even when a single thought arises, it is still the Buddha.
Because deluded thoughts have no substance and do not depart from the emptiness of nature, one need only directly believe and understand with perfect clarity;
it does not depend on further deliberation or inference. The *Huayan shu* says: "The Buddha within the minds of sentient beings preaches the Dharma for the sentient beings within the Buddha's mind.
This clarifies that while sentient beings are universally pervasive according to their nature, the Buddha remains present without destroying their distinct characteristics.
Within the minds of sentient beings, the Buddha-mind—which, by its very nature, is all-pervasive—remains present without the characteristics of sentient beings being destroyed.
This is illustrated by the analogy of water and milk mixed together in one place, wherein each serves as both the permeator and the permeated.
Furthermore, in terms of explaining and listening, the permeator is taken as the speaker and the permeated as the listener; thus, water is used as a metaphor for the Buddha.
Milk is a metaphor for sentient beings. One should say that there is water within the milk, and milk within the water. The milk within the water receives the water within the milk;
though they are of one flavor, the subject and object are distinct. Though the subject and object are distinct, they exist within one another, pervade one another, and encompass one another.
Listen, yet there is nothing heard; observe, yet nothing is seen.
The Dharma-body has no form; true listening has no sound.
It is eternally present, yet there is no need for further seeking; it is fundamentally luminous, so why labor over cultivation? The gates of the triple world have no substance.
"Sounds are transmitted from within a valley.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The phenomena of the triple world are produced by the grasping of objects; therefore, know that they have no substance, being like echoes in a valley—all are but my own voice.
The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* says: "All dharmas are like echoes in a valley," thereby illustrating the myriad [phenomena].
Because phenomena are solely mind, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In a single thought-moment, one completely encompasses the dharma-realm. It further states:
"In a single thought-moment, the three periods of time are fully present without exception. And it says: "In a single thought-moment, infinite manifestations appear."
The realms of the six sense objects are fundamentally empty; they are like reflections of a face in a mirror.
These realms of the six sense objects all arise from deluded thoughts, just as when a person looks into a mirror and sees their own face—there is no separate image.
In silent, empty penetration, there is nothing that is not harmonized. The Pavilion of Maitreya manifests universally.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "When the youth Sudhana entered the Pavilion of Maitreya, he saw that the pavilion was vast and immeasurable, identical to empty space, with asaṃkhyeya jewels forming its ground," and so on, until he beheld Maitreya.
From the Bodhisattva’s initial generation of the mind, through practicing the Bodhisattva path, to attaining Buddhahood via the eight manifestations—these are merely matters of three lifetimes.
Yet, within the womb of Māyā, they are infinite.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Within the womb of Lady Māyā, the entirety of a trichiliocosm is fully manifested."
In all these forms, within each of the ten billion Jambudvīpas, there were respective capitals and cities, and respective gardens and groves, each with different names.

In every one of them, Lady Māyā dwelt, surrounded by hosts of devas, manifesting the inconceivable signs of supernatural transformation as the Bodhisattva was about to be born. Furthermore, this was as vast as the Dharma-realm.
Ultimately, it is like empty space; this is the meaning of being "in the womb.
Within the crown of Mañjuśrī, the *Mañjuśrī-parinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that Mañjuśrī’s body is like a mountain of purple gold, and so forth. As for that crown of Mañjuśrī:
It was adorned with *vairocana* jewels of five hundred kinds of colors. Within each individual color, the sun, moon, and stars;
the palaces of the devas and nāgas; and the rare and wondrous phenomena of the world’s sentient beings were all manifested.
Within the eight-cubit room of Vimalakīrti, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* states:
"To the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of thirty-six Ganges Rivers, there is a world named Sumerukūṭa.
Its Buddha is named Sumerupradīparāja, who currently resides there. That Buddha’s body is eighty-four thousand [yojanas] tall."
It was one thousand yojanas [in extent]. That lion throne was eighty-four thousand yojanas high, the most exquisitely adorned of all.

Then, the elder Vimalakīrti manifested his supernormal powers; immediately, that Buddha dispatched thirty-two thousand lion thrones—lofty, broad, magnificent, and pure—which entered the room of Vimalakīrti, until even his room became vast and expansive.
It completely encompasses thirty-two thousand lion thrones without any obstruction;
even a mustard seed or the point of a needle is not cramped.
As the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* says: "The high and vast Mount Sumeru is contained within a mustard seed, yet it is not constricted. *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
The *Pán jīng* (Discourse on the Bowl) states: "Upon the tip of a needle, Bodhisattvas such as Anantagātra stand;
though near to dust and far from lands, they are entirely unimpeded.
A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Within each and every atom, one can realize all dharmas; thus there is nothing that is not [so]."
Unobstructed, it travels throughout the lands of the ten directions. It is also said: "Within a single atom, all lands dwell with vast spaciousness.
An ancient master said: "All inconceivable matters can be universally manifested in every place."
It is merely the application of the unique, pure *dharmakāya* of Vairocana. This *dharmakāya* is none other than the mind;
the mind is the body of the Dharma-realm. Therefore it is said: "If one can contemplate the non-duality of the mind with clarity, only then will one see the pure body of Vairocana.
If a single thought of evil arises, the *dharmakāya* likewise manifests accordingly; if a single thought of goodness arises [the same applies]."
The Dharma-body likewise manifests accordingly; this is called "mutual manifestation everywhere," extending even to manifestation in the realm of form and the realm of space, sovereign and unimpeded.
Do not seek the Buddhas elsewhere; they are simply the empty mind of a single thought-moment. The *Huayan Sūtra Commentary* states:
"It is like the Ocean Seal suddenly manifesting. The Sūtra says: "Because it manifests in a single thought-moment," meaning there is no before or after, just as with a seal.
It is manifested instantaneously and is constantly present, unlike a bright mirror which has times when it reflects and times when it does not.

Furthermore, it is not a manifestation that occurs only upon encounter, as a bright mirror only reflects when an object is brought before it; because it does not depend on such encounters, it is constantly manifest, encompassing the three periods of time.
All of the above is simply the meaning of the single true mind’s quiescent illumination universally manifesting itself.

Neither decreasing nor increasing, it is perpetually and subtly concentrated within the wondrous essence. Neither formed nor destroyed, it continues in succession without falling from the profound wind.
Spanning from antiquity to the present, penetrating both the mundane and the sagely, there is no other dharma; it is solely this one mind. When attained...
It increases; it does not decrease when lost, it is not completed when ascending, and it is not destroyed when falling. As stated in the *Huayan jin'guan* (The Brocade Crown of the Avataṃsaka):
"Regarding the *Mahāvaipulya-buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*: 'Great' (*mahā*) refers to the essence of the mind. Because the essence of the mind is boundless, it is called 'great.
'Vaipulya' (*fang*) refers to the characteristics of the mind; because the mind possesses the dharmas of virtuous characteristics, it is called 'vaipulya. 'Broad' (*guǎng*) refers to..."

The function of the mind: because the mind possesses a function that accords with its essence, it is called "vast. The Buddha is the fruit of the mind; the state where the mind is liberated is termed "Buddha.
The flower is the cause of the mind; the practices performed by the mind are metaphorically likened to flowers.
Adornment is the functional power of the mind; because the mind can skillfully embellish, it is designated as "adornment. The sūtra is the teaching of the mind. The mind...
Names and phrases arise to explain and manifest this; therefore, it is called a "sūtra. These are the seven characters beginning with "Great" (Mahā), all of which are not separate from the mind.
Yet, the single character "mind" is neither essence nor function, neither cause nor fruit, and neither meaning nor teaching.
Although it is not everything, it can serve as everything. Why is this? It is because the single *dharmadhātu*-mind is the essence.
If one can awaken to and understand this, then every thought-moment is the *dharmadhātu* of the *Avataṃsaka*, and every thought-moment is the *dharmakāya* of Vairocana.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If one accords with such contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), regarding all phenomena..."

Without giving rise to dualistic interpretations, all Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before them. At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, they shall attain perfect awakening and realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The great mechanism of karmic destiny; the lineage of the Golden Wheel.
Śākyamuni Buddha was of the lineage of the Golden Wheel Kings. A song by the Master Yibao says:

"For ten thousand generations, the Prince of the Holy Golden Wheel—this very true suchness and numinous awareness is it. Therefore, what has been transmitted through the patriarchal lineages is simply this indication.
The mind is the Buddha. As soon as one gives rise to faith and understanding, one immediately succeeds to the ancestral position.
It is like the kalaviṅka bird, whose melody suppresses all other sounds;
even before the kalaviṅka has emerged from its shell, the sound it emits within the shell already surpasses the voices of all other birds. This...
How much more so for an ordinary person at the very bottom of the beginningless cycle of birth and death, who, while still unliberated from the shell of afflictions,
is able to recognize the mind and think, "I shall become a Buddha," thereby surpassing all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
It is like a tree of excellent solidity that rises high above all other trees.
In the Western Heavens, there is a tree of excellent solidity that, as soon as it emerges from the earth, stands a hundred feet tall, surpassing the tops of all other trees.

This illustrates the person of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), who knows that the mind itself is replete with the Dharma-realm; through perfect understanding and perfect cultivation, they transcend the Two Vehicles.
For practitioners of the Tripiṭaka, Shared, and Distinct Teachings, if one discusses their progress, days and kalpas increase exponentially.
When a single film first arises, a profusion of flowers fills the void; when a fleeting thought just stirs, the myriad phenomena stand arrayed before the eyes.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Because from time immemorial your mind-nature has been deranged, false cognitions have arisen.

As these delusions arise without ceasing, the wearying faculty of vision gives rise to dust. It is like when the eyes are strained, there appear illusory flowers; these arise without cause within the serene and luminous clarity.
All that exists in the world—the mountains, rivers, the great earth, birth and death, and even nirvana—is nothing but this deranged weariness."
The inverted appearance of flowers: this is to know that the myriad dharmas arise from conceptualization and arrive according to thought.
Thus, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) says: The Buddha said, "From the beginningless past, I have not obtained a single dharma.

Having attained ultimate concentration, it is only now that I first know what is called 'non-thought' (*amanasikāra*). If one attains non-thought, one observes that all dharmas are entirely formless. Because...
This constitutes the attainment of the unsurpassed, true, and correct path. Furthermore, as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*:
"Therefore, the three realms are illusory; they are produced solely by the mind. Apart from the mind, the objects of the six sense-fields do not exist. What is the meaning of this?
It is because all phenomena arise from the mind through the production of deluded thoughts. All discrimination is, in fact, the discrimination of one's own [mind].

The mind does not see the mind; no characteristic can be apprehended. One should know that all worldly realms exist and are sustained solely by the ignorant, deluded thoughts of sentient beings. Therefore, all phenomena are like reflections in a mirror.

No substantial entity can be apprehended; it is merely the mind that is illusory. This is because when the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise, and when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease.
Furthermore, it is said: "All objective realms are nothing but the deluded movement of the mind. If the mind does not move,"
Then all objective phenomena cease, and only the single true mind pervades all places.

Thus one knows that the perception of external objects exists solely because they arise from one's own deluded thoughts and mental conceptions. Therefore it is said: "Emotion creates a barrier to wisdom; conception transforms the essence.

"Emotion creates a barrier to wisdom" means that by losing right wisdom, one produces deluded thoughts. "Conception transforms the essence" [means that through such conceptualization, the fundamental nature is altered].

This is because one becomes deluded regarding *tathatā* (true suchness) and thereby gives rise to names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*). The *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation for Returning to the Source) states:

"When true emptiness stagnates within the mind, it constantly becomes the field of discursive thought; when the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) resides before one's eyes, it conversely becomes the realm of names and forms.
The *Weishi shuyao* (Essentials of Consciousness-Only) states: "The arising of the marks of one’s own mind is twofold: first, the mark of images; all phenomena are the mind."
First, the images; second, the grasped characteristics. All objects lack intrinsic substance; they arise in accordance with grasping.
Originating from one's own mind, they in turn serve as the characteristics of that mind.

The Way cuts off frivolous talk; its ultimate subtlety is difficult to discourse upon. To transcend birth and death there is no other path; to ascend to nirvana there is but this single gate. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"All those who are unimpeded, through the One Way, transcend birth and death. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
"The Bhagavans of the ten directions [enter] the single path to the gate of Nirvana. These two teachings take only the Dharma of the One Mind as their fundamental principle for seeking liberation.
Therefore, having realized the One Mind and emerged from it, one neither dwells in saṃsāra nor dwells in nirvāṇa.
Because of great compassion, one constantly abides in saṃsāra; because of great wisdom, one constantly abides in nirvāṇa. This is the meaning of "abiding in both."
Because of great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*), one does not abide in *nirvāṇa*; because of great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), one does not abide in *saṃsāra*. Thus, one abides in neither.

Furthermore, regarding the clarification that one abides in neither, there are two reasons for not abiding in *saṃsāra*: first, because one perceives the faults and sufferings of *saṃsāra*, it is impossible to abide therein;
second, because one perceives that *saṃsāra* is fundamentally empty, there is nothing in which to abide. [End of] above.
Both [types of non-abiding] are based on wisdom and thus do not abide; this is due to two meanings regarding why they do not abide in nirvana.
First, because one sees that nirvana is inherently present from the beginning, one does not abide in it. Second, because it is not distinct from saṃsāra, one cannot abide in it.

In an instant, one returns to the mundane and reverts to the True; there is no peer to this principle. In a mere moment, one passes from the profane into the Sage; it is difficult to repay such grace.
Within the Gate of the Chan School, since time immemorial, as soon as one realizes that the mind itself is Buddha, one immediately enters the rank of the Patriarchs.

Sit upon the site of enlightenment; simply believe in this. Ordinary beings and sages are not separated by even a single thought. If you do not believe, heaven and earth will be as vastly different as they can be.
As a verse in a sutra says: "All Buddhas attain liberation from the mind; the mind is pure and called stainless. The five paths are fresh and clean, never subject to defilement.
One who understands this realizes the Great Way. Even if you have not yet believed in your own mind—

This Buddha, though submerged within the five realms of existence, possesses a mental nature that is eternally pure; defilements cannot stain it. Thus it is said that the five realms are fresh and clean, remaining unstained.

Because the *dharmakāya* of sentient beings is identical to the *dharmakāya* of all Buddhas—neither increasing nor decreasing—its nature remains unchanged whether it follows the current or flows against it.
Therefore, when following the current as a sentient being, it is not extinguished; when flowing back...

Even when one attains Buddhahood, it does not increase. Because all sentient beings have deep defilements and heavy obstructions, even if they encounter a virtuous friend who awakens them, they do not believe or accept [the teaching].
They merely follow their own emotions and fail to perceive their own nature. Thus, a former master said:
"How many years will it take for deluded emotions to cease their pulling? One only brings shame upon the single point of light in the numinous hall."
The multitude of scriptures all concur that few can surpass profound principles; yet swallowing a snake and falling ill is entirely due to the arising of doubt.
(As recorded in the *Book of Jin*, Biography of Yue Guang): Yue Guang had a close guest who, having been away for a long time, did not return. Yue Guang asked him the reason.
He replied: "Previously, while seated, I was granted wine. Seeing a snake within the cup, my mind felt deeply repulsed by it. Having drunk it, I fell ill.
At that time, on the wall of the Henan Hall there was a horned bow upon which a snake had been painted. I realized that the snake in the cup was actually the reflection of the bow's horn.
When the wine was set back down in its original place, the guest saw it as before, and his mind was suddenly enlightened."
[The illness] was understood; the chronic ailment was suddenly cured.
Just as hanging sand satisfies hunger, all [mental states] arise from thought (*saṃkalpa*).
As it says in the "Chapter on the Four Kinds of Food" in the Vinaya: "Regarding the food of thought (*āhāra-saṃkalpa*): it is like a time of famine when a small child [clings] to its mother."
Seeking food, he wept and would not stop. His mother then hung a sandbag and deceived him by saying, "This is rice.
For seven days, the child gazed intently at the bag, thinking it was specifically for his food. After seven days had passed, his mother untied it and showed it to him.
When the child saw it was only sand, he fell into despair and died as a result. Only then was it proven that birth, old age, sickness, and death are all one's own mind.
Earth, water, fire, and wind ultimately have no separate essence.

Even so, when Sun was in the Bamboo Grove and Meng Zong’s father fell ill, Meng Zong sought bamboo shoots during the winter; Zong then embraced the bamboo and wept, whereupon the shoots sprouted forth accordingly.
Fish leaped from the ice-covered shallows.
Wang Xiang of the Jin dynasty was exceptionally filial. Having lost his parents early, he lived with his stepmother, Lady Zhu, who delighted in eating raw fish.

During a cold spell, Wang Xiang stripped off his clothes and lay upon the ice; the ice suddenly melted of its own accord, and two carp leaped forth. Contemporaries regarded this as the result of his filial piety.
Moved by this,
he transformed his wine into the river.
When King Gou of Yue threw a single ladle of unfermented grain-liquor into the river, the entire three-pronged army reported that they were intoxicated.
An arrow pierced through a stone. When Li Guang was young, he lost his father. He asked his mother, "Where is my father? His mother said, "Your father was killed by a tiger long ago.
Guang then took up his bow and went to catch the tiger. As evening fell at the mountain, he saw a rock that resembled a tiger; he drew his bow and shot it, and the arrow passed right through.
Feathers. He went forward to examine them closely and realized they were actually stones, not produced by fermented yeast or malt. How could they have been achieved through mere human effort?
These four matters above were all moved by a heart of filial piety and a mind of equanimity.
There is not even a speck of dust that does not arise through the transformation of consciousness;

this principle is perfectly clear. These eight consciousnesses have four divisions: first, the seeing division (*darśana-bhāga*); second, the image division (*nimitta-bhāga*); third, the self-verifying division (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*);

and fourth, the verifying-of-self-verifying division (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*). The *Huayan ji* states: "As the sūtras say: 'All things are nothing but cognition; the objects of cognition [do not exist externally].'"
There is none at all of the distinction between the subject that perceives and the object perceived; each turns forth spontaneously. The commentary states: This refers to the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

The first half clarifies the absence of external objects, while the second half clarifies the existence of the two divisions of the seeing and the seen, each arising from its own causes and conditions, which is termed "turning forth spontaneously.
Below, the correct meaning is concluded. The treatise says: "To realize that there is nothing apart from consciousness..."

Regarding the "object-condition" (*ālambana*): that which is the transformed *nimitta-bhāga* (image-aspect) is the object-condition; the *darśana-bhāga* (seeing-aspect) is termed the "self-characteristic" (*sva-lakṣaṇa*);
and the self-substance upon which both the image and seeing aspects depend is termed the "entity" (*vastu*), which is the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying aspect).

The commentary states: Although this [system] establishes two aspects, its meaning already implies three. Therefore, the subsequent treatise says: "If there were no self-verifying aspect, this [consciousness] would not be able to know itself."

Regarding the mental factors (caitta-dharma) of recollection: just as one cannot remember an object that has never been experienced before, it must necessarily be the case that there is a self-cognizing portion (svasaṃvitti-bhāga).
The intent of this explanation is that apart from the aspect of seeing (darśana-bhāga), there is no separate intrinsic substance; rather, there are merely two functional capacities.

Therefore, there must be a distinct substratum that serves as their support. If there were no self-cognition, one would not be able to recollect [them] oneself, just as with the mind and its mental factors.

If it has not previously experienced an object, it can certainly not remember it; that is to say, just as the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) cannot remember the object of the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) because it has not previously experienced it, one must have previously experienced something in order to be able to remember it.
If there were no self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*), then mental factors (*caitta*) that have already ceased [could not be remembered].

In that case, one would be unable to recollect [the object], because it would never have served as the condition for self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*). This would be just like the seeing-portion (*darśana-bhāga*), which can never be recollected.
That we are now able to recollect it demonstrates that there was previously a self-cognition that had already taken it as its object.

This is just as when one recollects the seeing-portion, one recollects the objects encountered therein. Consequently, the three portions are established below. The treatise states: "However, when each mind and mental factor arises..."

When examined through reasoning, each [cognition] possesses three parts: the object of cognition (*prameya*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), and the result of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), because they are distinct. Furthermore, the aspect and the vision must necessarily have a supporting substance.

The commentary states: the object of cognition is the image-part (*nimittabhāga*); the means of cognition is the vision-part (*darśanabhāga*); and the result of cognition is the self-awareness-part (*svasaṃvittibhāga*).
This is because the self-awareness-part serves as the support for both the image and the vision parts. As stated in the *Pramāṇasamuccaya*.
It is said in the *Gāthā*: "That which has the appearance of an object is the cognizable; the appearance of the grasper and self-awareness are the means of cognition and the result.

These three are not distinct in essence. The commentary explains: The cognizable is like a piece of cloth; the means of cognition is like a person; and the result of cognition is like the knowledge that understands the number [of threads].
What is the meaning of "result"? It is the sense of the fulfillment of the cause. As for saying they have no distinct essences, it is because they are but a single consciousness.

Thus, there is no object apart from the mind. Next, the four divisions are established. The treatise states: "Furthermore, if one analyzes the mind and mental factors in detail, they should consist of four divisions:

the seeing division (darśana-bhāga), the image division (nimitta-bhāga), the self-verifying division (svasaṃvitti-bhāga) as previously described, and fourth, the verifying-of-self-verifying division (svasaṃvittisvasaṃvitti-bhāga)."
If this [self-cognizing part] did not exist, who would verify the third [cognition]? Since the mental discrimination would be identical [in all cases], it would follow that everyone should verify it.
The commentary states: The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is a division of the mind; it is said that there is a self-verifying part (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

If the self-verifying part did not exist, it would have no result, for all means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) possess a result. The commentary states: The seeing-part is the means of cognition; there must be a self-verifying cognition to perceive it.

[The opponent] asserts that there is a fourth fruit. Fearing that this might be refuted by the argument that the seeing-division (darśana-bhāga) is instead used as the third fruit, the subsequent treatise states:
"The seeing-division should not be the third fruit, for the seeing-division is either not subsumed under valid cognition (pramāṇa) [or is non-conceptual]."
Therefore, the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) does not realize the third [part]. That which realizes its own self-nature must necessarily be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The commentary states:

this clarifies that the seeing-part extends across the three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The three types of valid cognition are: direct perception, inference (*anumāna*), and non-valid cognition (*apramāṇa*).

This clarifies that when the seeing-part takes the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*) as its object, it may be either valid cognition or non-valid cognition; however, a phenomenon that is non-valid cognition cannot be the result of direct perception. Or, the seeing...
The objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) is an object of inference (*anumāna*). Furthermore, that which takes self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) as its object is direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Therefore, self-cognition is the essence of the mind; it can serve as the result for both inference and non-valid cognition (*aprāmāṇya*). The seeing aspect (*darśana-bhāga*), however, is not the essence of the mind;
it cannot serve as the result of valid cognition for self-cognition. Consequently, the seeing aspect cannot realize the third [aspect]. That which realizes its own substance—

It must be direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Since the third part, which consists of four sub-divisions, is already direct perception, it would follow that there is the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) as they would mutually require further proof.
The intention is this: if the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is taken as the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), then three parts alone would suffice;

however, if the seeing-part is taken as the object of cognition (*prameya*), the fourth part must necessarily serve as the fruit of cognition (*pramāṇaphala*). If one intends to provide a general analogy, [it is like] silk cloth...
Just as that which is measured is like the measuring instrument, so the fruit measured by cognition is the self-verifying portion (*svasaṃvitti-bhāga*).

If a person is that which is impelled and cognition is that which impels, then that which employs cognition is the person. Just as one verifies the self-verifying portion, the person can employ cognition and cognition can impel the person;
therefore, it can be further verified. It is also like a clear mirror, where the mirror-image serves as the characteristic mark (*nimitta*).

The clarity of the mirror is the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving part). The surface of the mirror is like the *svasaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying part). The back of the mirror is like the *svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga* (self-verifying of the self-verifying part).
Because the surface depends upon the back, and the back in turn depends upon the surface, they are able to verify one another. Furthermore, the bronze may be taken as the *svasaṃvittisaṃvitti-bhāga*;
the mirror depends upon the bronze, and the bronze depends upon the mirror.
It is not of a single kind, yet it is accomplished through the mind’s lack of reliance; words and thoughts cease.
As for the transformation of the mental consciousness, as stated in a verse of the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*:
"O sons of the Buddhas, why do you not see or hear that the essence of the ālayavijñāna is pure, upon which all things depend, or that it possesses the thirty-two marks of a Buddha?"
The Wheel-Turning King may manifest in various forms, which all the world beholds;
like the moon in the clear sky, encircled by the host of stars, so do the various consciousnesses abide within the body of the ālayavijñāna.

Like the Lord of the Desire Realm, attended by his retinue as he wanders through his jeweled palace, or like the spirits of rivers, oceans, and other realms who exercise mastery within the waters, so does the storehouse consciousness dwell in the world.
One should know that it is likewise so. Just as the earth gives rise to all things, this mind manifests many appearances.
It is like the Sun Deity, resplendent and riding his precious palace, circling Mount Sumeru and flowing everywhere to illuminate the world beneath;
gods and men alike see him and pay him homage. Within the Buddha-ground, the characteristics of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) are also like this. [This concludes] the Tenth Stage.

Practicing all manner of deeds, manifesting the Mahāyāna Dharma, universally bestowing happiness upon sentient beings, and constantly praising the Tathāgata—while abiding in the body of a bodhisattva, this is precisely what is called a "bodhisattva. Both the Buddha and all bodhisattvas are designated by the name Ālaya.
The Buddhas and their spiritual heirs—those who have received and those who shall receive the prophecy—attain perfect awakening within the vast ālaya.
Those practitioners of the Guhyasamāja who are endowed with sublime meditative concentration can clearly perceive the ālaya.
This is what is observed by the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, Śrāvakas, and those of other paths who, having seen the truth, are free from fear.
All these various objects of consciousness are transformations of the mind. Such things as jars, garments, and other manifold objects lack any inherent nature;
they all depend upon the ālayavijñāna. Sentient beings perceive them through delusion due to the power of their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
The transformation of the grasped and the grasper—this nature is not like a magical illusion, a mirage, or a mass of floating hairs.
It is neither produced nor unproduced; it is neither empty nor existent. Just as with long and short and so forth, when one is absent, all are non-existent.
When the wise contemplate illusory phenomena, they see that these are all merely magical arts; never has a single thing arisen simultaneously with an illusion. [Mirage...]
The appearance of floating hairs and other such various objects are all transformations of the mind; they have no substance and no names.
People in the world who are deluded find their minds lack self-mastery; they falsely claim there is a "magician" who creates various names through illusion.
Past and future are both unreal. Just as iron moves toward a magnet, so too does the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) evolve in accordance with conceptualization.
It pervades all worlds without exception; like the sun or a mani-jewel, it is devoid of thought or discrimination.
This consciousness is omnipresent, yet its appearance is called "transmigration"—it is never extinguished.

Nor does it arise; fundamentally, it is not a phenomenon of cyclic flow. When the practitioner observes with diligence that birth and death are like a dream, at that moment there is a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which is called liberation. This is the supreme teaching and principle of all Buddhas.
To examine and measure all phenomena is like a scale or a clear mirror.

If this single mind is taken as the definitive standard for all phenomena, it is like weighing an object on a scale where the weight is without error, or like a mirror reflecting an image where both beauty and ugliness appear.
Furthermore, regarding the "mind that accomplishes," ancient exegesis explains that there are four types of single mind: first, *ghṛtaya*, which is translated here as "flesh."

1. The "clumped mind" (*tuánxīn*). This refers to the heart among the five viscera within the body, as clarified in the *Huangting jing* (Scripture of the Yellow Court). 2. The "discursive mind" (*yuànlǜxīn*).
This consists of the eight consciousnesses (*ālaya-vijñāna*, etc.), as they are all capable of discerning their respective objects (*svaviṣaya*).

Form is the object of the visual consciousness; the physical body, seeds, and the receptacle world are the objects of the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Since each [consciousness] perceives only one portion [of these], they are called "respective" (*zìfèn*). 3.

*Ci-tta-ya*: This is translated as the "accumulating-arising mind" (*ālayavijñāna*). It is exclusively the eighth consciousness, which accumulates seeds and gives rise to active manifestations (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
*Catu-kandali-ta-ya*: This is translated as the "solid-core mind," also called the "authentic-core mind. This is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*).
Therefore, within the ancestral Buddha-dharma, all take this mind as the seal (*mudrā*), for it definitively establishes all phenomena (*dharma*). If one can...
Enter with resolute faith; I request that each of you set aside your doubts. Apart from this, there is nothing else extraordinary. Thus it is said that it transcends words and thought.
Whether in motion or stillness, all objects are sustained by my own conditions, like the moon appearing to move when the clouds drift, or the shore appearing to shift when a boat travels.
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: The Buddha said, "Good sons, all worlds—from beginning to end, from birth to cessation;

from prior to subsequent, from existence to non-existence; from gathering to dispersing, from starting to stopping—these continuous, successive moments, revolving in cycles, and these various acts of grasping and rejecting, are all saṃsāra.
To attempt to discern Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-vidyā*) without having escaped saṃsāra is for that nature of Perfect Enlightenment to likewise flow along with the current."
It is impossible for one to escape saṃsāra [if these delusions persist]. It is like moving one’s eyes, which makes the clear water appear to shake;
or like fixing one’s gaze, which makes a stationary fire appear to spin. It is just as when clouds move, the moon appears to move; or when a boat travels, the shore appears to shift.
Good son, if the various rotations have not yet ceased, even the prior stability of those objects cannot be found; how much less so can the cycle of birth and death be halted?
The defiled mind has never been purified; one contemplates the Buddha’s Perfect Enlightenment but does not return to it.
As for the analogy, "moving the eyes can shake the still water," the ancient commentary states: by gazing at water with weary eyes, one perceives the water as moving.
If the eyes do not blink, the pond water will not ripple. If false perceptions are eliminated, there will likewise be no appearance of the growth or decay of grasses and trees. If...

Raising the eyes to see forms is due to the existence of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). Raising the body to experience suffering and pleasure is due to the existence of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanāskandha*).

Raising the mind so that it immediately becomes distracted is due to the existence of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*). Raising the eyes to perceive arising and ceasing is due to the existence of the aggregate of mental formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).

That place where the spirit is brilliant, still, and unmoving is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Furthermore, if one perceives the simultaneous sensation of needles piercing the entire body without engaging in conceptual discrimination, then...

This is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). If one analyzes it sequentially, there are the remaining aggregates; thus, we know that as soon as a single thought-moment arises, the five aggregates arise together.

While the subtle consciousness has not yet perished, the six sense-objects have not ceased. If the lamp of the meaning of "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*) shines constantly, [the darkness of ignorance is dispelled].

From what cause does delusion arise? The mirror of wisdom within the single mind is eternally luminous; its essential meaning is never obscured. Furthermore, regarding the analogy of the revolving firebrand:
when one looks at a whirling circle of fire with a fixed gaze, the eye itself also revolves. In the former case, the water moves because the eye moves;
this means the objective realm moves because the mind moves. In the latter case, [the fire moves] because the fire-brand moves...
The eye moves; this is because the mind moves in response to the movement of objects. Thus, one knows that the mind is the object and the object is the mind.
Although subject and object are distinguished, they manifest as a single essence. Therefore, the *Huayan shu* states: "Their coming and going are boundless;
movement and stillness share a single source. It is likewise so with the saying, "The clouds move, the moon travels; the boat moves, the shore shifts. Thus, one knows the Truth.

The mind is unmoving; it is through deluded thoughts that differentiation arises. As stated in the *Treatise on the Awakening of Faith*: "Furthermore, to demonstrate how one enters the gate of True Suchness from the gate of Arising and Ceasing:
this means to investigate the five aggregates, both form and mind, and the objects of the six sense-fields, and find them ultimately to be without thought.
Because the mind has no form or characteristics, even if one searches for it throughout the ten directions, it can never be found. As it says:
Because people are deluded, they take east for west, yet the directions themselves do not actually shift. Sentient beings are likewise:

because they are deluded by ignorance, they take the mind to be thought, though the mind itself is truly unmoving. If one can observe and know that the mind is without thought, one will immediately attain accord with entry into the gate of True Suchness (Tathatā). Therefore.
When the mother fish remembers them, the fish eggs grow;
if the mother fish does not keep the scattered eggs in mind, they rot and perish. If the mother fish remembers them, the offspring grow and develop.
Just as with an object that appears as a solitary reflection, if the mind does not take past and other such phenomena as its object, those objects do not manifest.
Previously, it was stated that all phenomena are transformations of consciousness conditioned by the mind; if there were no mind, there would be no phenomena.
It is like when the queen bee arises, the swarm of bees follows.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "All dharmas enter into the Buddha's mind as the single gate of the samādhi of quiescent extinction (*ekānta-śānti-samādhi*).
This encompasses immeasurable samādhis, just as when one pulls a corner of a garment, the entire garment is raised; it is also like capturing the king of the honey bees."
All other bees are fully included; when the mind-king arises, all mental factors—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or otherwise—arise in its wake.
How much more so when it goes forth like a king, with all its hundred officials following in its train.
The seal is consistent from beginning to end without deviation; all worthies look up to it together. It is a model for the start and finish that is never erroneous; a thousand sages alike commend it.
Like a royal treasure-seal, its inscription appears instantaneously, without distinction between prior and subsequent limits.

Furthermore, it seals and stabilizes the world, just as within the Buddha-dharma, if there is no Mind-Seal (citta-mudrā), the Buddha-dharma cannot be established. Thus we know that the former is also mind, and the latter is also mind.
The mind. It was the mind in antiquity, and it is the mind now. Thus it is said: "It is not that it flourished in the past and declines now;
nor is it that the ignorant have perished and the wise have appeared. It is further said: "The myriad dharmas do not transcend the one mind. A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The mental activities of sentient beings are immeasurable, yet they can be made to enter equally into the one mind; through the gate of wisdom, all are opened."
Awakened, they do not regress from their spiritual practice. It is further said:
"In this way, the lords among all people, within a single thought-moment, fully awaken to all their various spheres of experience, yet they do not abandon the conduct of bodhi."
It is further said: "The deeds performed by the Buddhas according to their suitability are immeasurable and boundless, equal to the Dharma-realm.
The wise, by means of a single skillful method, can fully comprehend them all without exception."
Therefore, as soon as my footprints appeared, they were all established from this source. A swift horse responds to the whip, and Śāriputra knows before it is uttered.
As the Sūtra says: An outsider asked the Buddha, "When one neither asks about existence nor asks about non-existence, what then?
The Buddha sat in silence. The outsider praised him, saying, "How wonderful! Gautama, you have cleared away the clouds of my delusion and enabled me to enter."
Having paid homage, he departed. Later, Ānanda asked the Buddha, "By what principle did the non-Buddhists perceive that they praised him so highly?
The Buddha said, "It was like a swift horse seeing the shadow of a whip: it quickly enters the right path.

Regarding Śāriputra, who was known as Śāradvatīputra—he was also called Śāriputra—it was at the first assembly of the Dharma-exposition during the Lotus Sūtra that he was the very first to attain realization. Previously...
She received the prediction of enlightenment.
A fragrant elephant circled about as the dragon girl personally offered [the jewel].
As for the "circumambulation of the elephant king," Mañjuśrī turned his gaze back toward the eastern side of the city of Bodhimaṇḍa, like the circling of an elephant king.
He showed this to the fourfold assembly. At the beginning, the youth Sudhana was able to enter. During the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the dragon girl offered a pearl;
she was a female of the animal realm in the state of true retribution (*sabhāga-vipāka*). Because she had not yet attained a human body, her observance of the precepts was lax (*śithila-śīla*);

yet because she attained realization of the mind-essence of the Mahāyāna, her engagement with the vehicle was urgent (*tīvra-yāna*). As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "To know all dharmas within a single thought is the site of enlightenment (*bodhimanda*)."
Because they have accomplished all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Furthermore, the *Garbhāvakrānti-sūtra* states: "The daughters of Śakra and Brahmā neither receive a body nor discard a body;
they all manifest their bodies and attain Buddhahood. Moreover, a verse says: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is like a great ocean; it does not speak of right or wrong.
Whether ordinary fools, sages, or saints, all are equal without high or low. It depends solely on the extinction of mental defilements; thus one attains realization."

In the turn of a palm, the attainment of fruition and the determination of prosperity or decay are already fixed; all accord with prior causes. With a single thought, suffering or joy arises accordingly;
all harmonize with one's original vows.

The transformation of consciousness is fixed; abundance or scarcity arises from the mind. Each receives their portion for food and drink, experiencing retribution in accordance with their body, never failing to receive it.
Not only do human rewards and retributions follow the mind, but all supramundane merits are already perfected within the initial resolve (*prathama-cittotpāda*).
As the *Huayan Yanyi Ji* states: "At the moment of first generating the resolve, one attains the single body of the Tathāgata..."
When the body is measured, the Dharma-body is revealed; when ultimate wisdom is attained and the light of all wisdom is obtained, Prajñā is revealed;
because the mind is free from deluded grasping and quiescence and illumination flow as one, Liberation is revealed.
Therefore, within this mind, there is no virtue that is not subsumed; the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, all of which resides within the initial mind.

From the very moment of first generating the aspiration for enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), one attains perfect awakening. This is as stated in the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Brahmacarya-varga*). Furthermore, regarding the statement that the beginning and the end are mutually interfused:

the beginning is the beginning of the end, and the end is the end of the beginning. According to the principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), there is no end apart from the beginning.
Since there is no beginning after having left [the state of non-arising], the beginning is cited to encompass the subsequent.
If one considers the interpenetration of the *dharmatā*, all causes and effects do not depart from the nature of mind; they accord with the nature of mind, such that no virtue is not subsumed.

This is because all phenomena, according to where they abide, are suddenly and perfectly fulfilled within the initial mind. As it says in the "Chapter on Brahma-conduct": "If bodhisattvas are able..."
Corresponding with such contemplative practice, one does not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena. All Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before one;
at the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
One knows that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind itself; one accomplishes the body of wisdom not through awakening by means of another.
The *Sūtra on the Ten Paths of Wholesome Action* states: "At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Dragon King, saying: 'Because the mental conceptions of all sentient beings differ...'"
The creation of karma is also diverse; it is because of this that there is the revolving of the various realms of existence.
O Dragon King, do you not see how the forms, colors, and species within this assembly and within the great ocean are each distinct? All such things are created by nothing other than the mind.
Furthermore, observe these great bodhisattvas, whose sublime forms are adorned and pure; all of these arise from cultivation.

They are born from the accumulation of virtuous karma and merit. Furthermore, those among the devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings who possess great majestic power are likewise born from virtuous karma and merit.

Now, all sentient beings within the great ocean—whether their forms and colors are coarse or base, large or small—all arise from the various conceptualizations of their own minds, which produce unwholesome actions of body, speech, and mind.
Virtuous karma! Therefore, one receives retribution according to one's own karma. Thus we know that objects follow consciousness as it transforms;
for this reason, it is said that "all is but mind. Impure wealth turns into pus and blood; ill-gotten treasures transform into venomous snakes.
In the past, there was a courtesan who offered money to build Puguangwang Temple.
The administrators would not accept it, so she had it buried to the northeast of the temple. Later, when it was excavated, it had all turned into blood.
Furthermore, there was a butcher who gathered money inside a bamboo tube; after he died, his mother opened it, and it too had become red blood. It is just as in ancient accounts.

Dechun, the ocean-like worlds of sentient beings—their modes of abiding, their forms, their suffering and happiness, and their purity and impurity—are all adorned by the karmic retribution of the sentient beings' own actions;
they do not arise from anything else. This is also true for the ocean-like worlds of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
All are accomplished through the power of great vows, the power of the inherently pure *dharmatā*, the power of great compassion and wisdom, and the power of inconceivable transformations.
Thus, one should know that the dependent origination of defilement and purity does not transcend one's own mind;
the formation of the world as a fruit has no separate essence. As a verse in a sutra says: "Either arising from the ocean of the mind, or following what the mind conceives..."
Understanding abiding: like an illusion, it has no location; all is conceptual construction. Furthermore, a verse says:

"From a single thought-moment until the completion of an eon, everything arises based on the mental perceptions of sentient beings. All oceans of lands and boundless eons are purified through a single skillful means.
Moreover, the transformation of consciousness is fixed; retribution and response leave no room for error. Whether one possesses a thousand horses or but a single gourd, each [is determined].
One must accept one's lot. Whether one resides in a crimson gate or a magnificent mansion depends entirely upon one’s conditions;
these arise in accordance with the mind that manifests good or evil deeds, evoking corresponding environments of abundance or scarcity. As the *Qianding lu* (Records of Predestined Destiny) states:

When the Duke of Jin, Han, was serving in the Secretariat, he summoned an official who arrived late. The Duke grew angry and intended to flog him. The official said, "I have other duties to attend to and could not come."
He arrived in haste and begged for forgiveness for his crime. The Duke of Jin asked, "To whom else does an official of the Chancellor belong?

The official replied, "It is my misfortune that I also belong to the Office of the Netherworld. The Duke of Jin considered this insincere and said in anger, "Since you belong to the Office of the Netherworld..."
"What do you oversee? the official asked. The clerk replied, "I am in charge of the food provisions for those of the third rank and above.
The Duke of Jin said, "If that is so, what shall I eat tomorrow? The clerk said, "This is no small matter; it must not be disclosed.
Please write it down on paper so that it may serve as proof after the fact. He did so, and then had the clerk bound. The next morning, an imperial edict was suddenly issued.

Having finished his meal, he happened to encounter a high official presenting food; there was a vessel containing rice cakes and gruel. The Emperor took half of it and bestowed it upon the Duke of Jin.
It was delicious, so the Emperor bestowed the remainder as well. Shortly thereafter, his belly swelled. He returned to his private residence and summoned a physician to examine him.

The physician said, "This is caused by a blockage from the food you have consumed; you should take a small amount of tangerine peel decoction. At night, you may eat thin congee made with starch-water."

The next day he recovered. He recalled the words of the official from the previous evening and summoned him. Upon examining his records, they were all exactly as he had described. The Duke questioned him further:
"Do the food provisions for those in the human realm also have registers? He replied, "Those of the third rank and above receive their daily rations."
Those of the fifth rank and above who hold official positions receive a monthly stipend (*xun-zhi*). Those of the sixth rank receive a quarterly stipend (*ji-zhi*).
Those who do not consume a salary receive an annual stipend (*sui-zhi*). It is further stated that Li Minqiu of Zhao County in Jingzhao Prefecture was a candidate for the jinshi examination.

He entered the examinations at the Ministry of Rites but was unsuccessful. In the autumn of the ninth year of the Taihe era, while staying as a traveler in Xuānpíng Village, he sat with his knees drawn up in sorrowful contemplation toward evening.
Suddenly, he felt as if he were intoxicated; shortly thereafter, his spirit departed from his body.

After traveling approximately sixty or seventy li, he arrived outside the gate of a city, where several hundred thousand people were gathered. Suddenly, a man came out and prostrated himself before him.
Minqiu asked, "Who is he? He replied, "I am Li An. Minqiu said, "Last year you accompanied me on my travels and passed away in Jingzhou.

How is it that you are here? He answered, "Since leaving the Twenty-second Young Master, I have served the Eighteenth Young Master, whose office is very powerful and prosperous. Now that the Twenty-second Young Master has arrived here..."
"I must see him once. He was then ushered through the crowd into the inner hall. Upon entering the gate, many officials were present in the two corridors;
some stood dejectedly, some wore plain white robes, some carried wooden tablets, and some presented credentials.
Their attire was mostly dark purple or green. Having reached the hall, he performed a formal bow and sat down, conversing with him.
He said, "Sir, why have you come here? Are you not perhaps enticed by some other object? My strength reaches this far; you should depart quickly.
This is no place for a long stay. Minqu replied in this manner, and Liu ordered his attendants to escort him out.

As they were about to depart, Minqiu earnestly requested to know the matters of his future. Liu said, "In this world, for every meal and every night one lives, nothing is not predetermined beforehand.
The reason I did not wish others to know was only for fear that the gentleman might fail to advance in virtue and cultivate his studies, or that the commoner might become indolent in his farming.
Since you truly desire to see it, it is not difficult. He then ordered an official to lead Minqiu away.
Upon reaching the Eastern Courtyard, there were approximately one hundred or so buildings. From the ground up to the roofs, the bookshelves were filled with documents;
the labels on each scroll could be clearly inspected. An official took out a single scroll and read three lines from it. The first line stated:

"Dismissed from the imperial examination in the second year of the Taihe era. The second line stated: "In that same year, he received two hundred thousand coins from the residence of Yi Zai. The third...

The third section records his service under Zhang Pingzi; nothing further is seen of him there. Once Minqiu had awakened from his trance, he recorded everything in detail within the covers of his books.
The following year, he traveled as a guest to the Western Capital, but when the time for the examinations passed, he did not enter them.
The next year, he married into the Wei family. Wei’s maternal grandfather, Yi Zai, was about to sell a secondary residence and summoned Minqiu.
He sold it. Min-gu then visited his relatives and obtained two million won for the price. Yi Jae then presented two hundred thousand won to Min-gu as a gift.
Subsequently, regarding the vouchers to be used, he treated forty thousand won as actual currency.
At that time, Min-gu was on good terms with the Wan-nam Eo Huc-jo; he therefore requested him, and Yi also utilized the funds provided by the Jiu-shi-jun.

He was granted [this post]. It accumulated to twenty-four thousand [in total]. The following year, by virtue of his hereditary privilege (*yin*), he was appointed to the post of County Magistrate of Hebei.
There was the tomb of Zhang Pingzi; at that time, commentators had lost the name of the county, so it is left for those who know it to identify.
Beauty and ugliness have no inherent substance;
they exist because they are sustained by thought. All phenomena are sustained by the eighth consciousness, while all that is good or evil arises from the discrimination of the sixth consciousness.
Sound and resonance merge in the profound; form and shadow follow one another.
When the mind is upright, the matter is upright; when the mind is crooked, the dharma is crooked. Each and every phenomenon merely opens or closes according to the mind;

there is no other underlying principle. Whether it be intentional killing or accidental killing, a true retribution or a false retribution, not even a hair’s breadth is confused, nor does it shift for even a moment. Thus...
What one’s own mind and mouth have done is what one’s own mind and mouth receive in return. As the *Zijing lu* (Self-Mirror Record) states:
"In the past, to the west of the city of the country of Moṣika, there was a great mountain that served as the dwelling place of the Pratyekabuddha Revata.

Not far from there, a man lost his ox and, searching for it, arrived at this mountain. There he encountered this Pratyekabuddha lighting a fire to dye his robes; due to the power of his past karma..."
At that time, the alms bowl transformed into an ox head; the Dharma robes transformed into ox hide; the dyeing liquid transformed into blood;
the dyeing dregs transformed into meat; and the firewood transformed into bones. Since the traces were thus, he was seized by the owner of the ox and cast into prison.
The disciple searched for him everywhere but did not know his whereabouts. From then on, twelve years passed by.
Later, encountering the right conditions, he learned that [his teacher] was in prison and spoke to the king, saying, "My teacher is in prison;
I pray that Your Majesty grant him amnesty. The king questioned the jailer: "Is there any monk here? The jailer replied, "There is no monk.

He said to the king, "I pray you summon the śramaṇa from within the prison, and my teacher shall come out of his own accord. The jailer immediately called for him, and the Pratyekabuddha came forth. This Pratyekabuddha...
The Buddha had been in prison for a long time; his hair had grown long and his robes were tattered, so that his appearance as a śramaṇa had vanished.
His disciples prostrated to him and asked, "Why is the Master here? At that time, the Master answered with the aforementioned account.
The disciples asked again, "What causes did you create in past lives that have brought you to this state? The Master replied, "In the past, I slandered another for stealing."
It was the ox that caused this to happen. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created does not perish;
when the causes and conditions meet, one must receive the retribution oneself."
Its fundamental nature is extraordinary and inconceivable. It is like taking the medicine *agada*, or like consuming a meal of pure milk.
As a sutra states: "The *agada* medicine possesses powers surpassing all other medicines; it can cure every ailment. Furthermore, another sutra says:
"Just as one who has eaten a meal of milk porridge requires nothing more, so too for one who has realized the mind—everything is already fully possessed."
It is like a wish-fulfilling tree that rains down inexhaustible jewels.
This wish-fulfilling tree rains down jewels in accordance with whatever all sentient beings think of in their minds. The mind is also like this:
it gives rise to the myriad dharmas according to thought, without end.
It is like the water-clearing jewel that clarifies the turbid pools of the multitudes;
it is like the great water-clearing jewel that can purify muddy waters. Just so, awakening to the one mind can shatter all realms of worldly toil and affliction.

Ascending to the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning (*paramārtha-dhātu*), on the day he formally met with the Great Sage; entering the Hall of Universal Radiance (*samantaprabhā-prāsāda*), at the moment he presided over the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Because within the teachings there exists the Heaven of the Ultimate Meaning, the Buddha is titled the "God among Gods" (*devātideva*), and is also titled the "Great [Sage]."
"Immortal. As for the "Hall of Universal Radiance," it is where the Buddha ascended to the Hall of Universal Radiance within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to preach that sūtra.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* takes the Dharma-realm as its central tenet. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:

"By the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, he attained the land of the Dharma and reigns as king over the three realms. Furthermore, regarding the "Universal Radiance Wisdom," if one speaks of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), [it refers to this].

The teaching that "wondrous enlightenment" (*miao-jue*) pertains to the [stages of] position (*wei*) means that the "universal radiance wisdom" (*pu-guangming zhi*) does not belong to cause or effect; rather, it encompasses both cause and effect.

This is because self-realized noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*) transcends cause and effect. Thus, in the seven-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra*, beyond the stage of wondrous enlightenment, there is established the further stage of self-realized noble wisdom.
This is also like the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*), which possesses cause and effect, as well as the cause of the cause and the effect of the effect.
The fruit is apprehended by means of the cause; this is the Buddha-nature as cause. The cause is apprehended by means of the fruit; this is the Buddha-nature as fruit.
Thus, the Buddha-nature is neither cause nor fruit. Universal Radiance Wisdom (Samantaprabhā-jñāna) is likewise: its essence transcends both cause and fruit.
It serves as the basis for cause and effect, such that the fruit is only then finalized; therefore, it is called the Tathāgata’s Wisdom of Universal Radiance.
It darkly accords with the True and illuminates in stillness;
it contains the void while emitting brilliance. The *Zhaolun* states: "The profound Way lies in wondrous awakening; wondrous awakening lies in realizing the True. To realize the True is to have..."
There is no fixed perspective. When one possesses the perspective of the equality of existence and non-existence, then "the other" and "self" are not two.
Thus, heaven and earth share the same root as I, and the myriad things share the same body as I. To be identical with me, they are no longer subject to existence or non-existence;

to differ from me, they would deviate from the principle of universal integration. Therefore, it neither emerges nor resides elsewhere, yet the Dao exists within it. It is further said: "The Perfected Person is empty..."
The mind illuminates in profound stillness; there is no principle it does not encompass. It holds the six directions within its breast, yet its spiritual discernment remains more than sufficient;
it mirrors all phenomena within the square inch of the heart, yet its spirit is ever empty.
"Like the *wangxiang* obtaining a bright pearl.

When the Yellow Emperor sought the Dark Pearl at the Red Water, he had a minister named Li Lou, who could discern the tip of a hair from a hundred paces away; yet though he sought it, he could not find it, until the *wangxiang* obtained it.

The *wangxiang* is precisely "no-mind. Thus, the "Rhapsody on Playing with Pearls": The Yellow Emperor lost his Dark Pearl at the Red Water. He summoned the minister Li Lou, Who could see the tip of a hair from a hundred paces. Though he searched for it, he could not find it; Only the *wangxiang* obtained it. The *wangxiang* is indeed no-mind. Therefore, one should play with the pearl.
It is said: "The formless *wangxiang* obtains the pearl through having no mind; that which can see and can hear is but a fabrication.
In the realm of the rare and the profound (*xīyí*) lies the essential principle of the school:
not seeing with the eyes is called "rare" (*xī*); not hearing with the ears is called "profound" (*yí*). Thus it is said: "When the mind is absent, the Way manifests. Furthermore—
The true mind is formless; it cannot be understood through seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing.
Its grace covers all living beings, yet it remains unattainable. It neither acts nor exerts itself. As the *Zhao lun* says:
"The Sage’s merit exceeds that of the two polarities, yet he is not benevolent; his brilliance surpasses that of the sun and moon, yet he is ever more [subtle]."
Obscure. The commentary says: "Therefore, the sage is not benevolent; he regards the common people as straw dogs. Heaven and Earth are not benevolent; they regard all things as straw dogs.
A "straw dog" is something that has no utility for barking or guarding. To be "not benevolent" means to bestow grace without expecting a reward.
To be "even more obscure" means to illuminate without illuminating; this is precisely the state of being without mind.
Light encompasses the myriad phenomena while transcending thought; it forgets both cognition and illumination.
The *Yongjia ji* states: "If one uses cognition to know stillness, this is not cognition without an object, like a hand grasping a wish-fulfilling gem."
It is not that there is no "hand of suchness" (yid-bzhin gyi lag-pa). If it is known through self-knowing awareness, it is also not a knowing that lacks an object.
Just as a hand forming a fist is not a hand that is not a fist, so too this knowing is not a knowing of silence, nor does it know itself as knowing;

yet it cannot be said to be without knowing, because its nature is luminously clear and thus differs from wood or stone. It is like a hand that does not grasp an object, yet is not [without function].
One forms one's own fist; it cannot be said to be handless, for the hand remains at ease.
Thus, it is not like a rabbit’s horn—this is the marvel of the Chan school, and so it is employed here, though with slight variation.

While that [other method] merely reveals non-conditioned true wisdom as the true path, if one were to take this away, it merely reveals the original mind, which does not follow the deluded mind. It has not yet...

When wisdom illuminates and realizes the original source of the mind, it is said that one must directly attain the equality of subject and object. In this state, equanimity does not lose its illumination;
it is a knowing that is free from [dualistic] cognition. Only when this knowing knows the empty, quiescent, and unarisen nature of the Tathāgatagarbha can it be called wondrous.
In this way, even dust becomes a Buddha-land, and mindfulness accords with the perfect sound.
The *Xinyao jian* states: "Mind after mind becomes a Buddha; there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind. Everywhere, the Way is perfected."
There is not a single speck of dust that is not a Buddha-land. Furthermore, the *Vow of Mind-Only* (*Weixin jue*) states:
"The trees on the crags and the ferns in the courtyard each manifest boundless wondrous forms; the cries of monkeys and the chirping of birds all discourse upon the perfect sound of non-duality.
Moreover, when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, sentient beings each attain understanding according to their own kind, just as the full moon possesses only a single, perfect form.
It manifests many reflections according to the differences in the capacities of beings; thus, the many are identical to the one.
If the many were not identical to the one, it would not be a single sound. Furthermore, the one is identical to the many; if the one were not identical to the many, it would not be the perfect sound.
It merely manifests a world of golden hue.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "In all places, Mañjuśrī comes from the Golden World.
This "golden" refers to the pure, white color of the self-mind of all sentient beings. "Mañjuśrī" refers to one who has faith in their own mind.
The liberation of sublime wisdom that abides in non-reliance is Mañjuśrī himself. Whether persons or phenomena, all are dharmas manifested by one's own mind.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says: "To enter the Tathāgata’s chamber is to possess the great compassion for sentient beings.
How could one possibly enter a house of conditioned forms? This is why [he was] the foremost of the Oxhead [monks].
The Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai, in his commentaries on the Buddhist sutras, consistently employed the method of "contemplating the mind" (guānxīn) as his interpretation;
in doing so, he profoundly accords with the fundamental intention of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
One hears only of the *campaka* groves;
as stated in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra*, within the ten-foot square room, they discuss nothing but the principle of the Mahāyāna’s single mind. Hence it is said:

One perceives only the fragrance of the *campaka* flower and does not smell other scents; the breath of the Three Vehicles cannot be compared to the treasures of a merchant, which are left for the merchant to gather.
Even if one were to obtain a "black pearl" (*li-zhu*), it would still be but a worldly rarity; such efforts would be in vain, like looking through a narrow tube.
The Master said: "Where profit lies, there is no mountain of a thousand *ren* that one will not ascend, and no abyss of a deep source into which one will not enter.
When merchants engage in trade, they double their paths and travel in tandem, continuing by night as if it were day; even a thousand *li* is not far when profit lies before them.
When fishermen enter the sea, though the waters are a hundred *ren* deep, they brave surging waves and currents that flow against the tide, staying out through the night."
It does not emerge; the benefit lies in the water itself. This refers merely to the worldly pursuit of profit through diligent toil.

If, however, one resolutely seeks the Way with steadfast intent, forgetting fatigue from morning until night, seeking nothing outwardly, but with an open heart and clarified mind, sitting in stillness within a secluded chamber—this is the true path.
To remain composed with hands folded and the spirit at peace is to have one's benefit reside within the mind. Wherever there is benefit, whatever is sought will be obtained;

how much more so when the Way resides within the mind—there is truly nothing that cannot be attained. Therefore, know that the words of instruction and transformation must not be abandoned for even a moment;
they may be engraved upon the bones, written upon the sash, infused into the spirit, and permeated into consciousness. This is why King Zhuang of Chu disregarded a thousand [pieces of gold].

When Duke Cheng of the state of Song renewed the single word of his younger brother Shu, and Fan Xian valued the boatman’s brief discourse more than ten thousand acres of land—these were instances where establishing a family or a state still held words in such high esteem and lightened the value of material wealth.

How much more so when it concerns the Dharma-gate of the Mind-ground, the secrets of all Buddhas, through which one accords with non-arising upon hearing a single word and realizes the Great Way upon hearing it; how could one possibly afford to treat it lightly?
How arrogant!
Would you rather equate yourself with a woodcutter?
Suppose a woodcutter, returning home laden with firewood, encounters gold on his path; he immediately discards the wood to pick up the gold, for its value far exceeds [that of the former].

It is ten thousandfold greater. How much more so when one abandons the false to return to the true, not relying on provisional, gradual, or incomplete teachings, but entering directly through the gate of the One Mind’s teaching of ultimate reality;
then the progress of one's studies will increase day by day and kalpa by kalpa. As the "Solitary Chant" says: "To be undeluded, there must first be an undeluded mind;
when viewed it seems shallow, but in its application it is profound. If this pearl is gathered..."
It is attained. How could it be compared to a woodcutter carrying gold? Gold, through smelting and refining, becomes ever newer; yet this pearl contains its radiance without showing it to others.
When fully realized, one finds that the tip of a single hair swallows the vast ocean, and only then does one know that the great earth is but a single mote of dust.
Each drop and each mote of dust serve as metaphors for the One Mind, which encompasses all that is vast and great. How could it be likened to the treasures of the human world? This—

This is the treasure of the world-transcending; it marks the source of the myriad transformations. It unifies the root of ultimate truth and responds to conditions through application, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
It manifests forms according to objects, like a great round mirror. Therefore, it can encompass all phenomena and is the Great Dharma Treasury;
it gives birth to the inexhaustible and is the Inexhaustible Treasury; its wondrous wisdom is boundless and it is the Great Wisdom Treasury.
All phenomena are eternally as they are; this is the Tathāgatagarbha. Its original nature is formless; this is the Pure Dharmakāya.
Its essence is conjoined with true emptiness; this is the Ākāśakāya. Its marks and embellishments are void and profound; this is the Sublime Rūpakāya.

Its wondrous eloquence is inexhaustible; this is the Prajñākāya. Its concealment and manifestation are unimpeded; this is the Nirmāṇakāya. Adorned by the myriad practices; this is the Puṇyakāya. Contemplate...
Thoughts being unimpeded is the entrance into the Dharma-door of liberation. Each thought being vast and empty is the entrance into the Dharma-door of emptiness and stillness.
The six sense-faculties being sovereign is the entrance into the Dharma-door of non-obstruction. A single thought not arising is the entrance into the Dharma-door of signlessness.
Furthermore, regarding the essential purport herein: if they mutually support one another, then it is only expansive and only great, unfolding without limit. If...

When they are mutually sublated, they become increasingly subtle and minute until, upon investigation, no trace remains. This is to transcend both existence and non-existence without destroying existence and non-existence;
it is to mark both unity and difference without being either unity or difference. Thus, the fires of the four extremes cannot burn it, and the defilements of the hundred negations cannot stain it.
It merely manifests in accordance with conditions, like an echo in a valley. Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
It is said: For example, suppose there is one person who possesses many skills. When he runs, he is called a runner; when he harvests crops, he is called a harvester;
when he prepares food and drink, he is called a cook; when he works with timber, he is called a carpenter;
and when he smelts gold and silver, he is called a goldsmith. Thus, this single person has many names.

The Dharma is also like this. In its essence it is one, yet it has many names; thus we know that while it is divided into many according to its functions, its substance remains eternally unified and indistinguishable.
The Great Master Yuan of Mount Lu said: "There is only the single knowing mind, which is divided into many according to its functions;

it is not that apart from the whole mind there exist separate numerical categories. It is, for example, like gold being fashioned into various vessels; it is not that apart from the gold there exists something else.
There exists the substance of the vessel;
yet, while one may loathe difference and rejoice in sameness, their dispositions remain naturally divided.
The *Mahāyāna-śāstra-vyākhyā* states: "To loathe difference and abandon distinction is to realize that there is only True Suchness (*tathatā*). It is, for example, like a person who avoids..."
A shadow fears emptiness, yet can never escape it. Even if one follows the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths, they will always accord with the Perfect Teaching;
