even if one indulges in the eighty-four thousand afflictions, they will forever abide in the True Position. This is because none of them can ever be separated from the mind.
Abandoning this and grasping that, one constantly follows the principle;

yet this following turns one’s back on awakening and joins with the sensory dust, causing the mind to neglect its source and rush toward external objects. Nevertheless, the principle of the True Suchness of the One Mind has never shifted or changed.
As the *Śīla-mahāyāna-śāstra* states: "The essence of the One Mind as True Suchness is great and pervades the five types of people. It is impartial.
They are equal and without distinction. What are the five kinds of conventional persons? First, the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*);
second, the śrāvaka; third, the pratyekabuddha; fourth, the bodhisattva; and fifth, the Tathāgata. These are the five.
Although these five types of persons are conventionally five, in reality they are but one. Why is this? Because of *tathatā* (suchness).
The self-substance has neither increase nor decrease; it is neither large nor small; it is neither existent nor non-existent; it has neither center nor periphery; and it has neither coming nor going.
From the very beginning, it has been singularly self-constituted; it is identical in its own making and identical in its own nature. It loathes diversity and abandons differentiation.
There is only one suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, all phenomena have the single characteristic of suchness. As it is stated in the *Samādhi-sūtra*:
"Just as a diamond may take the form of the five destinies, yet the equality of the five persons remains likewise;
among all people there is neither increase nor decrease. Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "The suchness of mind is precisely this one [suchness]."
The essence of the Dharma-realm’s great universal dharma-gate is what is called the characteristic of the mind-nature being neither born nor extinguished.
All dharmas exist as distinctions only due to deluded thought; if one is free from deluded thought, then there are no characteristics of distinction among any objects of perception.
One perceives a snake upon a rope and becomes terrified. As the verse of the *Śāstra* says:
"In the daylight, looking at the rope, one sees it as hemp; in the night, looking at the rope, one sees it as a snake.
Even perceiving a rope upon hemp is still delusion; how much less can a snake arise upon that rope? This illustrates how the deluded mind creates objective realms.
A person is like a snake produced upon a rope, or a rope produced upon hemp; this is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
If a snake is produced upon a rope, this is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); it has no name and no substance, existing only as a mental projection while being non-existent in reality.
By analogy, when observing the myriad objects of experience, they are likewise all reduced to the mind of pervasive conceptual construction.
Seeing a ghost within a wooden stump, one hesitates;
it is like looking at a stump at night and suspecting it to be a ghost. Although there is no reality to it, a mind of fear arises.

This is also like what is seen in a dream, for the essence of all phenomena is empty yet gives rise to things. This, too, is a metaphor for how the deluded mind creates objects and gives rise to them of its own accord.
The mind of fear arises. If one realizes that all is the One Mind, there are no external objects to act as adversaries; naturally, neither delight nor aversion will arise.
It is like a deluded monkey grasping at the moon, exhausting its strength in vain, or a thirsty deer chasing a mirage, seeking in empty pursuit.

This also serves as an analogy for the fact that there is no logical principle for grasping phenomena external to the mind. Thus, the *Song of Realizing the Way* says: "Without leaving this very place, it is ever serene;
yet if you seek it, you will know it cannot be seen. The *Treasury of Jewels Treatise* (*Pao-tsang lun*) says: "To scrutinize with diligent effort is to needlessly give rise to dream-like anxieties;
to wander restlessly seeking outwardly is to lose the profound path all the more."
When one drinks the drug of madness, the mind follows its transformations as the sun turns; when one eats the *laṅdā* plant, flower-needles spread across the eyes.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "It is like a person who, when intoxicated, sees the sun turning. This illustrates how, as soon as the deluded mind stirs, such appearances arise.
Illusory phenomena arise and revolve. Furthermore, a sutra states: "It is like a person who, having consumed the *laṅgali* seed, sees flowers made of needles with their eyes;
this serves as a metaphor for those who fail to realize the single mind and thus falsely give rise to objective realms."

All arise from one’s own perceptions; though there are ten thousand species, their beginning and end are eternally quiescent. All originate from thought; though it is the single Reality, its realms are ever profound.
As the Sūtra says: "All lands are sustained by perception; if there were no perception, there would be no phenomena. Furthermore, all...

Objects of perception arrive in accordance with mindfulness; if there is no mindfulness, no objects arise. As the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) states regarding the "Contemplation of True Emptiness that Subsumes Objects and Returns Them to Mind":
it means that all phenomena within the triple world are nothing but this single mind, and outside of the mind not a single dharma can be found.
Therefore, it is called "returning to the mind. It means that all conceptual discriminations arise solely from one's own mind.
There has never been an external object outside of the mind that can serve as a condition for the mind. Why is this? Because the mind does not arise, external objects are fundamentally empty.
The Treatise states: "Because one relies on consciousness-only, objects fundamentally lack intrinsic substance; thus the meaning of true emptiness is established.
Since sensory objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness does not arise."

The internal scale of the Dharma and the worldly rules of conduct—this single Dharma-gate of the One Mind may be called perfect in every way. Why is this? Its essence contains void stillness, such that one cannot praise its excellence;
its principle transcends sight and hearing, such that one cannot record its faults. From this point downward, all fall into form.
Once one has a name, it is difficult to escape censure and praise. As an ancient said: "The Great Way is a chaotic unity without form;
it is silent and without sound. It cannot be seen by looking, nor heard by listening; it cannot be known through shadows or echoes, nor can it be designated by defamation or acclaim.
From this level downward, affairs cannot be doubly beautiful, and reputations cannot be simultaneously flourishing."
Despite the vastness of heaven and earth, the brilliance of the three luminaries, and the wisdom of sages and worthies, they still cannot avoid censure and praise.
Thus, heaven exhibits signs of fissuring; earth takes on forms of cracking; and the sun and moon undergo the anomalies of eclipses and blemishes.
The five planets exhibited the portents of planetary conflict and comets; Yao was slandered for lacking filial affection; Shun was accused of resenting his father;
Tang the Sovereign was labeled for banishing his ruler; King Wu was criticized for murdering his lord; Duke Huan of Qi was branded as greedy and licentious;
Duke Wen of Jin had a reputation for failing in ministerial loyalty; and Yi Yin left a record of deceiving his sovereign. Guanzi had...
Regarding the assumption of titles superior to one's station: even the spiritual power of the Two Polarities and the Seven Luminaries cannot avoid eclipse or obscuration;
even the sagehood of Yao, Shun, Tang, and Wu could not escape suspicion and slander; and even the worthiness of Huan, Wen, Yi, and Guan could not leave behind even the slightest fault.
Viewed from this perspective, how could the common run of people in the universe possibly avoid resentment and slander? And yet—
"Regret" means stinginess. If one employs the mind and wisdom to communicate with the numinous and accomplishes the transformation of non-action (*wuwei*), then the myriad burdens cannot interfere.
Furthermore, both the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—arise from the mind; the eighth consciousness is the support that maintains the seeds.
The *tathatā*-mind is the basis for both delusion and awakening. As the *Huayan ji* states:

"Relying on the eight consciousnesses of arising and ceasing to distinguish the two [aspects], it is revealed that the *dharmalakṣaṇa* (characteristics of phenomena) are merely the support of mind and objects, yet they are themselves the *tathāgatagarbha*.

To distinguish the reasons for these two, first there is a general overview, followed by the convergence of conditions into reality; below, the two aspects are specifically demonstrated. Thus, with...

The two gates of the arising of True Suchness (tathatā) and of birth-and-death (saṃsāra) in the *Awakening of Faith* constitute merely two aspects; their preservation and destruction are non-dual, being but a single dependent origination.
This concludes with the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, which brings together conditions to enter into reality, stating that the two gates are unimpeded and are nothing other than the one mind.
In the *Awakening of Faith*, the doctrine is established by relying on the single mind (*ekacitta*) to set forth two gates;

therefore, it must fully possess these two meanings to be called "complete-particular vijñapti-mātra. Question: The ninth chapter of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states that its transformed basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) has two kinds:
first, the basis that maintains seeds, which refers to the eighth consciousness; second, the basis of delusion and awakening, which refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*). Why is this so?
[The opponent] says: "However, based on the eight consciousnesses of arising and ceasing, there is only the support of mind and its objects.
[The respondent] answers: Although they speak of the basis for delusion and awakening, it is not the support of mind and its objects. This is because True Suchness (tathatā) is unchanging;

it does not follow the mind to transform into the myriad objects. It is merely that which is deluded about. When one later returns to purity, it is not that the characteristics are subsumed into True Suchness.
However, this is merely what has been realized. Now, the mind and its objects serve as the support;

they are thus true and false, yet not two distinct entities. Therefore, they are said to be one. Yet, because their meanings differ, they are divided into two aspects, and the two gates are distinguished. Thus the Treatise says:
"Nevertheless, these two gates each comprehensively encompass all phenomena, for these two gates are not mutually separated."

May there be nothing that does not follow [one's vows]; may there be nothing that is not accomplished through faith. One beholds the myriad phenomena within the palm of one’s hand and gathers the ten directions at one’s side.
The *Huayan ce lin* (Forest of the Avataṃsaka) states: "To take form entirely as the eye means to constantly perceive form without conditions.

Form is the object of perception (*ālambana*), while the eye is the faculty that perceives (*ālambaka*). Now, since this is precisely the eye itself, it is without conditions. This is what is meant by "taking form entirely..."

The eye takes form as its object; though it is always called "seeing," it is not the self. When the eye is the self’s faculty of seeing, yet now it is entirely occupied by form, at the very moment of seeing, it is no longer the self.
Being non-self, it is free from emotional conceptualization; being without conditions, it cuts off all craving and seeking.
It gathers the myriad images before its presence and encompasses the ten directions within the limits of its vision. Thus, the principle of its conditions is inexhaustible.
Following what is seen, seeing is inexhaustible; the nature of things is inconceivable. Responding to phenomena as they are, they are difficult to standardize.
When the Dharma is universal, the eye is universal; when the meaning is pervasive, vision is pervasive. Its substance is inherently hidden; its illumination is thus layered and manifold.

Thereafter, one exhausts the ten directions within the limits of the eye, reflecting both emptiness and existence with brilliant clarity. Gathering all myriad forms to form the body, it reveals itself.
Phenomena and principle are thoroughly penetrated;
manifestations appear solely in accordance with my mind; beauty and ugliness alike return to my consciousness.

This clarifies that those who possess the complete portion of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) take the unarisen and undying to be conjoined with the arisen and dying; they are neither one nor...
It is different. It is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is "complete" (*yifen*) because it possesses both the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing.

That which is non-arising-and-non-ceasing is the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is identical to the universal true mind (*zhenshin*). If one does not rely entirely upon the true mind, then phenomena do not rely upon principle;
therefore, to discuss only the arising-and-ceasing aspect would not be complete. Some say that there is a substance outside of its reflection. As for...
The "Half-Headed" (ardhavaināśika) Yogācāra holds that both the substance and the reflection are reflections; this refers to the "Full-Portion" (sakalavaināśika) within the Yogācāra school.
Furthermore, regarding the principles that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only, there are four meanings to the term "mind-only" (cittamātra).

First is phenomena (*vastu*). These are distinguished according to their objects as seen, heard, sensed, and known. Second is dharmas (*dharma*). In terms of their essence, they are merely the numerical categories of arising and ceasing phenomena.
Regarding these two meanings, they exist from the perspective of the conventional (*saṃvṛti*) but do not exist from the perspective of the ultimate (*paramārtha*).

Third is principle (*tattva*). When investigated to its limit, it is empty and quiescent. Fourth is reality (*bhūta*). When one discusses its fundamental nature, it is solely the true Dharma of the *tathāgatagarbha*. Furthermore, it is like...
The *Sūtra on the Expedient Means for Advancing toward the Mahāyāna* states: The Buddha said, "The realm of one reality refers to the essence of the minds of sentient beings.

From the very beginning, it is neither born nor extinguished. Furthermore, the minds of all sentient beings, the minds of all those of the two vehicles, the minds of all bodhisattvas, and the minds of all buddhas are all identical in their true nature of being neither born nor extinguished."

Because it is according to its true nature (*lakṣaṇa*). Even if one were to search throughout all worlds in the ten directions, as far as the limits of empty space, not a single portion of the mind’s form or appearance could be found.

It is only due to the causes and conditions of the habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*) of sentient beings’ ignorance and deluded darkness that false objects appear, causing them to give rise to thoughts of attachment. That is to say, this mind cannot know itself; it falsely [identifies with] itself...
This refers to the arising of the perception of cognition and the conceptualization of "self" and "what belongs to self," yet in reality there is no characteristic of cognition.
Because this deluded mind is ultimately without substance and cannot be seen, if there were no cognizer capable of making such distinctions, [it would not exist].
Then there would be no differentiated characteristics of the realms of the ten directions and the three periods of time.
This is because all phenomena cannot exist of themselves; they exist only through constant reliance on the discriminative activity of the deluded mind.

That is to say, each and every realm does not conceive of itself as existing. It is by knowing this that it is "self" and by knowing that which it is not that it is "other. Therefore, all phenomena...
Being unable to exist of itself, it has no distinct reality; it exists solely in dependence upon the deluded mind.

Because one fails to understand and lacks knowledge of its internal non-existence, one falsely gives rise to various conceptualizations of phenomena regarding external objects of cognition that are supposedly present before one, asserting them to be either existent or nonexistent.

That is to say, one conceives of good and evil; one conceives of right and wrong; one conceives of gain and loss—and so on, until giving rise to immeasurable and boundless conceptualizations of phenomena (*dharmasaṃjñā*).
One should understand it thus: all phenomena arise from false conceptualization and take the deluded mind as their basis.
However, because this deluded mind lacks any intrinsic characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), it also exists in dependence upon objects; that is to say, it is conditioned by them.
Because it recollects and cognizes preceding objects, it is called "mind" (*citta*).

Furthermore, although this deluded mind and its preceding objects mutually depend upon one another and arise without temporal sequence, this deluded mind is able to act as the primary source of all objects.
Why is this so? It is because, based on the deluded mind's failure to realize that the *dharmadhātu* has a single characteristic, it is said that the mind exists.
Ignorance (*avidyā*). Because it relies on the power and cause of ignorance, false objects appear; likewise, because ignorance is extinguished, all objects are extinguished.
It is not because objects themselves lack self-cognition that one says objects possess ignorance, nor does ignorance arise based upon objects. This is because all Buddhas, regarding all...
Because ignorance does not arise from objects, and because it does not depend on the cessation of objects for its own cessation, the mind of ignorance is extinguished;
for all objects have, from the very beginning, been self-extinguished by their very nature and have never truly existed.
Based on this principle, it is said that all phenomena take the mind as their fundamental basis. One should know that all...
All phenomena (*dharma*) are entirely designated as "mind" (*citta*), because their essential nature is not different and they are subsumed within the mind.
Furthermore, all phenomena arise from the mind, act as its characteristics, and exist through conjunction with it; they arise and cease together with it, and likewise lack any abiding.
This is because all objective spheres merely follow the objects of the mind's perception, continuing in an uninterrupted succession from moment to moment. Thus, [they] are attained.
The abbot’s tenure was but temporary;

yet from his hand emerged a golden-haired lion, all through the power of his roots of goodness. The city transformed into a pond of seven-jeweled flowers, entirely sustained by the force of his compassion.
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states: King Ajātaśatru, wishing to harm the Tathāgata, released the intoxicated and rampaging elephant Dhanapāla.
The Buddha immediately extended his hand toward it and displayed five lions upon his five fingers. Upon seeing this, the elephant—
They prostrated themselves on the ground in reverence. The Buddha said, "At that time, there were actually no lions upon the five fingers of my hands;
rather, it was through the power of the roots of goodness cultivated from compassion and kindness that I caused them to see such a thing.
He further said, "In the kingdom of South India, there was a great city named Śobhāvatī. Within that city, there was an elder named Luṭi."

The leaders of the multitude: when the Buddha desired to go to that city in order to transform and deliver its people, those Nigaṇṭhas, hearing that the Buddha was about to arrive, subsequently destroyed the groves and springs, firmly closed the city walls, and each prepared their weapons to guard and defend it with great firmness.
"Even if they should come, do not allow them to advance. The Buddha said, "At that time, when I had reached that city, I saw no trees or groves at all;
I saw only people arrayed with weapons, defending their walls."
Having seen this, I immediately gave rise to compassion and directed a mind of loving-kindness toward them. All the trees grew back as they were before;
the rivers, ponds, springs, and wells became pure and overflowing. Like a pristine pond blooming with various flowers, I transformed the city walls into deep blue lapis lazuli.
At that time, I truly did not create these various trees through supernatural transformation.
The Pure Flower Pond—know that all these are the power of the roots of goodness of loving-kindness (*maitrī-kuśalamūla*), which enables them to see such things.

Therefore, know that whenever there are any realms of suffering or joy, they rely upon the Buddha’s power as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*); they are merely manifested by the resonance of one's own mind.
To take the real objects currently before one as an example: all are produced from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Outside of the mind, not a single dharma exists in reality.
It is merely a transformation of consciousness.
Its expansion and contraction are indeterminate; its concealment and manifestation take a thousand forms. At times it is utterly silent and traceless; at other times it is brilliantly visible.
It dwells amidst complexity without becoming disordered, and traverses perilous paths while remaining ever secure.

The phenomena of mind and world mutually displace and mutually support one another; they merge and interpenetrate. If they mutually support and interpenetrate, then both essence and appearance coexist, vividly manifest and visible.
If they mutually displace and mutually dissolve, then both principle and phenomenon are empty, silent and traceless.
This is because the myriad dharmas arise from the mind and are established according to conditions; because they lack intrinsic nature, they exist through conditions. Because...
Because they lack intrinsic nature due to their dependence on conditions, they are empty. As stated in the "Profound Preface to the Jewel Seal" (*Bao yin zhong xuan xu*):
"The scrolls of the *Mahāsāhasra-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* do not emerge from the dust of sensory objects; the clouds of the most pure body-mass constantly abide in defiled lands.

One realizes quiescent extinction at the juncture of causes and conditions, and attains perfect permanence within the wheel of birth and death. Principle and phenomena manifest together yet both vanish; such is the nature."
They are mutually formed together yet mutually negate one another. The One Truth is profoundly still, yet not quiescent; the myriad transformations are chaotic, yet not profuse.
All phenomena are suddenly rendered void, yet not empty; manifold activities arise everywhere, yet do not exist. Without grasping a single dharma, the essence of the mind is secretly transmitted;
without uttering a single word, the perfect sound constantly revolves. The single body pervades all multiplicities, just as...
The bright moon divides its reflection across a thousand waters; many bodies enter into one. Like a clear mirror, its light casts forth ten thousand forms.
The ocean of *amṛta* (clarified butter) is profound and deep, engulfing all tributary streams; the mountain of *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) rises toweringly, surpassing all surrounding peaks.
The Lotus Sūtra states: "For example, among all streams, rivers, and great waters, the ocean is the foremost.
This Lotus Sūtra is likewise so; among all the sūtras preached by the Tathāgatas, it is the most profound and vast.
It further states: "And among the ten jewel mountains and all other mountains, Mount Sumeru is the foremost. This...
The Lotus Sūtra is likewise so; it is the most supreme among all sūtras.

This scripture is the teaching of the finest cream (amṛta) and constitutes the primary heart-essence. Therefore, the sūtra says: "In the lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma."

The essence of principle is harmoniously pervasive; its fragrant fame resounds with power. When viewed in terms of time, its distinct characteristics are difficult to exhaust; when entering through a single gateway, one penetrates deeply into the One.
If one observes through phenomenal forms, one becomes lost in their differences and fails to grasp the ultimate intent; if one illuminates through the single mind, one accords with equality.
Thus one returns to the root. Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "If you enter deeply through a single gate, then the six faculties of cognition will all become pure at once.
It also says: "Entering the One, there is no delusion. Master Li’s Commentary states: "Entering the One, one is entirely true.
As the Verse on Awakening to the Way by Master Xin-feng says: "Previously, I sought penetration in every object; it was only because..."
In the past, I did not awaken to the fundamental principle; now that I have awakened, there is nothing at all. Only then do I know that the myriad dharmas are originally empty.
Having taken the medicinal elixir of King Sudarśana, all ailments are completely eliminated. Having strummed the lute strings of the lion’s sinew, all other sounds are suddenly silenced.
The medicinal herbs of King Bhaiṣajyarāja can cure all manner of ailments; the sublime medicine of the mind is likewise able to cure all phenomena. Thus a verse says:
"A single pill cures ten thousand diseases, rendering many prescriptions unnecessary. It further says:

"If a lute string is made from a lion’s sinew, its sound, once played, causes all other sounds to cease. How much more so when one speaks of how a single-mindedness can encompass ten thousand [virtues]."

The Dharma is such that its brilliance surpasses the bright sun and its virtue exceeds the Great Clarity (*Mahāvyoman*). It arises in function according to conditions and accords with things without birth.
Question: For a beginner practitioner who awakens to and enters this school, and whose faith and understanding are perfectly realized, what superior power do they possess? Answer: If...
With right understanding perfectly clear and bright, one enters with resolute faith; thus there is the merit of transcending kalpas and the power of sudden realization.

Although remaining within birth and death, one constantly enters nirvana; though perpetually dwelling amidst the defilements of worldly toil, one eternally resides in pure lands. Though appearing to possess only the physical eye, one truly sees.
Thus, the radiance of the eye of wisdom is opened. Without altering the ordinary mind, one immediately shares the knowledge and vision of the Buddha's mind.
Then, the dust and toil of afflictions will extinguish themselves without needing to be severed; the wondrous fruit of Bodhi will become perfectly fulfilled without relying on cultivation.
This extends even to equalizing enemies and kin, harmonizing disputes, leveling the ordinary and the sage, dissolving self and other, and transcending coming and going—thus it is sealed.
It unifies identity and difference; it merges the long and the short; it blends the center and the periphery.

This power—which is of the mundane and the supramundane, which is ineffable, immeasurable, and beyond description—is unsurpassed by anything else. It is called the Power of the Buddha; it is called the Power of Prajñā;
it is called the Power of the Mahāyāna; it is called the Power of the Dharma; it is called the Power of Non-abiding. For this reason, the former masters...
The commentary states: "That which is sustained by the power of non-abiding means that a great kalpa is not separate from a single thought-moment.

It further states: "The equality of form is the power of the Buddha. Since form is equal, the principle of "mind-only" is established. Thus, one knows that among all gateways for contemplating the mind, this one is without flaw;
it is most honored and most noble, peerless and unsurpassed. Through it, the merit of attaining Buddhahood in a single kṣaṇa is instantly realized.
Regarding the power of the wheel of suffering, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "For example, there is a medicinal tree called the 'King of Medicines.

Among all medicines, it is the most excellent and is able to eliminate all diseases. The tree does not form the thought, 'If one takes my branches, leaves, bark, trunk, or other parts,' yet even though it forms no such thought, it can cure all ailments. Nirvāṇa is also like this. Therefore, if one—

With single-mindedness, there are those who possess perfect faith and perfect cultivation, even down to those who merely see, hear, rejoice in, or give rise to a thought of awakening for a single moment.
There is not one among them who does not eliminate the ailments of the eighty thousand afflictions, the three obstacles, and the two deaths. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"It is like a maṇi jewel; wherever it resides, no non-human spirits can find an opportunity to harm. If the jewel is worn upon the body, in the midst of darkness..."

One attains clarity; in heat one finds coolness, and in cold one finds warmth. Just as when it is in water, it reflects the colors of whatever objects are present—this is a metaphor for realizing that this mind of one’s own is like a wish-fulfilling jewel.
When one’s perfect faith is firm and solid, at all times and in all places, one cannot be harmed by the non-humans of ignorance and afflictions.
Thus, one remains undisturbed amidst the profusion of the world and stays ever secure while treading upon perilous paths.
High yet not precarious; full yet not overflowing.

Neither different nor the same; filling the entire realm of phenomena (*kṣetra*) while appearing perfectly level. Neither large nor small; pervading all of space, it is spontaneously and naturally perfected.
This single dharma of the one mind is the Great Truth. It does not arise dependent on conditions, nor does it arise without conditions, because it is the essence of all dharmas.
It pervades all places; according to what beings perceive, it manifests inexhaustibly.
It is different yet not different, the same yet not the same, great yet not great, small yet not small—like a flower.
A verse from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: Within each and every atom, one can realize all dharmas;
The minds of all sentient beings are universally present throughout the three periods of time. In a single thought-moment, the Tathāgata clearly and fully comprehends them all.
The Terrace of the Spirit; the Secret Treasury.
This Dharma of the One Mind is the nature of spiritual liberation; because it can penetrate the numinous and the sagely, it is called the "Terrace of the Spirit.
Furthermore, as it is the ultimate destination of all dharmas and the universal essence of a thousand paths, it is termed the "Secret Treasury."
The sick encounter a skilled physician; the people meet a sagely sovereign. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"It is like a merchant finding his master; like a child finding its mother; like one crossing water finding a boat;
like the sick finding a physician; like those in darkness finding a lamp; like the poor finding treasure; like subjects finding their king; and like merchants finding the sea."

This is even more so for those encountered in the human realm. If one within the Buddha-dharma directly realizes the mind, they can forever escape the toil of worldly dust and dwell eternally in the sacred ground.
They treat the grave illness of afflictions and become the unsurpassed Dharma King. When comparing the gain and loss of these two states, the difference is as vast as that between heaven and earth.
Using the fundamental to encompass the derivative: this serves as the bridge and ferry across the ocean of wisdom.
Taking the single mind as the fundamental and all phenomena as the derivative, those who wish to cross the ocean of birth and death should do so by means of the mind-intellect.
To cite one and thereby encompass all: this is the rule for opening the profound gate.
By citing the Dharma of the single mind, everything is gathered up without exception. This one dharma-gate is able to establish the realms of both ordinary beings and sages.
The Gate of Gathering and Transforming Beings: therein the six perfections and myriad practices are fully complete. As the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) states:
"From the essence of the one mind, two functions arise: [the three pervasions,] the four virtues, the five stillnesses, and the six contemplations.

Regarding the "one essence," it is the essence of self-nature, pure and perfectly luminous; it serves as the common essence for the ten samādhis. Regarding the "two functions," the first is the ocean...

The seal that eternally abides throughout the myriad phenomena is the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*). The sovereign function of the perfect luminosity of the two dharma-realms is the Flower-Adornment Samādhi (*avaivartika-samādhi*).
Regarding the three types of pervasiveness: first, the pervasiveness of a single atom universally encompassing the entire dharma-realm;
second, the pervasiveness of a single atom giving rise to the inexhaustible; third, the pervasiveness of a single atom containing both emptiness and existence. These three are all...
The *Indrājāla-samādhi* gate. Regarding the four virtues: first, the virtue of wondrous function that adapts to conditions without fixed direction;
second, the virtue of maintaining proper conduct and decorum with established rules; third, the virtue of gathering and sustaining sentient beings through gentleness and straightforwardness;

fourth, the virtue of universally taking the suffering of sentient beings upon oneself. Regarding the five types of cessation (*śamatha*): first, the cessation of detachment from conditions through the clear and empty illumination of phenomena; second, the cessation through contemplation... [text continues]

1. The cessation of quiescent detachment, which severs desire; 2. The cessation of natural law, wherein the proliferation of the three natures arises and subsides; 3. The cessation of non-conceptualization, wherein the radiance of Dīpaṃkara appears; 4.

The cessation of signlessness, wherein phenomena and principle are mysteriously interpenetrated. Regarding the six contemplations: 1. The contemplation of true emptiness, in which objects are subsumed into the mind; 2.
The contemplation of wondrous existence, in which objects manifest from the mind; 3. The contemplation of the secret, perfect interfusion of mind and object.

1. The contemplation of the manifestation of the bodies and shadows of the four wisdoms within all conditions; 2. The contemplation of the single body manifesting as many; 3. The contemplation of the many bodies entering into one; 4. The contemplation of the manifestation of the bodies and shadows of the four wisdoms within all conditions;

5. The contemplation of the mirror-image of many bodies entering into one; 6. The contemplation of the Indra’s Net of mutual manifestation between principal and attendant. The above *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are both gateways to the samādhi of boundless quiescence and function.
It serves as a mirror for rectifying the age and a scale for weighing all things.
This Dharma of the One Mind can examine antiquity and infer the present, exhausting the nature of the ordinary and penetrating the state of the sage.

It is like a balance that knows weight and lightness, or a mirror that reflects beauty and ugliness. Once this One Mind is understood, there is nothing among all dharmas—whether vast or minute—whose source one will not know.
When they contend with one another, object and wisdom mutually dissolve; when they support one another, both self and other arise together.
When the object contends with wisdom, wisdom dissolves; when wisdom contends with the object, the object perishes.
When the other supports the self, the self is established; when the self supports the other, the other arises.
Upon the tree of ignorance, the flower of awakening suddenly blossoms; within the ocean of the eight sufferings, the single flavor remains eternally pure.
As the Sūtra says: "Within the great remorse of afflictions, there is the Perfect Tathāgata," proclaiming the principle of the eternal abiding of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Within the true nature of original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇajñāna*), there are sentient beings of ignorance who give rise to immeasurable and boundless afflictions.
The *Śāstra* states: "Only the Real cannot stand alone; solitary delusion cannot be established. It is through the mutual conditioning of the Real and the delusory that they can be established.
It is like water giving rise to waves due to the wind; for the wind and the water are not mutually separable."
The whole is manifest before one; why use further thought regarding wondrous awakening? It is originally complete; why need one laboriously wait for its perfection?

The Buddhas take the minds of sentient beings as their own Buddha-nature, while sentient beings take the minds of the Buddhas as their own sentient-being nature. They are of one essence, without distinction.

It is so. There is only a distinction between delusion and awakening; because the mind itself is Buddha, although the three bodies (trikāya) are differentiated, they ultimately possess no separate essence.

Thus it is said: "The marks and signs of the Dharmakāya are of one limit, without difference. Furthermore, an ancient worthy said: "A new Buddha and an old one already perfected have never had two distinct bodies.
When the Saṃbhogakāya is considered in relation to the Dharmakāya, it is like an image cast from a mold; the image is fundamentally the old [mold].
It is accomplished; therefore, there are not two distinct entities. A new Buddha is formed from an ancient Buddha, such that the Dharma-body and the Reward-body appear to be divided.

This is like taking gold to form an image: the gold and the image appear to be distinct because there was previously gold that had not yet been fashioned into an image. Now that the image has been completed, [the two are one].

They appear to be divided into two: the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are like gold that has already been fashioned into an image, while sentient beings are like gold that has not yet been fashioned into an image.
Although the formed and the unformed seem to be distinguished as prior and posterior, the essence of the gold remains fundamentally no different from beginning to end.

It manifests the extraordinary and marks the unique; its brilliance and purity reach ultimate perfection. It is like the spreading light of the bright sun, resembling the dissemination of the mandate of Goumang.
This Dharma of the One Mind is like the sun illuminating the world—there is no phenomenon that it does not clarify—and like spring pervading the entire realm.
There is nothing that does not manifest.
The three poisons and four inversions are no different from the ordinary; the eight liberations and six supernormal powers are no different from the sage.
Being among the ordinary, one is not ordinary; dwelling among the sages, one is not a sage. Because these are but one’s own mind, there is ultimately no separate principle. Treasure!
The *Zanglun* states: "In the realm of ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), not even a hair's breadth of ordinary or sagehood can be found.
When the supreme treasure dwells within one’s breast, one should never seek it elsewhere; when the numinous pearl is held in one’s grasp, one ought to rejoice."
The *Zhao lun* states: "How distant can the Sage be? To embody him is itself the numinous. Why is this so?
Because the minds of sentient beings are all *prajñā*. If one can realize the ultimate principle, then the mind is itself the Buddha;

that is to say, the true nature of the numinous awakening of this very day is precisely the holy wisdom of *prajñā*. This clarifies true wisdom; such a person is a sage who has awakened to the principle.

It is not the fruit of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Furthermore, regarding what is called "sacred wisdom of *prajñā*": if it is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), it is the *prajñā* of contemplative observation;
if it is suchness (*tathatā*), it is the *prajñā* of the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*). This correct wisdom and suchness are precisely the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
The perfected nature is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha mind. The Tathāgatagarbha mind is precisely the [Dharmakāya] of all...
The nature of spiritual awakening of sentient beings; the nature of spiritual awakening of all living beings is precisely the true wisdom of *prajñā*.
Out of compassion for those who share the same essence, one gives rise to non-referential [compassion].
When a Bodhisattva contemplates all sentient beings as being of one and the same essential nature, they feel pity for those who do not realize this and thus practice great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
"Objectless" refers to objectless compassion (*apraṇihita-maitrī*). Like a magnet attracting iron, it spontaneously draws in all sentient beings without the conceptualization of "delivering" them.
It overflows with the wealth of the Dharma to sustain the life of wisdom.
There are seven kinds of Dharma-wealth: first, hearing; second, faith; third, precepts; fourth, concentration; fifth, diligence; sixth, relinquishment; and seventh, shame and remorse.

As for the "life of wisdom," it is the inexhaustible nature of True Suchness within one's own mind. These seven kinds of Dharma-wealth, up to and including the ocean of wisdom and virtue as vast as the sands of the Ganges, are all mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*).
For those who awaken to and enter them, these provide inexhaustible sustenance and benefit.
One who attains the essence of the One finds their doubts suddenly dispelled.
Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; humans attain the One and the Way is perfected. The Sūtra says:
"If one attains the One, the myriad evils are extinguished. It also says: "If one attains the One, all matters are completed. This refers to realizing the single true mind.
What principle would not be complete? What matter would not be finalized? As an ancient master asked:
"If it is said that the nature of the mind is one, how can the realm of sentient beings be seen as having such variety? He replied:

"Because the true suchness (tathatā) of the nature of the mind is one, yet it gives rise to various forms through the conditions of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, the eighth consciousness is precisely the mind that is perfumed.
The substance contains various seeds and is perfumed into various forms; this is precisely the meaning of True Suchness (tathatā) conforming to conditions.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "the nature of the mind is one," there are two interpretations in the ancient commentaries.

First, the nature of the deluded mind and the nature of the accomplished mind are distinct because their characteristics differ, whereas the nature of the true mind is such that the true mind is itself the nature. Second, they are identical in their accomplishment, meaning:
These two natures separately clarify the two *garbhas*. The former two natures both possess the two *garbhas*, yet because they are shrouded by delusion, they are called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

To speak directly of the essence of the *garbha*, it is the mind of self-nature (*svabhāvacitta*). This true mind of self-nature purity, when not conjoined with delusion, is called the "empty *garbha*" (*śūnyagarbha*);
when it possesses virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is called the "non-empty *garbha*" (*aśūnyagarbha*). The former [section] has clarified this.
This is "neither identical nor separate. This clarifies emptiness and existence; therefore, it is stated again. As for the statement that "all are equal and non-dual":
the preceding two [pairs] differ in being both identical and separate. Because the nature of the mind is [the mind], they are not identical; because the mind is the nature, they are not separate.
Being neither identical nor separate constitutes the nature of the mind. The latter two [pairs] mean that the reality of emptiness is non-empty, and that which is identical to reality...
Emptiness is the treasury of emptiness. Emptiness and existence are non-dual; this constitutes the nature of the mind.
Thus, the nature of the non-duality of emptiness and existence is precisely the nature of neither identity nor separation; therefore, it is simply called "one."
Entering the gate of non-duality, one is vast and empty, free from contention.
To perceive that there are dharmas external to the mind is to see duality; this immediately gives rise to counteraction, which constitutes contention.

If one realizes that objects are identical with the mind, such that subject and object merge into a single unity, then there is no contention. Since one does not engage with subject and object, there is neither emotion nor non-emotion.
This discourse merely discusses directly the gate of perceiving one's nature; it does not fall into the path of right and wrong.
Therefore, the subject and object are not the same, yet one must not cling to either as singular. Mind and phenomena are of one flavor, yet they cannot be called different.

If one follows nature through conditions, then emotion and non-emotion differ, and even nature itself becomes distinct. If one dissolves conditions to return to nature, then there is neither awakening nor non-awakening. If...
When the two natures are mutually fused, there is nothing that is not awakening. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"There is not even the slightest portion of True Suchness (tathatā) that is not awakening. Thus, True Suchness pervades all places, whether sentient or insentient.

If there were not even the slightest portion that was not awakening, could it be that the insentient are not Buddha-nature? Furthermore, the intent of the sutra merely excludes the clinging to [insentient objects such as] tiles and pebbles.
Regarding the perception of insentient things: it is not that the Buddha-nature can be removed; rather, this nature is omnipresent.

Since its measure extends throughout empty space, how could it ever be removed? Furthermore, an ancient master said: "The nature of awakening is principle (li), while the act of awakening is phenomena (shi).
Thus, within insentient things, there exists only the nature of awakening, but no act of awakening—just as within wood there exists only the nature of fire, yet there is no fire to illuminate. Now...

Regarding the term "nature" (*xing*): it refers solely to the fundamental principle; who would discuss its secondary ramifications? Furthermore, that which involves cognition, wisdom, and mental apprehension is called "sentiment" (*qing*);
that whose self-nature does not change is called "nature. The deluded person is confused about nature and gives rise to sentiment, and thus object and wisdom are not one.
The wise person realizes that sentiment constitutes nature, and thus things and self are non-dual.
Great Justice is impartial and level; it neither diminishes nor overflows. The nature of the Way is thus: there is no sending off and no welcoming.
It is solitary and lofty at the bottom of the thousand-fathom sea, yet level and plain atop the ten-thousand-fathom peak.
Master Fu’s Song on Walking the Road: "Mount Sumeru and a mustard seed are father and son; A mustard seed and Mount Sumeru are grandfather and grandson.
Mountains and seas are level and smooth; I strike the ice to come brew tea."
The elder bamboo sways in the wind and grows of its own accord; the young paulownia turns toward the sun and blooms in secret.
The several peaks of green mountains remain forever; a single fleck of idle cloud suddenly arises.
Master Danxia, forgetting himself, composed this verse: "The green mountains need not be visited by white clouds; The white clouds need not be governed by the green mountains.
Clouds always abide in the mountains, and the mountains always abide in the clouds; The green mountains are naturally at ease, and the white clouds are naturally unhurried.
All of these compare to the nature of the single mind: the realm of wisdom is tranquil and leisurely.
The mental ground is suddenly empty, as sharp as a rabbit’s horn; the intellect and mind are entirely stilled, like the clarity of water in a mirage.
Master Xin’feng’s verse says: “Smoke and dust arise from the bottom of a well; Waves surge upon a high mountain. A stone woman gives birth to a son;
Turtle hair grows many fathoms long. If you wish to study Bodhi, You must observe this model.”

Greatly erecting the Dharma-banner and deeply lifting the Treasure-Seal; dwelling low yet ever high, abiding in opposition yet always harmonious—this Dharma-gate of the single mind is the lofty erection of the Dharma-banner and is also the heart-seal of the patriarchs and Buddhas.
It is the gate of equality and the ground of the single limit. High and low naturally incline toward one another; compliance and resistance naturally cease their conflict. If one enters the Truth...
Wisdom is necessarily without differentiation. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Wisdom enters the three periods of time, all of which are entirely equal.

This clarifies that the substance of the conventional is fundamentally true; therefore, it is called "equality. When encompassed by the six characteristics, the whole is simultaneously the particular.
It is distinct yet entirely universal; it is identical yet simultaneously diverse; it is diverse yet eternally identical; it is established yet simultaneously disintegrating;
it is disintegrating yet simultaneously established.
He grasps the true form of the royal treasury sword and strokes the authentic tones of the Asura lute.
Within the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that the Buddha-nature of sentient beings is like a true, precious sword within a king’s treasury that no minister is able to recognize;
those who are ignorant do not see it. Furthermore, the sutra states that the lute of the Asura King is not even stroked.
The rhyme: This illustrates that the minds of sentient beings constantly turn the fundamental wheel of Dharma without ever ceasing.
As the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The lands speak, sentient beings speak; throughout the three periods of time, they speak all at once."
Having found the path, the dark road is opened wide; why seek much more? Once one thing is understood, ten thousand matters are simultaneously at rest.
Simply give rise to deep faith. The *Xinxin Ming* says: "The One is all; all is the One. If one can be thus, what need is there for worry?

End. A verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "With various transformations of infinite bodies, as numerous as the atoms of all worlds, desiring to fully comprehend that they arise from the mind—the Bodhisattva thereby first resolves his mind."
He was sovereign and unimpeded, transcending the ancients and surpassing his peers. Thorns were transformed into rows of trees, and the cries of owls and jackals became the Brahma-wheel.

The *Biographies of Eminent Monks* records that Shi Zhitong said: "As for those who seek the Mahāyāna and cultivate right contemplation, they examine the ultimate limit of the subtle atom and recognize the primordial source of a single thought-moment; thus, they may take thorns to chant upon the impermanence [of all things]."
As for sounds, even the cries of owls and manticores preach the most profound Dharma; it is not certain that the pure lands of the ten directions surpass this.

Generally speaking, when one speaks of the "pure land of the mind-only," then one being pure means all are pure; it can be said that within the very dust and toil of worldly afflictions, one accomplishes the Buddha-land.
The tip of a hair seems to contain a precious moon.
Pang Jushi’s verse says: "Within the tip of a hair, a precious moon is contained; one sees the true source to the very bottom.
It is like a golden body appearing within lapis lazuli.
A verse from the Lotus Sūtra says: "Like a pure lapis lazuli vessel, within which the image of true gold appears.
To expound this doctrine and bring forth wondrous wisdom is to strip away the marrow and bones of the Mahāyāna and to extract the very root and stem of the udumbara flower.

Mahāyāna is the mind of the Great Vehicle. The Udumbara flower is a miraculous and auspicious flower; it symbolizes that when this mind is expounded, it is difficult to encounter and difficult to understand.

Even if one were to gather the brushes of Mount Sumeru, not even a hair’s breadth could be written; and though one possessed the gate of eloquent exposition, it would be difficult to unfold even a single verse.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Even if one were to take Mount Sumeru and grind it into a single brush, it would not suffice to write even a single sentence or a single verse of the *Puyan Jing* (Universal Eye Sūtra).
It seals both the identical and the different; it dissolves the distinction between the center and the periphery; it equalizes coming and going; and it transcends the partial and the perfect."

The essence of one's own mind is not subject to views of identity or difference, center or periphery; it is like the great void of space, devoid of any distinct characteristics. Therefore, a sutra states:
"The Bodhisattva knows that all phenomena are the very nature of the mind itself; they accomplish the body of wisdom without depending on another for awakening.
Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* says: "Next, as for the essential characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*), all ordinary beings..."
Indeed, the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and buddhas neither increase nor decrease; they are not born in the past limit, nor do they perish in the future limit.
They are ultimately eternal and constant. Since beginningless time, their original nature has been fully endowed with all merits, namely:
the sense of possessing the great light of intrinsic wisdom, the sense of universally illuminating the dharma-realm, and the sense of true and authentic cognitive awareness.
The meaning of the intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*); the meaning of permanence, bliss, self, and purity;
the meaning of coolness, immutability, and sovereignty.

Regarding "the waters flow eastward," it is like the *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) which says: "The Yangtze and Han rivers flow toward the sea as their sovereign. "Sovereign" (*zong*) means honorable or revered. It is similar to this.
In the morning, it is as if the mind is the sovereign of all phenomena; there is not a single phenomenon that does not return to the mind.
Regarding the stars bowing to the North, the *Analects* states: "The Master said: 'To govern by means of virtue is like the Northern Dipper (Beichen).
It dwells in its place, and the myriad stars bow toward it. To govern by means of virtue refers to the virtue of non-action (*wuwei*), just as the Northern Dipper does not [move]."
They shift, yet the myriad stars revolve around them as if with a single unmoving mind;

all practices converge upon it, like a valley cradling the wind or the ocean receiving the rivers—all this is *dharmatā*, thusness, the natural state of the nature of the Way (*mārga*). As the *Ratnakośa-śāstra* says: "The wind in the valley never ceases."
A spring never runs dry; this is also compared to the nature of the Way (mārga), which is without interruption. Thus, the Way is not separate from the mind, and the mind is not separate from the Way.
Therefore, the former masters said: "That which is supremely wondrous and spiritually penetrating is designated as the Way. Furthermore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says:
Your spiritual mind is all-enlightened; is this not the True Way?
It is tranquil and soundless, yet the myriad echoes and clamors roar across the earth. It is vast and signless, yet wondrous forms and strange shapes reach toward the heavens.
Thus, appearance is non-appearance, and non-appearance is appearance, because this is the realm of the one mind.

As described in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, the realms are layered upon one another and the Buddha-bodies are inexhaustible; they mutually penetrate each other, being both identical and distinct, entirely different and entirely the same.
Pure and impure lands are without obstruction or hindrance, regardless of the distinction between sentient and insentient beings.
All are the realm of the true wisdom of the single mind.

To distinguish them according to principle and to speak in accordance with reality: honey is uniformly as sweet as all that is sweet within the seas; fire is equally as hot as all that is hot throughout the world.
One drop of honey is sweet; all the honey throughout the world is sweet. One fire is hot; all the fires within the realm are hot.
This is an analogy for the fact that if this single dharma is the mind, then all dharmas of the mundane and supramundane worlds are likewise the mind.
This is the manifestation of the state of correct realization, established by means of the *dharmatā*.
This "Treatise on the Mind" contains two contemplations: first, the contemplation of mind-only (*cittamātra*); second, the contemplation of the reality of *tathatā*.
One first contemplates mind-only and subsequently enters *tathatā*. As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The noble wisdom of self-realization causes one to awaken to one's own mind."
[The *Śrāvakabhūmi*] says: "To realize that [objects] are merely mental verbal discriminations (*manojalpa-vikalpa*) and that no real dharmas exist is the skillful means for entering Vijñaptimātra.
By not grasping at external signs, one enters Mind-only. The *Sūtra on Examining the Grounds of Practice* (*Sīkṣānanda-samādhi-sūtra*) states: "First is the contemplation of mind-only consciousness;

second is the contemplation of the reality of True Suchness (*tathatā*). The contemplation of mind-only is shallow; the contemplation of True Suchness is deep, as it is able to enter the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*)."
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is a synonym for suchness (*tathatā*). As the *Awakening of Faith* states:

"If the mind wanders and scatters, one should immediately draw it back and cause it to abide in right mindfulness (*samyak-smṛti*). Regarding this right mindfulness, one should know that it is 'mind-only' (*cittamātra*), with no external objects.

This is the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). It continues: "Furthermore, this very mind also lacks intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); it cannot be apprehended in any single moment of thought."

This is precisely the true contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*). If one realizes that there is only mind, one accomplishes the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*). If one realizes the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one accomplishes the true contemplation of suchness.
When both mind and object have vanished, one then accomplishes non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).
Not engaging in activity yet not losing one's essential nature; it is neither one nor many. Not maintaining a fixed self yet responding to conditions;

it is both identical and distinct. As previously stated regarding the "manifestation of the position of correctness": there has never been a single dharma that transcends the correct position of the mind.

As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "This dharma abides in the station of dharmas; the characteristics of the world are eternally constant. Furthermore, as previously mentioned, this is the *dharmatā*.
Regarding "provisional designation," the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "There has never been a single dharma that arises apart from the nature of dharmas (*dharmatā*).

True Suchness (*tathatā*) and the one mind do not maintain their own inherent nature; they establish themselves in accordance with phenomena. Therefore, it is said that they are both identical and distinct.
Although they establish themselves in accordance with phenomena, they do not lose their own essence; therefore, it is said that they are neither one nor many."
The fundamental and the derivative are presented together;

the provisional and the ultimate coexist. The *Treatise by Zhaolun* states: "Without the fundamental, there would be no way to manifest the derivative; without the derivative, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental. Although the fundamental and the derivative differ,"
The inconceivable is one. The mind is the root; phenomena are the branches.
Within these words, the essential framework is fully presented; by pointing downward, the source is entirely revealed.
Although the myriad dharmas differ, they are all encompassed within a single word; although the thousand moons are not the same, each reveals its source with a single finger.
As the *Jin'guan* says: "Within each and every phenomenon, there is fully present such inexhaustible virtue."

It is like a single drop of the ocean, which already contains all its rivers; yet each individual phenomenon does not destroy its original characteristics nor depart from its original position, while being perfectly interfused and entering into one another.
Thus, if one wishes to speak of its characteristics and functions, they are identical with its essential stillness; if one wishes to call it stillness, [it is not separate from its functioning].
The interplay of characteristics and functions is manifold; thus, the Preface to the *Huayan* Commentary states: "It transcends words and thought and stands far apart.

It not only transcends words and thought, but also emerges from that very transcendence of words and thought. Both the transcendent and the non-transcendent emerge together. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
Although one does not rely on the path of language, nor does one cling to wordlessness;
yet, by the very cessation of speech and the forgetting of thought, one accords with the principle of transcendence.

Just as a single piece of gold takes on the forms of various vessels, so too is the principle of the Way that remains unchanged while following conditions; like a thousand waves containing the nature of moisture, such is the gate of following conditions without changing.
Gold is unchanging; the vessel is that which follows conditions. Waves follow conditions; moisture is unchanging. Thus, the gateway of the One Mind possesses both meanings:
following conditions and being unchanging. As the *Yanyi ji* states: "Because following conditions is itself unchanging, one negates the distinctions so that the essence is realized as empty;
this is the quiescence of the derivative. Because the essence is empty, distinctions are negated... [The text continues with the negation of the primary].
Transformation follows conditions; therefore, the fundamental is quiescent. Because the fundamental is taken as the derivative, the fundamental becomes hidden;
because the derivative is taken as the fundamental, the derivative vanishes. Thus, when True Suchness follows conditions to become sentient beings, it never loses its true essence;
this causes sentient beings to be non-sentient beings. The emptiness of the essence of sentient beings is the Dharmakāya.
At that time, there has never been a time when sentient beings did not exist; therefore, the Dharma-body is not a non-Dharma-body. Thus, the two pairs are both transcended.
Since these two are mutually transcended, truth and delusion are equal, with nothing to distinguish them.
If one attains this tenet, there is neither "being present" nor "not being present.

The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha teaches that all dharmas are neither present nor not present. This is because, in terms of the reality of principle (*li*), they are hidden and thus said to be "not present";
in terms of the appearance of phenomena (*xiang*), they manifest and thus said to be "not not present. This is precisely the concealment and manifestation of the single mind.
It is unimpeded and sovereign.
Entering the body of a sage, it is not exalted; dwelling in the body of an ordinary person, it does not change. Taking the narrow as broad, the tip of a hair extends throughout the ten directions.
Subsuming the long within the short, a single instant encompasses an ocean of kalpas.
The former masters said: "Dust contains the Dharma-realm; its magnitude is neither diminished nor increased. A single thought encompasses nine aeons; extension and contraction are simultaneous.
This is precisely the opening and closing of the one mind, manifesting its supreme excellence. It is like the morning mushroom, which perishes at evening."
How could this compare to the lifespan of the Great Chūn tree? This is merely the perception of extension and brevity among worldly beings.
As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies, when the Rishi Vimala took Sudhana by the hand, many kalpas passed while they traveled through boundless realms;
therefore, it cannot be conceived in terms of long or short durations. If one manifests supreme transcendence, one may achieve sudden and perfect realization in a single lifetime. If...
Regarding its profound depth, it cannot be fathomed even over many kalpas; one must not dogmatically fix upon its duration as either long or short. What is valued is entry into the mystery;
thus, those of provisional capacity and shallow learning cannot fathom its boundaries. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"From a single thought-moment until the completion of a kalpa, all arise in dependence upon the thoughts and perceptions of sentient beings. The oceans of lands and the kalpas are all boundless; by means of a single direction..."
"Then all are purified. The commentary explains: "The single skillful means is one's own mind. Extension and contraction depend on the mind as the standard of measure.
If one realizes the single mind, kalpas—whether long or short—are naturally exhausted; therefore, it is said that 'all are purified. A verse from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
'All kalpas, whether numbered or unnumbered, the Bodhisattva knows to be but a single thought-moment. In this regard, he is skilled..."
Entering the conduct of enlightenment, one constantly and diligently practices without regressing.
When a single leaf falls, autumn comes to the world; where a single speck of dust rises, the vast earth withdraws its support. Thus, one passes the imperial examination at the Gate of Emptiness.
Master Pang’s verse says: The ten directions gather together as one; Each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
With an empty mind, one returns having passed the imperial examination.
In the garden of dhyāna, one is enfeoffed as a marquis.
In the world, one is enfeoffed for achieving success and establishing virtue; in the supramundane, one is enfeoffed for awakening the mind and attaining the records of realization.
It is the armor against the army of birth and death; it is the spear and halberd against the ranks of the afflictions.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Wei-shi shu) states: "If there are phenomena external to the mind, the cycle of birth and death continues; if there are no phenomena external to the mind, birth and death are forever severed."
One attains the Great Dhāraṇī, which can serve as the foundation for transcending the mundane world.
The mind is the central court of this dhāraṇī; there is no dharma that it does not encompass.
It possesses the sovereign samādhi and is fit to be the gateway for entering the Way.
To be able to contemplate the nature of the mind is called the supreme concentration (*samādhi*).
This mind is the *tathatā-samādhi*, the root of all concentrations; therefore, the mind is the king of concentrations, termed the "King Samādhi.

Thus, by awakening to the mind, one accomplishes the Way, and the myriad practices are simultaneously perfected. Now, if one realizes that the mind itself is Buddha, one naturally becomes humble. Why is this?
Therefore, by trusting in one's own mind, one knows that all sentient beings possess a mind and that they are all, without exception, Buddhas.
Because one knows that the single mind is equal, one neither indulges in self-conceit nor treats others with contempt. As a sutra says:
"The practice of gentleness accords with the Dharma-realm; humility is the root of patience. The *Book of Changes* (*Zhou Yi*) states: "Humility brings success."
"The noble person has a successful conclusion. The Tuan says: "Qian brings success. The Way of Heaven descends to provide succor and is thus luminous;
the Way of Earth is humble and thus ascends. The Way of Heaven diminishes the full and augments the humble. The Way of Earth transforms the full and flows toward the humble.

Ghosts and spirits harm the full and bless the humble. The way of humanity detests the full and loves the humble. Therefore, with respect to both self and others, there is no cause for praise [of pride]."
Not to disparage others is not [the mark of a great man]. To praise oneself is the characteristic of one who is self-aggrandizing and deludes others;
to disparage oneself is the mark of a deceitful and sycophantic person; to disparage others is the mark of a slanderous and treacherous person; and to praise others is the mark of a flatterer.
Therefore, Master Fu said: "Whether seeing good or seeing evil, simply lower your head; such conditions will lead to the development of illness.
Thus we know that when the ground is attained, all things are born; when the principle is attained, all practices are perfected. This is the principle of Mind-Only.
It must not be forgotten. Until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is neither increase nor decrease.
It is the model for the patriarchs of learning, the archetype of Bodhi, a forest of merit, and a treasury of True Suchness (Tathatā).
The eighth consciousness of all sentient beings is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness) and is also termed the "dwelling consciousness.

As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas know that skillful means for teaching the Dharma and manifesting *nirvāṇa* in order to deliver sentient beings are all established by the mind's conceptualization; they are neither delusions nor..."

It is deceptive. Why? Because the Bodhisattva understands that all phenomena are equal throughout the three periods of time, unshakable like suchness, and non-abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
He does not perceive even a single sentient being who has been transformed, is being transformed, or will be transformed;
nor does he himself perceive anything to be practiced. There is not the slightest phenomenon that arises or ceases.
That which can be attained relies upon all dharmas, causing one's vows not to be in vain; this is the ninth dwelling in accordance with reality.
Transverse and vertical illusory phenomena merge into emptiness within a single nature; the quiescent and numinous void manifests its signs by relying upon a thousand gateways.
The single nature is the nature of all phenomena; the thousand gates are the characteristics of all phenomena. Nature and characteristic are divided into two, yet when fused, they return to one.
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Buddha-nature is called the emptiness of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
The emptiness of the ultimate meaning is called wisdom. These two are non-dual; this constitutes Buddha-nature. Thus, the emptiness of the ultimate meaning is...
Buddha-nature is called wisdom; it is the characteristic of Buddha-nature. The ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) does not reside in wisdom, but is merely termed "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*).
Because it resides in wisdom, it is named "Buddha-nature. If one follows the nature through its characteristics, then only sentient beings possess Buddha-nature, because they possess wisdom.
Walls, tiles, and rubble lack wisdom; therefore, they have no Buddha-nature.

Regarding nature (*dhātu*): if one follows from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) to nature, then since the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is omnipresent, walls and such are all the emptiness of the ultimate truth;
how then could they not be nature? Therefore, a sūtra says: "Know that all phenomena are the very self-nature of the mind. A treatise says:
"Because the nature of form (*rūpa*) is the nature of wisdom (*jñāna*), the essence of form is formless and is called the body of wisdom (*jñānakāya*). Because...
Because the nature of wisdom is itself form, it is said that the Dharma-body pervades all places; its essence is fundamentally uniform.
Now, by distinguishing between its nature and its characteristics, two aspects are differentiated.

The wondrous traces are peerless; within the world, nothing is more intimate than this, for throughout the realm of heaven and earth, nothing surpasses the mind. This is because all phenomena arise from the mind;
apart from the mind, not a single phenomenon exists. Thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "Because all jewels arise from the pāramitās..."
Namely: canopies of all flower curtains produced from the pure understanding of the realm of all Buddhas;
all garments produced from the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); and all nets of bells produced from the unimpeded mind that enters the vajra-dharma.
All solid fragrances produced by the mind that realizes all phenomena are like illusions;
all exquisite jewel thrones of the Buddhas produced by the mind that pervades all Buddha-realms;
all jeweled banners produced by the tireless mind that makes offerings to the Buddhas; and the Buddhas produced by the joyful mind that realizes all phenomena are like dreams.
All the jewel palaces where they dwell; all the clouds of jewel lotuses produced by roots of goodness free from attachment;
and boundless exquisite delicacies emerging from small vessels.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: There was a laywoman named Paripūrṇā who attained the bodhisattva liberation door of the "Inexhaustible Treasury of Merit.

She was able to produce various delicious foods and drinks within a small vessel according to the diverse desires and inclinations of sentient beings, filling them all completely. With this small vessel, she could likewise satisfy the gods among the devas.
He provided food, even to humans, satisfying them with human sustenance, as well as to all the Buddhas, śrāvakas, arhats, and those throughout the realm of hungry ghosts.
Then he said, "Good son, wait but a moment; you shall see for yourself. As he spoke these words—
Sudhana then saw immeasurable sentient beings entering through the four gates; all had been invited by the original vows of the laywoman (upāsikā).
Once they had assembled, she prepared seats for them to sit upon and provided them with food and drink according to their needs, until all were fully satisfied.
As for those [who received] from small vessels, these were the vessels of the mind; the mind is an inexhaustible treasury that provides according to one's thoughts.
This Dharma-gate gives birth to all mundane and supramundane treasures; how could it ever come to an end?

Like looking up at the sky as it rains down unfathomable and extraordinary jewels, the wise layman (Upāsaka) in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "I have attained the liberation of the treasury of merit that gives birth [to wealth] according to one's wishes."

The Gate of Liberation. Whatever was required, all their wishes were fulfilled—namely, clothing, necklaces, elephants, horses, carriages, flowers, incense, banners, parasols, food, drink, medicinal decoctions, and so forth.

At that time, the householder, knowing that the assembly had gathered everywhere, focused his mind for a moment and looked up into the void; then, whatever was required descended from the sky, one by one.
The entire assembly was universally and completely satisfied. Thereafter, he preached various dharmas for them;
that is to say, for those who had been fully satiated by obtaining excellent food, he taught various practices for accumulating merit and so forth. The commentary states:

Regarding the objects raining from the sky, first, they emerged from within the minds of the householders; therefore it is said they were produced according to their wishes. It is also said [they appeared] in an instant.

Fixing the mind. Second, it is that which manifests through the resonance of the minds of those beings to be converted; the capacity of the stimulus and the response are in dark harmony, being neither one nor different.
To accomplish this matter, "gazing up at empty space" means that it appears within the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
Thus, the *Dharmapada-sūtra* says: "Within ultimate emptiness, the Bodhisattva establishes [the teachings] with fervent vigor."
When the rishi grasped his hand, time passed for aeons as numerous as motes of dust.
As described in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, when the rishi Vimala grasped Sudhana’s hand,
Sudhana immediately saw himself traveling to worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields in the ten directions, reaching those ten buddha-fields.
At the abodes of Buddhas as numerous as atoms, he beheld those Buddha-fields and their assemblies, as well as the various adornments of the marks and signs of those Buddhas;
this continued even for as many eons as there are atoms in hundreds of thousands of billions of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Finally, when that seer released Sudhana’s hand, the youth Sudhana immediately saw his own body.

It returns to its original place. Thus we know that while remaining unmoved from its fundamental station, the body pervades the ten directions without departing from a single thought-moment, even as time passes through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust.
An ancient commentator said: "When Sudhana follows the distinctions of phenomena, he enters the Dharma-realm;
yet in the gate of perfect interfusion (*yuanrong*), raising a single gate immediately fuses all gates. Nevertheless, by means of principle fusing phenomena, it causes..."

The phenomenon conforms to the principle, and the principle manifests the phenomenon, causing the principle to conform to the phenomenon; therefore, it is said that the principle is not without parts.

This means that the principle is identical to the phenomenon. Since the phenomenon has parts, the principle also has parts. Were it otherwise, the true principle would not be identical to the phenomenon.
Since the principle conforms to the phenomenon, if one raises a single dharma, it is the single Dharma-realm; if one raises many dharmas, they are the manifold Dharma-realms.
As Sudhana personally realized, by merely grasping [the Bodhisattva’s] hand for a moment, many kalpas passed; this clarifies the perfect interfusion of all time.
