Subsequently, he entered the pavilion and saw the infinite everywhere; this clarifies the perfect interfusion of all places.
Thus, that Sudhana was able to accomplish the practices of many kalpas within a single lifetime was due to the power of the spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra); in an instant, there may even be a Buddha.

As for what has been seen in the sūtras—practicing for as many eons as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—how could one attain [enlightenment] in a single lifetime without passing through many eons?

It is because the power of the rishi grants mastery over the duration [of time], just as when King Qi of the world encountered the rishi during a game of chess and caused the axe-handle to rot away. Even three lifetimes are considered but a single meal; since this is so, how much more so for that which is extended?
The short can also be made long, as when King Mu of Zhou followed a phantom man; though many years passed, in reality it was but a moment.
Therefore, the conclusion states: one should not determine the ultimate meaning based on the duration of time, whether long or short, nor on the extent of space, whether broad or narrow.
On the day the youth ascended the tower, he suddenly beheld his past causes;
that is, when the youth Sudhana ascended Maitreya’s pavilion, he saw the events of Maitreya’s three lifetimes.
Although the Perfect Way has been fully realized and manifested, its broad propagation depends entirely upon the person.

It is the person who can propagate the Way; it is not the Way that propagates the person. All Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time have all attained Buddhahood by awakening the mind.
Mind is itself the Dharma, and the Dharma is itself the mind. Therefore, it is through the faith of the person that one is able to propagate it.
Furthermore, the person is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the person. Apart from the person there is no Dharma; apart from the Dharma there is no person. Therefore it is said:
"This Dharma was already taught by previous Buddhas; subsequent Buddhas have followed it accordingly without adding a single word.
Thus it is said that the Buddha takes the Dharma as his teacher. As the Duke of Yan, Zhang Yue, asked the Good Knowledge of South of the Water: "The Dharma comes first."
[The opponent asks: "Is the Buddha prior, or is the Dharma prior? He replies: "The Dharma is prior, for that which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma.

Thereupon, he is challenged: "If that is so, then regarding the first Buddha to attain enlightenment, since there was no preceding Buddha to teach him, by what means did he awaken to the Dharma? He replies: [as follows].

Awakening occurs spontaneously. It is like the otter offering sacrifice to Heaven during the *Yueling* (Monthly Ordinances); how could there be anyone instructing it? Lord Yan was profoundly submissive;

his extraordinary merit alerted the world, and his great function penetrated the divine. Music harbors wondrous tones; when the fingers strike the sublime notes, the *gong* and *shang* pitches accord with the rhythm. The mind—
Possessing the nature of awakening, one employs wisdom and skill to move in accordance with the profound truth.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "For example, though lutes, harps, *konghou*, and *pipa* lutes possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skilled fingers, they can never produce music.
You and all sentient beings are likewise so; each possesses the precious, awakened true mind."
Each is fully perfected. Just as when I press my finger, the Sea-Seal (Sāgaramudrā) emits light, yet when you briefly raise your mind, afflictions (*kleśa*) arise first;
this shows that because your finger is not skillful, the five notes are not produced, and because your wisdom is not clever, the single mind does not manifest.

Thus, the Tripitaka Teaching is a clumsy means of deliverance, while the Shared Teaching is a skillful means of deliverance. Furthermore, one need only realize the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena; there is no need for...
To practice with diligent effort is called skillful deliverance.
The merit of the Ten Powers is sublime; only the most eminent sages can tread this path. The sun and moon conceal their radiance; the mountains and rivers turn back in retreat.
Master Pang’s verse says: “The kalpa-fire blazes, yet the heavens do not grow hot; The gale-force winds blow, yet no sound is heard.
A hundred rivers compete to flow, yet the sea does not overflow; The Five Peaks and famous mountains show no form. In pure clarity and tranquil contemplation, there is no trace;
The thousand paths all enter together into non-arising. Thus we know that there is not a single dharma that does not enter the One Mind.”
The principle of non-arising crushes the peaks of pride and dries up the river of craving; it tears down the city of doubt and severs the snares of Māra.
If one realizes the single mind and awakens to the truth of the emptiness of phenomena, one enters the realm of equality and dwells in the gate of the true mark; only then can one...
They topple the mountain of pride, pull out the arrows of craving, tear asunder the net of doubt, and break through the encirclement of Māra. Why is this?
Because they realize that the realm of Māra is itself the realm of the Buddha, having returned to the single, true mind. As a metaphor in the treatise states:
"For example, a fly can alight upon all things, yet it alone cannot alight upon a flame; for if it were to alight upon a flame, it would be burned. Māra is likewise [incapable].
They take all phenomena as their object, yet they alone cannot take the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena as their object. If one enters the true nature, then Māra is itself the true nature;
what, then, could cause delusion? Therefore, the Treatise says: "The suchness of the realm of Māra is the suchness of the realm of the Buddha; it is a single suchness, not two suchnesses."
All are the seal of the *dharmadhātu*. How could the seal of the *dharmadhātu* further destroy the seal of the *dharmadhātu*? Furthermore, the treatise states:
"The Bodhisattva who has severed views and understandings is like a fisherman who sees a great fish enter deep waters beyond the reach of hooks and nets;
he then falls into despair and sorrow because it has escaped the net of the sixty-two views."

When one is enlightened, the Dharma is present within every phenomenon; even a massive mountain may be moved. When one is ignorant, every matter follows after others; not even a hair’s breadth can be discerned.

The *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) says: "The enlightened person’s virtue flourishes in this very day; the ignorant person’s hope is cut off for many lifetimes. Furthermore:
The Treatise of Master Li states: "Those who are deluded practice in vain through kalpas; those who awaken realize the inherent stillness of the essence itself.
Both are but the single mind; it is through delusion and awakening that these gains and losses arise."
The Dharma is neither difficult nor easy; transformation depends upon the person.
When deluded, the person pursues the Dharma; when awakened, the Dharma follows the person. When deluded, one clings to the mind as being the objective realm and is turned about by that realm.
When awakened, one realizes that the realm is none other than the mind, and everything is governed by oneself.
It hastens many lifetimes into a single thought-moment and transforms a cold valley into a fragrant spring.
To realize the Truth in a single thought-moment is a merit that surpasses that of countless kalpas; it is like a cold valley encountering spring, where sprouts suddenly burst forth.

Thus, the *Huayan lun* (Treatise on the Avataṃsaka) says: "It is not as good as a single thought-moment of dependent origination and non-arising, which transcends the provisional views of those who study the three vehicles."

As the *Huayan Cailin Wen* asks: "In achieving success and establishing virtue, the cultivation of the Three Teachings is the same. Why then does this sutra praise 'effortless action' (*anābhoga*)? Answer:
When one accumulates practices through conditioned cultivation, it is said that one establishes merit. However, when reaching the ultimate and realizing the true essence, one must forget all effort.
Effortlessness is itself merit; its flow extends to the limits of the future. This function of non-function pervades the ten directions. There is no... [text ends]

The function of function is called true function. It is like boarding a ship to enter the sea: if one suddenly ceases the use of the oar and pole and raises the sail to follow the wind, ten thousand *li* are not far away.
When the practice of effort and function ceases, this is the stopping of the oar and pole; when signless wisdom is perfected, it is like the brocade sail being raised high.
Being without dependence and without dwelling, once there is no longer effortful function, one abides within the flow of the Dharma and wanders eternally in wisdom.
Master Hai held fast to the great compass to illuminate the obscure gates; the essential meaning was brilliantly revealed. He steered a swift vessel across the deep river;
in an instant, he ascended to the Truth.
If one directly realizes the single mind, bodhi is easily attained; it is like boarding a carriage and arriving at a distant land, or stepping onto a boat and reaching a thousand li away.
This is the essential method for being born into the family of the Tathāgata.
If one acts with the mind directed toward external phenomena, one is born into a worldly family; if one realizes that the mind is itself the Buddha, one is born into the family of the Tathāgata.
This single dharma of the One Mind is the fundamental lineage of all Buddhas; whether in speech or silence, in contraction or expansion, it always accords with the Way of the Single Truth.
In managing one's livelihood and engaging in worldly occupations, one does not contravene the gateway of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
In every movement and application, moment by moment, one does not depart from the *dharmadhātu*. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, at every step one is constantly within it.
For those who do not believe, [the truth] is as if a thousand li away even when face-to-face. As the poem of Han Shan says: "That precious, natural thing is solitary and has no companion."
It is compressed within the space of a square inch, yet extended throughout all places. If you do not believe and accept this, though we meet, we shall not truly encounter one another.
For those who are clear-sighted and discerning, they attend to things with every glance and are able to perceive them beforehand; as for those who have not yet met [this truth], it is otherwise.
One can know this through one's actions; every movement and deed is never interrupted. For example, Cai Shun, whose courtesy name was Junzhong, lost his father while young and raised his mother.
Once, he went out to gather firewood when a guest suddenly arrived. His mother, seeing that Shun had not yet returned, bit her finger.
Shun’s heart immediately stirred, and he abandoned his wood to rush home. Kneeling, he asked the reason for his mother’s distress. She said, "I have an urgent visitor."
"Come! I shall bite my finger to awaken you. Furthermore, during the Tang dynasty, Pei Jingyi’s father was executed by the Censor-in-Chief for King Chen.
At that time, Jingyi was in the city; he suddenly felt his tears flow and ceased eating.
He said to others, "Whenever my father had pain anywhere, I immediately felt uneasy. Today my heart aches, and my hands and feet have all failed me. The matter is at hand."

Cè then returned home to visit his father, only to find that he had indeed already passed away. Furthermore, there was Zhì'ān of the Tang dynasty, who was renowned for his filial piety in his village.
He was appointed as a village head (*lǐyīn*) and was serving in the county when he suddenly announced that his mother was critically ill.

When the magistrate questioned him, Zhì'ān said, "My mother is ill; I am also ill. I have just been afflicted with a pain in my heart, and by this I know that my mother is ill. The magistrate, because of this—

He dispatched an official to verify this, and it was indeed as he had described. Subsequently, the Emperor issued a proclamation to honor his gatehouse and promoted him to the rank of Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary (Sanqi Changshi).
This was due to the causes accumulated from practicing the path of the Bodhisattva.

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "If there are those who have not yet heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, you should know that these persons have not yet skillfully practiced the bodhisattva path.
If there are those who do hear this sutra, they will then be able to skillfully practice the bodhisattva path.
Furthermore, the myriad practices cultivated by bodhisattvas all arise from the unchanging nature of the true mind, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
Regarding merit: as stated in the *Awakening of Faith*, "Furthermore, based on verbal designations and conceptual discrimination, there are two meanings of True Suchness (tathatā).
What are these two? First, it is 'emptiness according to reality,' because it can ultimately manifest the reality.
Second, it is 'non-emptiness according to reality,' because it possesses its own essence, which is fully endowed with the nature of untainted meritorious qualities. (*Huayan ji*)
It is said: The intrinsically pure mind (*prakṛti-viśuddha-citta*), when not conjoined with delusion, is termed "empty. Its nature, which is replete with myriad virtues, is termed "not empty.
If one is separated from the deluded mind, there is truly nothing that can be called empty; thus, the treasury of emptiness is revealed through delusion.

The essence of the treasury of non-emptiness (Amogha-garbha) is manifested as non-empty only through the overturning of defilements. For example: the virtue of generosity (dāna) that is inherently present is now obscured by stinginess;

the virtue of ethical discipline (śīla) that is inherently present follows after the five desires; the tranquil concentration (samādhi) that is inherently present is now occupied by distracted thoughts;
and the great wisdom (prajñā) that is inherently present is now clouded by ignorance. Thus, stinginess conceals generosity, and so on, until ignorance conceals wisdom. Therefore...
The Treatise says: Because one knows that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is free from stinginess and greed, one practices the *dānapāramitā* and other perfections in accordance with it;

all ten thousand practices are likewise so. Therefore, there is the meaning of the originally existent, true cognitive awareness. It says: "If the mind has movement, it is not true cognitive awareness.
This clarifies that the movement of the deluded mind conceals True Suchness (*tathatā*). Thus, the emptiness within the very midst of delusion conceals [the truth].
This is because emptiness possesses the myriad virtues. Thus, a sutra says: "Knowing that delusion is fundamentally true, one sees the Buddha as pure.
Because it can ultimately manifest reality, it is called "emptiness. Therefore, know that the treasury of emptiness is able to store that which is not empty;
since the container is empty, it reveals that the treasury of non-emptiness is primordially possessed. Furthermore, the conduct of Samantabhadra traverses and enters the ten directions.

Briefly, there are ten gates: First, entering the world of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*). This is because one enters directly into the dependent origination of the *dharmadhātu*. Second, entering the realm of sentient beings (*sattvadhātu*).

This is because the realm of sentient beings and the Buddha-realm are non-dual in essence. Third, making offerings. This is because every single offering implement accords with the truth. Fourth, clarifying the request for the Dharma.
This is because the wisdom that exhausts the *dharmadhātu* never fails to request the Buddhas at any time, and never fails to... [request the Dharma].

1. Because of raining down the Dharma, the five great wisdoms encompass and give rise to all beings; they thoroughly understand the delusions of birth, yet there are no sentient beings, for they do not obstruct transformation.
2. Sixth is the manifestation of supernormal powers: throughout the dust-motes and lands of the ten directions, they enter one another in infinite layers;

they shake the earth and manifest signs without ceasing. 3. Seventh is the eternally quiescent concentration: never for a single thought-moment is there any stirring or movement. 4. Eighth is the vast production of mindfulness...
This is because one contemplates that all realms appear from every pore without end. Ninth is the teaching of the Dharma:

in every thought-moment, there is a constant rain of boundless Dharma, raining upon all beings. Tenth is the general summary: the nine preceding meanings encompass the whole by citing a single part, for there is no sequence of before or after.
Though there be ten thousand distinctions and a thousand variations, none transcend the nature of empty space. Whether noble or lowly, high or base, none can escape the ford of equality.
The nature of all phenomena is precisely the mind-nature of sentient beings; the mind-nature of sentient beings is precisely the nature of empty space.
Question: Truth and falsehood are as contrary as water and fire; how can these two interpenetrate? Answer:

Because the two dharmas of truth and falsehood are of one and the same mind, they are able to interpenetrate. It is like the case of Yan Ruduo, who, because he was mad, lost his head and then regained his original mind.
His head had never actually been lost; even when he was mad, his head was not lost. This is due to his deluded state of mind.

As soon as it ceases, it ceases; this cessation is itself bodhi. This intrinsically pure and luminous mind is not obtained from others. It is like being deluded regarding the truth and clinging to the false:
once that deluded state is awakened to, one immediately returns to the true mind. Even when one is in the midst of delusion, the truth is never lost.

He shears away delusions and trims away doubts, setting forth the ultimate truth and manifesting the orthodox path. Thus he causes the majesty of the Buddha-dharma to soar and the lineage of the school to flourish, like ten thousand reflections interlacing upon the autumn river.
Within the sutra’s elucidation of the ten similes, the first is the simile of a shadow. The first [aspect] illustrates that its substance is empty and lacks reality;
the second illustrates the meaning of having utility and being able to provide shelter and concealment. Thus, the *Huayan ji* states:

"Just as when a bright and pure object catches the radiance of the sun, a shadow appears upon the walls of a house, so too does the Tathāgata manifest a body in response to the capacities of beings. This is what is meant by the 'simile of the Tathāgata.'"
The bodies, trees, and other substances are used as metaphors for sentient beings. While the sun has no differentiated essence, the substances differ in ten thousand ways.

When the substance is tilted, the shadow is slanted; when the form is upright, the shadow is straight. The shadow does not appear within the sun itself; it merely manifests in myriad ways at the periphery of the substance.
According with the mind, myriad things appear like a thousand lamps in a cold room reflecting one another;
in a single room, the light of a thousand lamps interpenetrates. One mind encompasses ten thousand objects, and ten thousand objects are one mind—just as light is without [obstruction].
Obstruction.
Like a bird soaring through the air, or like a fish diving into the deep abyss to swim;
the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "If all is but mind alone, where does the world abide? Upon what do coming and going depend?"
Dharma. How is it so within the ground of vision? Just as a bird in the empty sky moves by means of the wind of the mind—neither dwelling nor observing—it likewise moves upon the earth.

In this way, all sentient beings move according to the activity of the discriminating mind, coming and going within their own minds like birds flying in the sky. Seeing these vessels of livelihood, the Buddha taught that the mind is thus. Therefore...
Know that when you lift your foot and set it down, you do not depart from your own mind.
If a bird were to leave the sky, how could it soar? If a fish were to leave the water, how could it float or dive?
Therefore, the Patriarch Micchaka asked the Patriarch Vasumitra, "From what direction have you come, and where will you go? He replied, "I come from my own mind; I go to nowhere."
In weeping and laughing, the Buddha-wisdom is distinct; in walking and sitting, the source of awakening is pure. The *Zhangzhe lun* (Treatise by the Elder) states:
"Without deviating from the present thought, the accumulation of merit is itself the Buddha. There is no phenomenon of temporal transition whatsoever;
the self-nature of the Arhat constantly turns the Wheel of Dharma. It further states: "Not even a speck of dust separates it from the ten directions; a single hair..."
How could this obstruct the ocean of lands? It is further said: "The three periods of time are a single thought-moment; past and present are entirely identical.
The inexhaustible kalpas of the past and future are simultaneous and unimpeded—this is the moment of attaining perfect enlightenment in a single thought.

The Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness enter the flow of the Dharma in every thought-moment, spontaneously reaching Buddhahood. The initial water and the subsequent water are of one and the same nature."
Therefore, because the Buddha as cause and the Buddha as fruit are of one nature, there is no beginning, middle, or end within them;

for they are not separated by even a single thought-moment. Because they rely upon the fundamental Dharma, there is no thought-moment that can create a separation. Thus, cause and effect reach their consummation in a single thought-moment of correspondence—a single Buddha.
This does not concern the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) nor supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); for these marks and powers arise from this very perfect enlightenment.

It is attained. If one realizes perfect enlightenment, one does not cling to any marks; yet because of being in accord with the path of awakening, the marks of supernatural powers and physical excellence arrive spontaneously without being sought.
Furthermore, it is said: because the world of sentient beings is itself the Dharma-realm; because the nature of sentient beings is itself inconceivable;
and because the conceptual discrimination of sentient beings is itself the wisdom of the Tathāgata. Moreover, it is the faculty of the Tathāgata.
Fundamental wisdom is the discriminative mind of sentient beings; because it accords with non-duality, it is sovereign within the dharma-realm.
This wondrous understanding belongs solely to me, the true self—the very lifeblood of the successive patriarchs.

This "Treatise on the Mind" speaks only of the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) and does not refer to deluded consciousness (*vikalpa-vijñāna*). This is because the true mind and the deluded mind each possess their own nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, the true mind takes luminous awareness and quiescent illumination as its mind; it takes non-emptiness and non-abiding as its essence (*svabhāva*), and the true mark (*bhūta-lakṣaṇa*) as its characteristic.

The deluded mind takes the reflected images conditioned by the six sense objects as its mind; it takes the absence of inherent nature as its essence, and clinging to conditions and discursive thought as its characteristic.
"Contemplation as a characteristic" refers to this deluded mind that contemplates, discerns, and cognizes objects; it has no independent substance of its own.

It is merely the sensory realm, existing in accordance with the presence or absence of objects. When an object comes, it arises; when the object departs, it ceases. Arising because of objects, the entire object is the mind;
furthermore, because the mind illuminates objects, the entire mind is the object. Each lacks self-nature; they are solely causes.
Therefore, the *Dharmapada* says: "The shimmering light has no water; it is merely vaporous heat. Within the shadows there is no form; it is merely a condition of air.
When the shimmering vapors of the hot season are scorched by the sunlight, they appear from afar to be water.
This arises solely from perception and is nothing but vaporous heat. These illusory forms and mind are likewise so: they have one's own karma as their cause."
With the external objects of the parents as conditions, they combine to produce what appears to be form and mind; it is merely a condition of vapor.

Thus, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* says: "One falsely identifies the reflected images conditioned by the six sense-objects as one's own mind-nature. Therefore, we know that this is the mind capable of deliberation.
If there were no causes and conditions, nothing would arise; it is only from conditions that things are born.

All phenomena born of conditions are impermanent, like a form in a mirror—lacking substance and entirely dependent on external objects—or like the moon in water—unreal yet appearing as a hollow reflection in the sky.
To take this for true is the height of folly. This is why Ānanda clung [to such views].
Yet there was no basis for this; he was at a loss in all seven places. When the Second Patriarch realized that [the mind] is unborn, a single word brought him into accord with the Way.
Thus, the Second Patriarch could not find this mind of restless conceptualization, and thereby knew that the true mind pervades all places.
Taking this realization as the fundamental principle, he was thus the first to succeed to the Patriarchal seat.

Because Ānanda had been led by the Tathāgata to shatter his deluded mind, [the Buddha] proceeded to interrogate him exhaustively on each and every detail regarding the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve spheres of perception (*dhātu*), the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the seven great natures (*prakṛti*).
Ultimately, these were found to be entirely empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); they arose neither from causes and conditions, nor from self, nor from others.
They exist through conjunction; furthermore, they do not arise spontaneously or without cause. All are but the conceptualization and discrimination of mental speech and consciousness.
Through this, one suddenly awakens to the wondrously luminous true mind, which is vast, all-encompassing, and pervasive in all places.
Then, together with the great assembly, one realizes this mind and praises the Buddha with a single voice, saying: "O Wondrous, Profound, Total-Mastery, Immovable Honored One. First...
The Śūraṅgama King is a rarity in the world; it eliminates my inverted conceptions of billions of kalpas, enabling me to attain the Dharmakāya without passing through the aeons of *saṃghī*.
This is identical to the First Patriarch’s direct pointing to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha. This single true mind is the very throat of all the successive patriarchs.
Penetrating the mind, one should not entertain further thoughts.
Regarding the nature and destiny of the multitude of sages, the *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta Sūtra* states: "That which is the profound meaning is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
That which is the ultimate truth is the realm of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*). That which is the realm of sentient beings is the Tathāgatagarbha. That which is the Tathāgatagarbha is..."
The Dharmakāya. The commentary states: Now, as for the mind, it is the gateway that upholds all dharmas and constitutes the true nature of all phenomena;
therefore, it is called the *paramārtha-satya* (ultimate truth). Because it gives rise to various and manifold mental conceptions, it is termed "sentient beings" (*sattva*).
This realm of the mind is itself the realm of sentient beings. Arising from the nature of *tathatā* (suchness), it is named the Tathāgata. It is without any deficiency whatsoever. Thus...
The eye is the treasury; because it can accumulate merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, it is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Therefore, the *Ratnarājasūtra* states: "In the very first moment of thought, one is fully endowed with the eighty-four thousand *pāramitās*.
Among all the constituent parts of the body, the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is supreme; among all the gateways of the Dharma, the mind is their sovereign."
Commentary on the Mind: Fascicle One;
Commentary on the Mind: Fascicle Two.
Composed by Chan Master Zhijue Yan-shou of Huiri Yongming Temple in Hangzhou, Song Dynasty.

Whether contrary or favorable, they converge in the same destination; whether walking or staying, one is never apart from them. Like the rain of jewels, the *maṇi* gem transcends intentional thought; like the sounding of the celestial drum, the teaching is impartial.

Both the *maṇi* gem and the celestial drum are devoid of effortful activity (*anābhoga*); their impartial accomplishment of tasks serves as a metaphor for the True Mind, whose quiescence and function are non-dual.
This is "stagnation. As the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source) states:

"The manifestation of the light of concentration through non-conceptual contemplation" refers to the white, pure jewel-net of the One Vehicle teaching—the precious pearl of the Ten-Thousand-Syllable Wheel-Turning King. The essential nature of this pearl is transparent and penetrating, illuminating the ten directions simultaneously.
It accomplishes its work without partiality, and all who contemplate it follow it. Although it manifests extraordinary powers, its mind is free of conceptual thought.
If a person enters this gate of great and wondrous *śamatha-vipaśyanā*, they are free from thought and deliberation, and things are accomplished spontaneously.
Like that precious jewel, it illuminates both near and far equally, appearing with vivid clarity, vast and transparent as space. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"At that time, a voice issued from a celestial drum, announcing: 'O sons of the gods, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas are not [limited] by this...'"

Having ended their lives, they were born in that realm. By means of their supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they cause all sentient beings to behold them according to what is appropriate to each being's mind.
O sons of the gods, just as I am now not seen by the eye yet am able to produce sound—just as it is said in the Preface to the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*:
"The perfect voice unfolds eternally without being struck; the ocean of fruition transcends thought while the mind..."
The tradition [holds that] one practices all myriad deeds simultaneously, forgetting both illumination and objectivity;

one enters both the gradual and the sudden without obstruction, where principle and phenomenon mutually support each other in their layered depth. Therein, essence and function are eternally present; within each and every thing, emptiness and form manifest together. It is eternally quiescent and eternally cognizant.
Principle is established through the mind; phenomena manifest from principle. The essence is merged with principle; function arises from phenomena.
Thus, the essence within function does not lose its nature, and the essence within function does not perish. Therefore, it is said that the essence is eternal and the function is eternal.

Furthermore, existence is created from the mind, and emptiness manifests from the mind. Because it is empty, it is eternally quiescent; because it exists, it is eternally cognizant. It is thus quiescence itself that is cognition.
Knowing does not lose its quiescence; it is knowing that is itself quiescence. Quiescence does not lose its knowing; therefore, it is called "ever-quiescent and ever-knowing. Thus it is said:
conditioned phenomena arise from the mind, and unconditioned phenomena manifest from the mind.
Welcomed, they do not come forward; followed, they do not lag behind. Subtler than a speck of dust, they are not non-existent; yet throughout the ten directions, what can be found?
Within the revolving *dhāraṇī*, one should always maintain the mind of a Great Being (*mahāsattva*).
The Lotus Sūtra says: "At that time, those who receive, uphold, read, and recite the Lotus Sūtra shall behold my body;
they will experience great joy and become even more diligent. Because they behold me, they immediately attain a samādhi called the *svādhiṣṭhāna-dhāraṇī* (the dhāraṇī of revolving).
There are hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of such revolving dhāraṇīs. This Lotus Sūtra is for this one great matter."
Appearing in the world through causes and conditions, [the Buddha] directly reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within the minds of sentient beings.
This "Buddha’s knowledge and vision" is precisely the true mind of all sentient beings. If one upholds this sutra, one is a Bodhisattva of Great Mind;
therefore, it is said that one should always maintain the mind of a Mahāsattva.
Within the Lion’s Roar Samādhi (*siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*), one does not fall into the hands of the two vehicles.

As for the Lion’s Roar Samādhi: this clarifies that the Tathāgata’s essence of function is none other than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and the function of that essence manifests as the myriad differences of dependent origination. Since both principle and phenomena are without obstruction, it is named "Lion."

Regarding the "lion’s roar" (*siṃha-vijṛmbhita*): as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, "At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing the thoughts in the minds of all the bodhisattvas, with great compassion as his foremost [quality], entered the samādhi of the lion’s roar.

At that moment, the assembly of bodhisattvas in the Jeta Grove all beheld everything throughout the entire dharma-realm and space-realm, including all buddha-fields, and even [the Buddhas] entering..."

The great supernormal transformations of the samādhi in which he dwells are without distinction; thus, he immediately realized them within the Jeta Grove, yet the śrāvakas and others neither knew nor saw them, being like the deaf and the blind.
When the single principle meets the point, the myriad phenomena are all harmonized. It encompasses the very depths of the source of wisdom and crowns the summit of the ocean of Dharma.

Having thoroughly realized the one mind, there is no matter that is not reached and no principle that is not penetrated. Encompassing the past and including the present, it gathers everything without exception.
As stated in the *Treasury of Jewels Treatise*, in the "Chapter on the Primordial Limit’s Profound Emptiness": The Sūtra says, "The Buddha-nature is equal and vast."
It is immeasurably great. Ordinary beings and sages are non-dual; all are perfectly complete.
It is fully present in grasses and trees, pervading even ants, down to the finest speck of dust and a single hair—there is nothing that does not contain this One within it.

Therefore, it is said: "If one can thoroughly understand the One, all matters are concluded. For this reason, all sentient beings are born by riding upon this One; thus, it is called the One Vehicle (Ekayāna). If...
Because of delusion, there is differentiation; because of awakening, there is unity. Thus it is said that the preceding thought is ordinary and the succeeding thought is sagely.
It is also said that in a single thought-moment one knows all dharmas. Therefore, the one is all, and all is the one.
Hence, we know that by knowing through the one, the function is perfected in the myriad phenomena. Thus the Sūtra says: "If all have a mind, they are deluded."
If all things were without mind, they would pervade the ten directions; thus, true oneness is ten thousand differences, and ten thousand differences are true oneness.
It is like the ocean surging with a thousand waves: the thousand waves are the ocean itself, and there is no difference between them at all.

Now, as for the term "one," it is used in contrast to the perception of difference. Since that perception is not different, "one" is also not one. Being neither one nor not one, it is a provisional designation.
True Oneness. Now, as for that which is called "One," it is not something governed by names and designations. Therefore, the One is not the seeing of oneness.
If there is anything seen, then there is duality; it cannot be called true oneness.
It is like beholding a thousand layers of reflected images within a mirror, or as if peering through a window crack and seeing boundless space.
These are all metaphors for the single mind possessing such great function—like seeing the waves and knowing the ocean, or seeing the soil and knowing the mountain.
Although the myriad phenomena are diverse, they ultimately return to a single totality.
This Dharma of the One Mind expands to pervade the entire Dharma-realm and contracts to fit within a single speck of dust. Thus, the mind is the ultimate destination;
it reaches the very source of the myriad dharmas, the foundation of all wisdom, and the core of boundless vows and practices. Without attaining this teaching, one cannot reach this truth.
There is no path to Buddhahood that does not pass through the gateway; this is surely what is meant.

The expositions of the various Mahāyāna scriptures provide manifold proofs, all of which state that [the mind] mirrors the profound ultimate of the one mind and contains the source of the myriad dharmas. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"The Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are his own mind. It further states: "One understands that the world is entirely like [a reflection]."
Through transformation, they clearly realize that sentient beings are nothing but this single Dharma. Furthermore, a verse says:

"Throughout all kalpas—counted and uncounted—the Bodhisattva understands them to be but a single thought-moment; thus skillfully entering the practice of Bodhi, they constantly and diligently cultivate it without ever regressing.
Another verse says: "The deeds performed by the Buddhas according to their suitability are immeasurable, boundless, and equal to all dharmas."
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): the wise are able, through a single expedient means, to fully comprehend them all without exception.
The moisture of the Bohai Sea is the same as that of a small stream; the emptiness of the ten directions is equal to the space within a mustard seed.
Moisture and emptiness are both without magnitude; how much more so is the true mind of universal equality, which possesses neither superiority nor inferiority?

It is like the sun of today and of antiquity, whose illumination is no different in its clarity; it is further comparable to the wind of the past and the present, whose movement is no different in its force.
The sunlight is impartial; its dynamic nature is non-dual. All these manifest the virtues of the True Mind.
Treading upon the ground of ultimate reality and soaring into the sky of nirvana, one digs into the parched earth of sentient beings, causing the wisdom-spring of the Sugata to gush forth.
The Lotus Sūtra says: "Suppose there is a person who, parched with thirst, needs water. He digs for it on a high plateau;
seeing only dry earth, he knows the water is still far off. Yet, without ceasing his efforts, he gradually sees moist earth and eventually reaches mud.
His mind becomes certain that the water must be near. Sentient beings are like the dry earth, and the śrāvakas are like the moist earth."
The earth is like the bodhisattva; the Buddhas are like water.
As for the shrivelled sprouts of the śrāvakas, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:
"The two vehicles are like scorched sprouts and rotten seeds; they cannot give rise to the mind of unsurpassed enlightenment. Hereafter...

Within the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra, he deeply entered the One Vehicle and received the true prediction of enlightenment. He once again sprouted the seeds of perfect faith and brought forth the fruit of Bodhi;
thus was the ultimate fruition of the King of Flowers perfected.
The minds of sentient beings are the source of the fruit of all Buddhas. Thus, the *Huayan shu* (Commentary on the Avataṃsaka Sūtra) states:
"The Buddhas of the ten directions realize the essence of sentient beings and employ the function of sentient beings. Furthermore, a sūtra says:

"The Buddhas of the ten directions, within the mental activity of a single small sentient being, attain perfect enlightenment and turn the wheel of Dharma in every thought-moment; yet sentient beings do not perceive this."
I understand.
It is like obtaining the "soul-returning incense," by which withered roots sprout anew; it is like ingesting the "returning-elixir" medicine, by which cold flames are kindled once more.
Just as the power of soul-returning incense can raise the dead, so too does the efficacy of the returning-elixir have the capacity to transform the mundane.

How much more so, then, the power of single-minded cultivation! To attain a holy body within an ordinary frame, and to enter nirvana from the midst of birth and death, is like flowers blooming on a withered tree or flames erupting from cold ashes.

It is as when the śrāvakas at the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* beheld the Tathāgata-nature and received the Buddha’s prediction; it is like sprouts growing from parched grain, or the blind and deaf regaining their sight.
Upon hearing this, the corpse rose again and the cold flames blazed up once more.

Having attained complete realization beyond doubt, what need was there for formal judgment? He mounted the ox-cart and arrived at the Jeta Grove; he boarded the boat of compassion and sat as he ascended to the other shore.
Simply by trusting one’s own mind, the doubts of others are instantly severed. Thus, the *Xinxin Ming* says: "When doubt is completely purified, right faith becomes straight and upright.
Furthermore, if one has faith in the mind, one does not believe in any phenomena apart from it. As an ancient master said:
"One believes in the wisdom of one's own mind, which in turn believes in its own mind; it is not that there is some separate agent of belief existing outside the mind. Moreover, as for this faith...
Not to have faith in one’s own mind is not called right faith; the mind is itself the essence (*tattva*). Thus, essence and faith are non-dual.
Therefore, the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "One has confidence in one's own mind, knows that the mind is delusively active, and practices the dharma of detachment.
This shows that all matters such as wisdom and phenomena (*jñāna-dharmas*) mentioned therein are not separate from the mind. Consequently, we all possess this potential (*bhāga*).
A thousand-year dark chamber is destroyed by a single lamp; the cage of beginningless bondage relies solely upon wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
A thousand-year dark chamber can be destroyed by one lamp; the karmic fetters of beginningless time are truly dissolved by authentic contemplation.

Authentic contemplation is precisely right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*); right contemplation is precisely the contemplation of the mind. Therefore it is said: "If one contemplates oneself, this is called..."
This is right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
When facing a foreign land, there is not the smallest territory that he does not subdue. How could a single speck of dust disturb the Buddha’s borders?
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The three realms are mind-only; the three periods of time are mind-only. How, then, could there be even a single object or a single atom that contradicts this?
Furthermore, as a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Awakening to the true Dharma of the Dharma-King, therein is neither attachment nor bondage.
Thus, with sovereign and unimpeded mind, one has never seen a single dharma [that exists apart from it]."

Arising, it transcends the realm of feelings and cuts off all conceptual understanding; facing this, there are no words. Its purport is darkly merged with the ultimate truth, and its Way accords with the profound source.
Now, to directly realize the one mind: it is neither true nor false, neither identical nor separate. Why is this? Because both the true and the false lack inherent nature.
Constantly conforming to the single source, how could there be two minds?
Yet they are mutually identical because the source of nature is undefiled and delusion cannot be found—just as a hook or a blade cannot cut stone, nor can mist defile the void.
It is for those who do not understand this single mind that "identity" (ji) is taught. As the Tiantai teachings ask: "Ignorance is identical to the Dharma-nature; there is no longer..."
Regarding ignorance (*avidyā*): with what is it identical? Answer: It is like a person who does not recognize ice; they point to water and call it ice.
Since there is merely a name, how could there be two distinct things that are identical? Thus, one knows that it is only the seasons that differ.
The process of congealing and binding follows conditions, yet the nature of moisture remains ever-present and never undergoes change; even so it is with the identity of the ordinary and the sage.
"Ordinary" and "sage" are merely names; in essence they are one and no different. Thus, the former masters, in their commentary on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, said:
"That which is so for one world is likewise so for the entire Dharma-realm" means that one knows the suchness of a single eye;
the suchness of all eyes is exactly the same. To use an analogy: just as one person has hands and feet, so do all people have hands and feet.
If one does not understand this single mind, one falls into dualistic views. If an ordinary person clings to this mind, they create saṃsāra.

Karma. The followers of the Two Vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) loathe and abandon this mind, seeking instead the fruit of extinction like ashes. Furthermore, ordinary beings lack the eye of wisdom;

when they attempt to illuminate with the wisdom of Bodhi, it becomes a fire of afflictions that burns them. They are like a blind child of great wealth sitting amidst a treasury of jewels; every movement is obstructed, and he is wounded by the very treasures.
The followers of the Two Vehicles take the secret treasury of the Tathāgata’s four virtues to be the impermanent five aggregates.
That is to say, regarding thieves, tigers, dragons, and snakes, one flees in terror; yet whether bound or liberated, both grasping and rejecting are equally lost.

If one clearly realizes and thoroughly penetrates this, there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither attainment nor birth. Understanding that this deluded mind has no substance from moment to moment, from where could attachment arise?
Moment by moment it naturally detaches itself; there is no need for deliberate severance or extinction, for even "one" cannot be found.
How much more so for the two [other natures]? Therefore, one knows that all phenomena accord with Suchness (*tathatā*) and realize the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*);

thus, while the object is non-existent, the mental state is existent. The multitude of sentient minds oppose this intent by clinging to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); thus, while the object is existent, the mental state is non-existent. When one accords with reality, one is always in opposition; yet within this single path, how has the essence ever been lost?
When the mind does not deviate from principle, though there be a thousand paths, they have never for a moment branched apart. To penetrate this is to understand both principle and emotion.

Names are extinguished; having realized this, there is no ground for either compliance or opposition. Thus, every dharma completely accords with the Way beyond words, and every thought returns to the school of non-attainment.
This is the natural spontaneity of the Heavenly Truth; it has nothing to do with artificial fabrication.
Inferable through the two truths yet unknowable; supreme within the principle. Sought throughout the three periods of time yet unobtainable; honored as preeminent within the Dharma.

This single mind-dharma is neither mundane nor separate from the mundane; it is neither ultimate nor separate from the ultimate. Furthermore, although it is neither ultimate nor mundane, it can manifest both the ultimate and the mundane.
Thus, it cannot be sought through conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) nor grasped through ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya); therefore, it is called "two."
One investigates thoroughly yet knows nothing of it. Furthermore, this single mind is not a dharma of the past, for it does not abide in the prior limit;
it is not a dharma of the future, for it does not abide in the posterior limit; it is not a dharma of the present, for it does not abide in the intermediate limit.

Therefore, it is said that one seeks it throughout the three limits and finds it nowhere. If one lacks faith, the myriad practices are established in vain. Thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* says: "If one..."

One knows that all phenomena have no differentiated characteristics. Even regarding the three refuges and the five precepts, they are not established [as discrete entities], because one has not realized the root of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*), does not know the essential nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and lacks clarity regarding the reality of all objects.
Therefore, the former masters said: "When a Bodhisattva first awakens to the equality of the self-nature of all phenomena, how..."

It is equality, because one enters into the true nature (*tathatā*) of all phenomena. That is to say, within this true nature, there are no marks of differentiation, no marks of variety, and no marks of multiplicity. All phenomena are of one suchness; how could there be anything unequal?
Upon what, then, is this true nature established? Furthermore, it clarifies the basis of non-reliance: namely, not relying on form, nor...

Relying upon emptiness: if all phenomena rely upon emptiness, then emptiness has nothing upon which it relies. Now, all phenomena rely upon the True [Suchness], yet the True has nothing upon which it relies;
this is because it is the Dharma-gate of the Seal of Non-reliance. Thus, one abandons the world.
The world consists of various distinctions, yet its nature is eternally non-established—how much more so its characteristics? Furthermore, form is not established by relying upon emptiness, nor...
Emptiness is not established by relying on form; it is neither different nor non-different. When there is no "is" and no "is-not," this very view is severed.

It is provisionally named "inner realization. Thus, a verse from the *Avataṃsaka* says: "Even if, in every moment of thought, one were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas, if one does not know the true Dharma, it is not called making an offering. Furthermore, another verse says: "Though [one may continue] until the end of the future..."
Even if one were to travel throughout all Buddha-fields, if one does not seek this wondrous Dharma, one will ultimately not achieve Bodhi. Furthermore, a verse says:
"Even if one were to offer wealth and treasures to the Buddhas for countless eons, if one does not know the true reality of the Buddha, this is not called giving.
Thus we know that among the six perfections and myriad practices, if one does not directly realize the One Mind, there is not a single gate of practice through which enlightenment can be attained.
This is the root of accomplishment, the foundation of the Bodhi tree, and the foremost principle of the teachings.
This Dharma of the single mind is the basis upon which all Buddhas attain the Way and the point from which Bodhisattvas enter awakening, as described in the *Mahāsannipāta Sūtra*.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Bhadrapāla, "I recall that in the past there was a Buddha, a World-Honored One, named Subhānu.
At that time, there was a man who encountered a vast wilderness; afflicted by hunger and thirst, he eventually fell asleep.
In his dream, he obtained all kinds of various exquisite and superior foods. Having eaten until full, he no longer felt hungry or empty. Upon waking from this, he returned..."
Furthermore, being hungry and thirsty, this person then reflects to himself: "All such phenomena are empty and without reality;

they are like what is seen in a dream, fundamentally not true. When he contemplates in this way, he awakens to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and attains non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is also like a person leaning a jewel against lapis lazuli.
Above, reflections appear within it, just as a bhikṣu, when contemplating bones, perceives various kinds of light. These have no one who brings them;
there are no such bones; they are merely created by the mind. Furthermore, the Mahāvaipulya Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra says:
"Moreover, Bhadrapāla, it is like a bhikṣu practicing the contemplation of impurity (aśubha-bhāvanā), who sees a recently deceased corpse whose form and color have just begun to change, or..."
Whether blue, yellow, black, or red, and even up to the visualization of bones scattered about—those scattered bones come from nowhere and go nowhere;
they are produced solely by the mind, and one thus sees them as one's own mind. They are also like reflections in a mirror.
It does not come from without; it does not arise from within. Because the mirror is pure, one sees one’s own form therein. When the practitioner’s nature is pure, that which is seen is pure.
If one wishes to see the Buddha, one immediately sees the Buddha; upon seeing him, one asks questions, and he immediately answers.
Hearing the sutra, one is greatly rejoiced. One then reflects to oneself: "From where has the Buddha come? I, too, have gone nowhere. That which I contemplate is..."
One sees. The mind creates the Buddha; the mind sees itself; the mind sees the Buddha; the mind is the Buddha; the mind is the self. The mind does not know itself, nor does the mind see itself.
When the mind has conceptualization, it is delusion; when the mind is without conceptualization, it is nirvana.
This Dharma cannot be demonstrated; it is all produced by thought. Even if such thought exists, it is fundamentally non-existent and empty.
Listen! This is called the Buddha-seal.
With composure, one performs the gait of the elephant king; with certainty, one accomplishes the roar of the Teacher.
The majestic demeanor of the elephant king’s gait represents the conduct of Samantabhadra. As for the lion’s roar, it is the lion’s roar.

There are four meanings. First, the hundred beasts' brains split open, which metaphorically represents the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma, whereby the hundred dharmas are simultaneously shattered.

Second, the fragrant elephants are subdued, which metaphorically represents the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma, whereby the celestial Māras are subdued. Third, the flying birds fall, which metaphorically represents the falling away of the heterodox views of non-Buddhists.
Fourth, the aquatic creatures hide away, which metaphorically represents the hiding of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*...
It is said: "The lion’s roar is the definitive teaching that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
It is further said: "All who possess a mind shall attain Buddhahood. And it is also said: "To have something to acquire is the howling of a jackal; to have nothing to acquire is the lion’s roar.
Since there is no phenomenon apart from the mind, there is nothing to be acquired.

If one wishes to recommend the method of silent transmission, it should be presented prior to words; if one intends to set forth the gate of the secret, how could one contemplate it after the opportune moment?
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he silently transmitted the mind-seal; yet even the single word "only silence knows" requires that the karmic conditions be met.
One never proclaims it outwardly, but waits directly to receive it from one’s own experience; only then is it confirmed. This is the Dharma-gate of self-realization:
like a person drinking water, the coldness or warmth is known by oneself alone and cannot be described in words. Furthermore, awakening falls into the "second head";
before the faculty [of the mind], there is no teaching, and after the teaching, there is no reality.
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), the fire of wisdom is such that it would be difficult for one’s hand to touch it.
The Treatise states: "The Prajñāpāramitā is like a great mass of fire; it cannot be touched from any of its four sides.

To touch it is to burn one's hand. This applies whether one speaks of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence—these being the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi).
Even the fourfold propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), the complete set of four propositions, and the ineffable (*anabhilāpya*)—all these constitute slanders against Prajñāpāramitā.
It is like touching fire at its four sides: they all burn the hand. Therefore, it is said that one must transcend the four propositions and sever the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*).
If one grasps the meaning of the four *siddhāntas*, one understands them as being like a cool pond; one may enter through any of the four gates and attain the Way in every case.
He drives the four propositions beyond the realm of emptiness and eradicates the hundred negations within the midst of stillness.
To fall into the four propositions is to become ensnared by extreme views; yet, if one perceives even a single dharma, one exhausts all hundred negations.

If one can suddenly realize the essence of the mind, the net of views will naturally be transcended. Thus, one attains the Way wherever one is, and every thought is the ultimate source. Therefore it is said:
A single color and a single fragrance are none other than the Middle Way. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Distant from the two extremes, one accords with the Middle Way.

An ancient commentary explains: "There are four kinds of two extremes: first, defilement and purity; second, regarding delusion and bondage versus liberation; and [the others] concerning afflictions and karma."
The third is existence and non-existence, which applies to both phenomena and principle. The fourth is identity and difference, which pertains to the mind and its objects.

Why is this so? It is because upon attaining *bodhi*, one is already free from subtle thoughts; once delusive afflictions are exhausted, the *dharmakāya* manifests and wisdom becomes purely immaculate.
If one views it in this way, one has not yet escaped the extremes. Thus, a sutra says: "If there is a view of the Perfectly Awakened One, liberation is still apart from all outflows (*āsrava*)."

Not being attached to any world is not yet the realization of the Dharma-eye. Now, having realized that the essence and nature of delusion are fundamentally empty, there is nothing further to be purified;

thus, one is free from the two extremes. Furthermore, because defilement and purity interpenetrate, there is no abiding attachment. This is called "leaving the extremes. Regarding "bondage and liberation":
it means that in the past, one was constantly bound by afflictions and karma, wandering through saṃsāra without end; now, one has attained Bodhi.

"Tī. He was released with clarity and liberation. If one were to say that this view is itself an abiding in extremes, the Bodhisattva’s wisdom realizes that from the very beginning there has been no bondage;

how, then, could there be liberation? Where there is neither bondage nor liberation, there is no attachment; thus, detachment is attained. Regarding the matter of "existence" and "non-existence" as penetrating both phenomena and principle:
if previously one thought something might exist, now one realizes it is perhaps empty. Both [extremes] are understood through emptiness; now they are known [as such].
The wondrous existence. Furthermore, true bliss is fundamentally present, yet one loses it without realizing it; delusory suffering is fundamentally empty, yet one attains it without awakening to it.
Only today do I begin to know this. If one knows in such a way, one has not yet departed from extremes.

Moreover, afflictions, karma, and suffering—which were fundamental but are now absent—and bodhi and the Buddha-body—which were non-existent but are now present—are all dharmas that exist throughout the three periods of time. This is the nature of bodhi.

Nature does not belong to the three periods of time. Existence and non-existence within the three periods are both subsumed under extremes. True wisdom accords with reality and transcends the three periods;

therefore, it is free from the two extremes of existence and non-existence, and so forth. Regarding the duality of identity and difference: first, if the mind and its object are not clearly understood, they become two;
if they are in accord, they are one—this too constitutes an extreme. Second, there is a difference between sentient beings and Buddhas; now...
To realize the single nature is also called an extreme. Now, one correctly awakens to the fact that existence and non-existence within this are non-dual, and even this non-duality is further absent.
One who possesses great wisdom and sees clearly abides in accordance with reality; therefore, they are free from these extremes. As for what was said previously:

although the pairs of views—such as annihilationism and eternalism, coming and going, birth and cessation, and the dependent and the primary—are dualistic dharmas, they are all subsumed under the category of extremes. Furthermore, [the text continues:]
Duality and non-duality are also termed "extremes. Now, being in accord with Bodhi, all things are entirely quiescent; therefore, it is said that one is "far removed" from them.
It is like the skill of Nala’s archery: his momentum pierces through iron drums.
Nārāyaṇa’s arrow can pierce iron drums;
it possesses a force like that of a vajra hammer, intended to shatter the mountains of the heterodox.
A vajra hammer can shatter mountains of gold.
One achieves the seven types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Regarding those who possess the seven types of eloquence: first, swift eloquence, providing instantaneous answers beyond thought; second, sharp eloquence, with clear and skillful vocal tones;
third, inexhaustible eloquence, wherein questions and answers are endless; fourth, uninterrupted eloquence, flowing in continuous succession; fifth, [eloquence] that accords with...
One should distinguish them as follows: (6) the eloquence of the primary meaning, which skillfully explains the true nature of reality;
(7) the supreme worldly eloquence, which transcends all other categories. These seven types of eloquence all arise from the wisdom of the mind.

He is endowed with the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*). The four fearlessnesses are: first, fearlessness regarding omniscience; second, fearlessness regarding the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*); third, fearlessness regarding the teaching on obstacles to the path;
and fourth, fearlessness regarding the teaching on the path to the exhaustion of suffering. A verse from the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: "Within one, he understands the immeasurable."
Within the immeasurable, one understands the one; by comprehending their mutual arising, one shall attain fearlessness. This is precisely the realization that the mind itself is Buddhahood.
Since there is no dharma external to the mind with which to contend, one is fearless in all circumstances.
It is the strategic manual for daily life among humanity, the warp and woof of the temporal cycles of the world.
Sentient beings use it every day yet remain unaware of it, like fish in water who do not see the water, or birds in the sky who do not see the sky;
likewise, people dwell within the Way yet do not recognize the Way.
If the myriad phenomena of the universe were to give birth and gestate, they would all be encompassed within the earth-element;
all things arise from the great earth, and all dharmas emerge from the mind-ground.
It is like the generation and growth of the myriad things, all of which contain the One Qi (One Vital Energy).
The *Yi Gouming Jue* states: "Before heaven and earth were divided, it was called the One Qi.

Within this, there are Taiyi (Great Ease), Taichu (Great Beginning), Taishi (Great Commencement), Taisu (Great Purity), and Taiji (Great Ultimate), which constitute the five movements (*yun*). A movement is precisely a numerical cycle."
This refers to the transformation of time; it first takes up the meaning of "change. When the primal qi (*yuanqi*) begins to disperse, it is called the Great Beginning (*taichu*).

The tip of the manifestation of qi is called the Great Commencement (*taishi*). When form undergoes change and possesses substance, it is called the Great Purity (*taisu*). Once substance and form are fully established, it is called transformation.
Because there are five qi, they are termed the Five Phases (*wuyun*); these are all the divisions of the Way of Heaven (*tiandao*).
Profound and remote, yet its power is naturally capable of being borne.
All sentient beings inherently possess the power of their own true mind. As the *Awakening of Faith* states:
"From the very beginning, the nature is spontaneously replete with all merits; that is to say, its essence possesses the great radiance of wisdom."
This refers to the meaning of "equality" and so forth.
Within the moon-islands and misty forests, they constantly discourse upon the wondrous intent; amidst the cloud-platforms and jeweled nets, they fully expound the perfect sound.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that within the cloud-platform of the great net of light, a verse was spoken: "The Buddha is the unequaled equal."

As vast as the entirety of space, the immeasurable and supreme merits of the ten directions—the most excellent among humans and the highest in the world—may the Dharma of the Lion of the Śākyas be bestowed upon them.
Furthermore, it is said that from within clouds of all manner of offering implements, a voice spontaneously issues forth, reciting this verse:
"The power and function of your supernormal abilities are immeasurable; may you preach according to the inclinations and joys of sentient beings. It is further said:
Within the Buddha’s radiance, before the entire assembly of bodhisattvas, he spoke in verse: "His sovereign supernormal powers are boundless;
In a single thought-moment, he causes all to attain liberation. The Elder asked: "Why does the great assembly not ask their questions with words?
For what reason do they harbor doubts through silent reflection? Why do they not praise and exhort him with their own speech?"

Question: What is the "Request by the Clouds of Offerings Emitting Sounds"? Answer: It clarifies that the Buddha has attained the mind of the *dharmadhātu* and shares the same mind as all sentient beings;
because their minds are not different, he knows the doubts in their hearts.

As for the verses spoken by the clouds of offerings, they clarify that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are, in their totality, the essence of the *dharmadhātu*. The *dharmadhātu* is inconceivable, and all phenomena are likewise so.
Because it is inconceivable. It clarifies that for the assembly of sages, the mind and its objects are non-dual. Ordinary beings are deluded regarding the *dharmadhātu*;
they perceive the mind and its objects as dual, and thus inversion arises.
To partake of the cuisine of the Fragrant Accumulation (Gandhavyūha) kitchen is truly worthy of entering the Vinaya.

The Vimalakīrti Sūtra states: "In the world-system of Fragrant Accumulation, when the bodhisattvas there smell the fragrance, they enter the Vinaya and immediately attain the Samādhi of the Treasury of All Merits.
If one enters the Dharma-realm through fragrance, one's own body is itself a multitude of fragrances.
The world: one's own mind is itself the Tathāgata Gandhavyūha, with immeasurable merit fully perfected within a single mind.
For one who awakens to and enters this, what need is there to seek elsewhere? As it is with the realm of fragrance, so it is with the eighteen realms;
all are places where the spirit may dwell and fields for attaining the Way.
Listening to the sound of wind in the branches, one may intimately transmit the mind.
The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "The water birds and the forest trees all constantly recollect the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha.

From this we know that the objective realm is the realm of the very mind, and the mind is the mind of the very realm. Though subject and object appear to be divided, they are of one essence and without duality.
This is different. If you can perceive the consciousness-mind that perceives objects, this is the essence of the secret transmission. Ultimately, not a single dharma is given to anyone;
do not esteem other schools, but must follow this command. The great task of appearing in the world is finished, and the fundamental study for entering Chan is complete.
Śākyamuni appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition: to open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision within the minds of sentient beings.
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he transmitted mind solely by means of mind. Now, simply awakening to the one mind, one awakens oneself and awakens others, thereby fulfilling one's original vow.
As the eminent monk Shi Tansui often said: "The three realms are illusory and false; they are but the one mind."

Chasing after external objects, one finds it difficult to cease such pursuits until awakening is attained. Furthermore, the eminent monk Master Jietuo (Śubhakarasiṃha) relied upon the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to practice the "Contemplation of Buddha-Radiance.
One clear moonlit night, amidst the light, he suddenly beheld a manifested Buddha who spoke this verse:
"The secret and most profound Dharma of all Buddhas, Only now attained after cultivation through vast eons. If a person can illuminate this Dharma-gate..."
All the Buddhas rejoiced in this. Liberation Master (Heshang Jietuo) then prostrated and asked, "How should this Dharma-gate be explained to others?
Thereupon, the transformation Buddha vanished from sight. From the sky, he answered in verse:
"Skillful means and wisdom serve as the lamp, Illuminating the realm of the mind. If you wish to know the true Dharma, In all things, nothing is seen."
These words are straightforward and unerring. The tracks of the guiding chariot are not in vain.
If one shows others through the mind, all shall return to the True Dharma and not fall into false views; they will be like the guiding chariot, all returning to the Right Path.
This demonstrates that there is no doubt. The patterns on a *jixi* (cock-antler) pillow are always regular.

There was a *jixi* pillow for startling the cock; when viewed from all four sides, its shape remained perfectly regular. This is like a person who contemplates the mind through the True Dharma (*saddharma*).
All things are fundamentally correct. It is like when a person of deviant views contemplates the True Dharma—the True Dharma also follows along as deviant.

When a person of correct views contemplates deviant teachings—the deviant teachings also follow along as correct. A student of the Path once asked Master Jia of Xinfeng, "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
He replied, "It is very much like the 'chicken-startling' horn."
A peerless and heroic spirit, perfected in a single thought, it transforms heaven and earth and moves the divine intelligences. Who would not rejoice upon seeing it?
Who would not be startled upon hearing of it? Universally manifesting the light of the mind, it bears ten thousand titles among humanity.
The myriad dharmas have no inherent substance; they receive their names because of the mind. Even when observing the minds of others, their subtle nuances can be discerned;

all of this is knowing the mind by means of the mind, appearing as if there were a distinction between subject and object. The Fourth Patriarch said: "All supernatural powers and functions are nothing but one's own mind.
Therefore, a sutra states: "The Buddhas manifest great spiritual transformations within the non-dual Dharma. (From the *Huayan*)

Yan Ji states: Regarding the explanation of the supernormal power of knowing others' minds, "subsuming the object within the mind without destroying the object" indicates whether the mind and its objects exist or not.
Dharmapāla says: "If one were to apprehend the objective essence, there would be a fear of destroying the principle of 'mind-only.

Since we do not destroy the object, what harm is there in apprehending it? What loss is there in [its] destruction? Because one has no [subjective] mind toward the myriad things, yet the myriad things have never been non-existent. This...
Success lies in the stillness of the spirit; failure lies in the emptiness of objects. This is because one assumes that objects truly exist.

If one merely destroys the object while the mind remains, then success lies in the emptiness of the object, while failure lies in the existence of the mind. Therefore, since objects are transformed by the mind, it is said that what is transformed by the mind alone is not non-existent.
Why must one necessarily destroy [the object]? If one considers that things lack intrinsic nature because they arise through conditions, then [the mind...]
Both object and subject are extinguished; therefore, it is said that one borrows the mind to eliminate the object, yet the mind itself is extinguished—it is not that the mind alone remains.

Second, regarding the phrase "both subject and object are extinguished, for neither alone remains": above, one did not destroy the object, but merely eliminated the ailment of fearing its substantiality;
now, one eliminates the principle of emptiness and existence. Thus, both mind and object are permitted to exist and to perish, for mind and object are mutually dependent.

Emptiness exists because it arises dependently upon conditions; "existence" is preservation, while "emptiness" is cessation. When emptiness and existence penetrate one another, both preservation and cessation are fully realized.
That the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is mind-only, neither identical nor different, precisely reveals the principle of partial mind-only (*pradeśa-cittamātra*).

Although it possesses the meaning of mind-only, it still pertains to the mind-only of arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha-cittamātra*); yet, although both [existence and emptiness] have ceased, it does not...

Although it was previously mentioned that the mind and its objects mutually encompass one another, it has not yet been explicitly stated that they are fully comprised of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).

Now, because this is clearly established as being exclusively consciousness-only, it is said to be "the ultimate truth of Mind-only" (*paramārtha-cittamātra*). Because it is identical to the ultimate truth, it is not different; because it does not destroy the distinction between subject and object, it is not one.

Because it is not one, there exist subject and object, and thus the principle of the object being established through dependence on another is fulfilled. Because it is not different, subject and object are equal; this is the meaning of Mind-only.
It is established. Regarding the statement, "Because at the very time one perceives another, it is oneself," this concludes that the essential nature (svabhāva) is attained;
there is no fault of [perceiving] something external to the mind, because it is precisely oneself. Thus, one does not lose the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Therefore, following the passage on "the minds of sentient beings being identical to the Buddha-mind," the second section correctly demonstrates the characteristics of the other-mind (*paracitta*) as *dharmatā*. This consists of two pairs of statements; the first pair is as follows:

This clarifies the object of cognition (*ālambana*). Subsequently, it contrasts this with the subject that cognizes. Here, the initial statement, "the sentient being's mind is precisely the Buddha-mind," clarifies that the sentient being's mind which is the object of cognition is identical to the Buddha-mind; these two are not different.
Next, the statement, "the Buddha-mind is not precisely the sentient being's mind," clarifies that the sentient being's mind and the Buddha-mind are not identical. They are not... [the same].
Regarding the phrase "that which has an object": because it is not different [from the mind], the principle of "Mind-Only" (cittamātra) is not undermined.
The statement "as an object" establishes it as the object of cognition, distinguishing it from that which is the subject of cognition. Next, below, the subject of cognition is explained:

"Because the Buddha-mind is precisely the mind of sentient beings. This sentence clarifies that the Buddha-mind, which is the subject of cognition, is identical to the mind of sentient beings, demonstrating that they are not different.
Next, the statement that "the mind of sentient beings is not identical to the Buddha-mind" clarifies that there is a sense of non-identity between the Buddha-mind and the mind of sentient beings.
Because they are not one, [the Buddha-mind] acts as the perceiving subject; because they are not different, the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) remains unimpaired.
To say that [the Buddha's mind] is the "capable perceiver" (ālambaka) establishes it as the perceiver and distinguishes it from the perceived object (ālambana).

To illustrate this further by means of an analogy: it is like water mixed with milk. The milk, which is the substance being mixed, represents the minds of sentient beings as the perceived object. The water, which is the agent of mixing, represents the Buddha’s mind as the capable perceiver.
Through the union of these two, they appear as if of a single flavor; yet when the king of geese drinks them, the milk [is separated].
When the water is exhausted and only the essence remains, one knows that they are not identical. Yet, this name "water" is the water of milk, and this name "milk" is the milk of water.
Although these two are similar, there is a sense in which they are not identical; therefore, they should be illustrated by analogy.
That which is the milk of water is not the water of milk, serving as the substance being mixed; whereas that which is the water of milk is not the milk of water.
As for milk, its capacity to harmonize [ingredients] can be understood through this principle.
It pervades the nature of consciousness, much like the thousand names of Śakra Devendra.
The celestial lord Śakra has a thousand names; one is named Śakra, another is named Kauśika, and so forth, as it is said:
