Without seeking with the mind, one reaches the very bottom of the mud step by step,

like a fragrant elephant crossing a river, stepping down to the bottom at every stride; this is a metaphor for the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), which differs from the provisional and gradual teachings, just as an elephant differs from a rabbit.

The horse crossed the river. Thus, the Treatise of the Elder Li says: "It is not as good as realizing non-arising in a single thought-moment, thereby transcending the provisional views of those who study the three vehicles.
A verse from the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says: "Mañjuśrī, the person of great wisdom, deeply penetrates the very source of all phenomena."
It is like shooting at a target:
if one takes the target as the target, one will mostly miss and rarely hit; but if one takes the ground as the target, there is no shot that does not hit.

Likewise, if one takes the mind as the target, there is nothing that does not accord with the fundamental principle. Furthermore, Yang You was skilled at archery; he would hit the mark every hundred times he fired.
To pierce the willow leaves at a hundred paces, not a single arrow misses its mark; thus it is said: "If one confronts the principle of the Mahāyāna, ten thousand cases will not fail once.
When the lapels are aligned, one thinks only of lifting the collar; when the main cords are straightened, one seeks only to grasp the handle.
How much more so this secret dharma-gate of the single mind! It is like grasping the main rope and lifting the collar;

it speaks by seizing the essential points and is also called "entering directly with a single blade. Within the teachings, there are explicit explanations and secret explanations, true explanations and expedient explanations, as well as negational definitions (*paryudāsa*) and affirmative definitions (*vidhi*). This [teaching] is an explicit explanation, a true explanation, and an affirmative definition that enters directly.
This expresses the essence of the mind; it is not a provisional teaching intended to negate or refute attachments. Thus, a verse in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says:
"Directly abandoning expedient means, he teaches only the unsurpassed Way. Regarding this explicit teaching, as a verse in the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* states:
"There is no mind and no objects; both the subject and object of cognition are absent. It relies solely upon the one mind," and so forth.

And they make conceptual distinctions. Furthermore, a verse says: "Like a fire-wheel, falling hair, or a city of Gandharvas—failing to realize that it is only one's own mind, one falsely gives rise to all manner of conceptual distinctions."
One bathes in the vast ocean and yet employs the waters of all rivers; one burns a single mote of dust and yet it contains the fragrance of all flavors.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "It is like a person who enters the sea to bathe and yet uses the waters of all rivers.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* says: "It is like pounding ten thousand kinds of substances into a pill; if one burns a single mote of it, the full array of their essences is present. All [are thus contained].
It is like this: if one understands the single mind, all dharma-gates will be in perfect accord.
It is like the Caitraratha Grove of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where no perception of difference arises.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is a Grove of Various Delights (*Caitraratha-vana*), produced by the power of the collective merit of the various devas."

It is wondrous. If the hosts of devas were not in this grove, when they experienced the pleasures of their palaces and other such things together, there would have been distinctions of superior and inferior, and they would have experienced them with the differentiation of "I" and "mine.
But if they are in this grove, whether in terms of objects or experiences, there is no superiority or inferiority at all;
everything is equally sublime. They experience these things in harmony without "I" or "mine," which enables them to attain equanimity.

Therefore, it is named the Grove of Intermingled Forests (*miśraka-vana*). This is because, through the sovereign power of the meritorious karma cultivated by the various devas in equal harmony, the *ālaya-vijñāna* of those devas manifests this grove; they occupy the same place, exist at the same time, and possess the same characteristics.
Due to the sovereign power of this Grove of Intermingled Forests, their evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) likewise manifest in the same way. Although...

Each experiences [its own state] while claiming there is no difference between them. Therefore, if one realizes that all phenomena arise from the mind’s perceptions, one immediately enters the sphere of the noble ones through the gateway of conventional truth.
This is like the southern face of Mount Sumeru, which radiates nothing but pure golden light.
On the southern face of Mount Sumeru, there appears exclusively a golden radiance. When birds of various colors enter the mountain, they all become the same color as gold.
This is because, just as all phenomena return to the mind, they all share the nature of the mind.
It was like awakening from a state of intoxication, or as if rising from a dream. A non-Buddhist practitioner bestowed a mantra upon him in the heavens; a woman sought a son within a forest.
In the Western Heavens, there was a non-Buddhist who made offerings to Brahmā to seek a mantra; consequently, he saw the deity bestow the mantra upon him in a dream.
However, Brahmā did not actually descend; rather, he relied upon the heaven as a dominant condition, and all such matters were merely what was evoked by the dreaming mind.

Furthermore, have you not heard that those who seek offspring may enter a secluded forest and, having dreamed of engaging in sexual union with someone, subsequently obtain a son? All of these are transformations produced by the mental consciousness within a dream.
However, it is merely one's own mind; in reality, there are no external objects.

Being unconditioned and without affairs, it fully accords with the gateway of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). It is solely quiescent and solely profound, providing an immediate realization of the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*).

The thousands of sutras and myriad treatises correctly discourse upon the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena, leading one to awaken to and enter the principle of the One Mind and the source of the eight consciousnesses.
This One Mind and the eight consciousnesses are subtle and difficult to know; only a Buddha can fully comprehend them. Furthermore, regarding the eight consciousnesses as the sovereign mind-kings:
Taking the eighth ālayavijñāna as the fundamental basis, it is able to give rise to the preceding seven consciousnesses.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "The cessation-and-arising and the non-cessation-and-non-arising are conjoined; being neither identical nor different, they are called the ālayavijñāna.
An ancient master’s commentary explains: "The non-cessation-and-non-arising mind and the cessation-and-arising [mind] are conjoined, being neither identical nor different."
Taking the seven consciousnesses as defiled dharmas, they are subject to arising and ceasing; taking the Tathāgatagarbha as pure dharma, it is neither arising nor ceasing.
Because this non-arising, non-ceasing mind moves throughout its entire substance, the mind does not depart from the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

Since these characteristics of arising and ceasing are none other than spiritual understanding (*vijñapti*), arising and ceasing do not depart from the characteristics of the mind. Because they are thus inseparable, they are termed "conjoined" (*saṃyukta*).

The *ālaya-vijñāna*, by virtue of its integration (*saṃyoga*), is neither identical nor different. If it were identical, there would be no integration; if it were different, there likewise would be no integration.
Because it is neither identical nor different, integration is possible. Furthermore, the activity of the Tathāgatagarbha—the pure mind—arises and ceases without being separate from it;
therefore, it is called "integration. This does not mean that there is a distinct arising and ceasing apart from it.
Coming to unite with the True [Suchness] is like stirring water to produce waves; the waves do not unite with anything external. This refers to the mind of arising and ceasing.
Because the arising and ceasing of the mind have no [independent] characteristics, the arising and ceasing of the mind are established through ignorance (*avidyā*).

This mind of arising and ceasing arises from original enlightenment (*mūlapratibodha*), yet they possess no dual nature and are never separated from one another; therefore, they are said to be "harmoniously united," just like the water of the great ocean.
Due to the wind, there is movement and fluctuation; the characteristics of water and the characteristics of wind are not mutually separable.

If arising and non-arising were one and the same, then when the characteristics of consciousness—arising and ceasing—are extinguished, the essence of the mental spirit would also necessarily perish, falling into the extreme of nihilism.
If they were different, then at the time when the mind is stirred by the perfuming of the winds of ignorance, the essence of the tranquil mind would [not follow].
If one were to follow conditions, one would fall into the extreme of eternalism. Free from these two extremes, [the nature of reality] is neither identical nor different.

Furthermore, regarding the aforementioned two dharmas—awakening and non-awakening—they mutually permeate one another to constitute defilement and purity. Since they possess no intrinsic substance, they are entirely one awakening.
Why is this? Because of ignorance, non-awakening arises; and because the meaning of non-awakening permeates original awakening, it gives rise to [defiled phenomena].
All defiled dharmas arise from the permeation of fundamental awakening upon non-awakening; furthermore, all pure dharmas arise from the same permeation.
Based on these two meanings, everything is universally produced; therefore, it is said that consciousness has two meanings by which it gives rise to all phenomena.

The hundred schools have returned to the dark mystery; ten thousand ages cannot shift this truth. Based on the fact that prior objects (pūrvadhātu) lack intrinsic substance, there is only the activity of the Dharma itself.
It is like a puppeteer manipulating wooden puppets, or like a performer displaying his skills upon a stage.
The *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: A verse in the Sūtra says, "The Buddha taught that the Tathāgatagarbha is the ālaya;
those of evil intelligence do not know that the Garbha is the ālayavijñāna. Ālaya is a Sanskrit term; here it is translated as "that which is clung to with self-love" (*ātma-sneha-abhiniveśa-ālaya*).
This is precisely the eighth fundamental consciousness-heart of all sentient beings. The eighth consciousness-heart is the Tathāgata...
Regarding the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness): because all non-Buddhist practitioners and sentient beings cannot fully comprehend it, they grasp it as the *ālayavijñāna*.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not undergo transmigration; they do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of *nirvāṇa*.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure, is accompanied by their causes, and undergoes birth and cessation. Explanation: The seven consciousnesses arise and perish from moment to moment.
It is impermanent; arising and immediately passing away, how could it undergo transmigration? Since its own substance is not established, it does not experience suffering or pleasure.

Being neither the basis for defilement nor the basis for untainted nirvana, it is like the Tathāgatagarbha—truly eternal and omnipresent—which, while existing within the six realms, causes delusion to manifest as phenomena through conditions, resulting in the experience of the fruits of suffering and pleasure. Together with the seven...
It is co-existent with consciousness; it is co-existent with name and its causes, and is formed without abiding in its own nature.

Therefore, the seven consciousnesses depend upon this to undergo arising and ceasing—whether they arise or cease. This clarifies that the Tathāgatagarbha is precisely True Suchness (Tathatā) following conditions, and thus experiences suffering and pleasure.
It further states: "It is constantly co-existent with ignorance and the seven consciousnesses, without interruption. This is the meaning.
It is said: Because the Tathāgatagarbha accords with conditions, it is called the ālayavijñāna; therefore, it coexists with ignorance.
The great ocean is explained as being like the ālayavijñāna, the waves like the seven consciousnesses, and the water like the Tathāgatagarbha.
Regarding the phrase "without interruption": because it has been a continuous succession from beginningless time, the Tathāgatagarbha is that which is...

Regarding the phrase "the perfuming of the pure nature becomes false and so forth according to defiled conditions": this refers to the defiled illusory nature of the perfumer; the "ālayavijñāna" is that which is produced by it.

Regarding the phrase "acting as the cause for the wholesome and unwholesome": this means that when this nature arises with wholesome conditions to produce various wholesome dharmas, the nature itself acts as the cause of the wholesome;
when it arises with unwholesome conditions to produce various unwholesome dharmas, the nature [itself acts as the cause of the unwholesome].

This is precisely the cause of unwholesomeness. Regarding the experience of suffering and pleasure together with their causes: following what is wholesome, one experiences pleasure, and the nature [of that experience] is inherent therein;

following what is unwholesome, one experiences suffering, and the nature [of that experience] is likewise inherent therein. As for arising and ceasing, this refers to the cycling through the various realms of existence (*gati*).

"Ten thousand deaths and ten thousand births are like a performer; they are like a person putting on a play, changing their costume and appearance, yet the body remains one person who has never actually changed.
Thus, a verse in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: 'The mind is like a skilled performer; the intellect is like the assistant;
the five consciousnesses are like the musicians; and deluded thoughts are the audience watching the performance. Therefore, the Verse of Master Caotang [says]:..."
It is said: "The musician was originally but one physical form; now he is a high official, now a slave.

Though his titles and attire have changed, from beginning to end there is no difference between him as a slave and as a master. Thus we know that the pure Tathāgatagarbha, this single point of true mind, neither increases nor decreases;
it is serene and eternally abiding. Because it does not cling to its own nature, it follows along with defilement and purity."
Through conditions, it thus forms the ten dharma-realms of ordinary beings and sages. Although it follows conditions, it does not lose its own nature;
it does not diminish among the ordinary, nor does it increase among the sages. It is like water that, when following the wind to form waves, does not lose its moist nature.
The true mind of all sentient beings is also like this: though it transforms according to appearances, its nature is eternally unmoving. Therefore, it returns...
Yuan Guan said: "The nature of True Suchness naturally accords with conditions; when it accords with conditions, it naturally returns to its nature.
Whether superficial or profound, nothing transcends the realm of the single mind."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "O Son of the Buddha, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, through the samādhi of supernatural powers, successively visits all buddha-fields.
Even within the span of a single thought-moment, he diligently seeks the sublime Dharma in the presence of all Buddhas.
Yet, regarding such phenomena as the appearance of the Buddhas in the world and their entry into parinirvāṇa, he perceives that none of them can be apprehended."

Just as a distracted mind cognizes an object, yet when the mind arises it does not know from what object it arises, and when the mind ceases it does not know to what object it ceases—so too is this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.
He does not discriminate between the appearance of a Tathāgata in the world and the marks of his parinirvāṇa. Son of the Buddha, it is like a mirage in the midday sun; it does not arise from clouds.
It arises from the pond; it does not abide on land, nor does it dwell in the water. It is neither existent nor non-existent; neither good nor evil; neither clear nor turbid.
It is unfit for drinking or rinsing, yet it cannot be defiled. It has no substantial body, yet it is not without a body;
it has no flavor, yet it is not without flavor. Through causes and conditions, it manifests the appearance of water, perceived by consciousness when viewed from afar.
It is like water; one gives rise to the perception of water, yet upon approaching it, the perception of water vanishes of its own accord.
This Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva is also like this: they do not perceive the appearance of a Tathāgata arising in the world, nor the appearance of his parinirvāṇa.
Whether Buddhas possess marks or are markless—all such things are merely conceptual constructions of the mind. Son of the Buddha, this samādhi...
This is called the practice of the pure profound mind. When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva has entered this samādhi and emerges from it, they do not lose what they have attained upon emerging.
This demonstrates that it is not only the Buddha’s teaching that takes the mind as its fundamental principle; rather, it is the ultimate destination of all three teachings.
All say that turning within oneself is supreme. As it is said in the *Kongzi Jiayu*:
Duke Ling of Wei asked Confucius, "Someone has told me that for one who governs a state, if they are careful within the ancestral temple, then the administration will be orderly.
What do you think? The Master said, "That may be so. But those who love others will be loved by others; those who hate others..."
People detest this. What is called "knowing the world without leaving one's round-walled room" refers to the knowledge of turning back upon oneself.
Thus, if one knows how to turn back upon oneself while responding to external things, there will be no activity that does not return to the mind.
When acceptance and rejection are forgotten, beauty and ugliness share the same essence. Thus we know that once the single mind is realized, formlessness manifests spontaneously;
then the dusty prison of the six realms is naturally transcended. To go forth, one must pass through a gate, and none do so except by this path.
As the ancient masters said: "The deluded multitudes of the six realms emerge from this door, yet they have not returned for a thousand kalpas—how tragic!"

How painful this is! This is why the Buddhas were startled and entered the burning house, why the Patriarch came from the West in person, and why even the thousand sages lamented with grief—all because people fail to realize that the way of transcendence is found solely within the mind.

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* clarifies that a single thought-moment can perform infinite deeds; thus it says, "The one mind is transcendentally supreme. As the Sūtra states: "The first is the Buddha's oneness..."
1. Sitting in the full lotus posture, they pervade the immeasurable worlds of the ten directions. 2.
All Buddhas speak a single phrase of meaning, which is fully capable of revealing all Buddha-dharmas. 3. Emitting a single ray of light, it is fully capable of illuminating all worlds. 4.
Within a single body, they are fully capable of manifesting the bodies of all Buddhas. 5. Within a single location...
Sixth, they are able to manifest all worlds. Seventh, within a single moment of wisdom, they are able to decisively comprehend all phenomena without any obstruction.
Eighth, within a single thought-moment, they are able to travel everywhere throughout the worlds of the ten directions.
9. Within a single thought-moment, one fully manifests the immeasurable majesty and virtue of the Tathāgata.
10. Within a single thought-moment, one universally takes as objects the Buddhas and sentient beings of the three periods of time, with a mind free from confusion or distraction. These are the ten.
The *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation on Returning to the Source), citing the *Śāstra*, states: "This is because one relies upon consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*)."

Therefore, objects fundamentally lack intrinsic substance; thus, the meaning of "true emptiness" is established. Because sense-objects do not exist, the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) does not arise.
From this, one comes to know that objects are manifested by the mind and the mind is revealed by objects. The mind does not reach the object, nor does the object reach the mind.
Constantly maintain this contemplation; such wisdom is profoundly deep. As the *Preface to the Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: "Objects separate from the mind..."
The dust of consciousness is thus present; the designation "endowed with numbers" becomes manifest, and the appellation "consciousness-only" emerges as a sign.
Consequently, the principle of the single mind is transmitted forever without end, and the lamp of the eight consciousnesses remains eternally inexhaustible.
It is left to you to deliberate and urge yourself forward.
However, at the time of "consciousness-only," it is as the sutra says: "Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was staying in Śrāvastī," and so forth.

This "time" is precisely the time of the single mind of consciousness-only; therefore, it is said: "A single thought-moment is immeasurable kalpas; immeasurable kalpas are a single thought-moment. (The Lotus Sutra)
The *Xuánzàn* commentary states: "As it is said in the Sūtra, 'at one time,' this refers precisely to the time of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*).
Upon the mental consciousness of both the teacher and the listeners, the appearances of the three times arise through transformation. In reality, these are present phenomena limited by the mind;
they are transformed into durations—whether short or long—and the entire sequence of events is collectively termed 'one time. It is like what is seen in a dream. Thus it is said.
There are many lifetimes. In the state of awakening, there is only mind; there are no real external objects at all. It is the same for the listener’s mind transforming the three periods of time:

these are merely objects of the mental faculty (*manas*), belonging to the formations dissociated from thought (*viprayukta-saṃskāra-skandha*), and subsumed under the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) and the dharma-base (*dharmāyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "at one time," the ancient masters say there are four types: first, it is not necessarily restricted to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*); second, it is not necessarily restricted to a single continuum (*saṃtāna*).
Third, the time is indefinite, being reckoned as four periods, six periods, eight periods, twelve periods, and so forth.

Fourth, the time is indefinite, being reckoned by the number of years and seasons following his attainment of enlightenment, designated simply as "one time. This is merely because the faculties of the listeners have matured.

The Buddha was moved to preach; his preaching was out of compassion, spoken in accordance with the capacities of his audience. When the matters of speaking and listening were concluded, it was collectively termed "at one time.
Here, the term is not restricted to a single *kṣaṇa* (instant) and so forth, because among those who hear the Dharma, some may have dull faculties;

though the time of the teaching is short, the time for their understanding is long. Or, the speaker’s time may be long, and the listener’s duration likewise extends over many moments within a single *kṣaṇa*.
That [explanation] was still not understood; therefore, it is not momentary (*kṣaṇika*), nor is it definitively stated [to be so].
If one were to rely on continuity (*saṃtāna*), then a speaker who has attained *dhāraṇī* could explain the meaning of a single syllable and all would understand it;

or a listener who has attained the purity of the ear and mind could understand everything upon hearing a single syllable. Therefore, it is not continuous, because [it occurs] through a single [moment].

The faculties of those who listen vary, being either sharp or dull. Through the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) of the Tathāgata, a brief moment may be extended into a long kalpa, or many kalpas may be condensed into a brief moment;
since these are not fixed, it is not definitively stated that the duration from the beginning of the teaching to its conclusion constitutes "time.
If one were to calculate based on four periods, six periods, eight periods, or twelve periods, it would amount to one day.
The moon illuminates the four continents; yet the lengths of days and nights, the warmth and cold, and the distances between day and night vary across different regions.

This is because its function always arises simultaneously in two continents at once. Furthermore, from the heavens below [the sun] upward, the higher celestial realms lack these four seasons as well as the eight periods of time and so forth.
The sutra intends for this to circulate among the various regions of the upper realms; if it were to speak of the four seasons and such, it would only apply to the current world.

Because it is not universal, it is also not definitively stated. If one were to calculate based on the number of years and seasons following the attainment of enlightenment, the bodies of the Buddha perceived by those of the three vehicles—whether ordinary beings or sages—as well as the length of their lifespans and the duration since his attainment of enlightenment, would each differ according to whether they are seen as the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) or the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
The commentary states: What has been explained above is not fixed with respect to either the momentary (*kṣaṇa*) or the continuous (*prabandha*) time.

Whether reckoned by four periods, six periods, eight periods, twelve periods, and so forth, or according to the number of years and seasons following the attainment of enlightenment, what is termed "one period" is indeterminate in length due to the varying sharpness or dullness of faculties.
Furthermore, because time is not fixed across the higher and lower realms, one should rely solely on the "single period of the mind-only" as the definitive measure; this is free from all faults.

Lost. When the facts and the principle correspond, and one has already eliminated the sentiment of grasping and rejecting, while also severing the views of annihilationism and eternalism, it is not merely a matter of interpreting consciousness-only for a single moment;
rather, all myriad meanings truly converge within the One Mind. Thus, this is what may be called the core tenet of the teaching.
It perfectly accords with the profound and secret intent, is able to open up right view, and forever extinguishes all doubts. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All dharmas take the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) as their definitive measure. It also says: "Explain only by means of the Mahāyāna, so that they may attain all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
From this we know that there is no fault in speaking only of the Great [Vehicle]. Now, what is called the Mahāyāna is precisely the One [Vehicle].
The Vehicle of the Mind. "Vehicle" (yāna) carries the meaning of transport. When discussing transport, how could it transcend the mind?
Furthermore, those who do not recognize the mind, even if they listen to the Dharma or read the sutras, merely follow names and appearances and fail to grasp the essential purport of the scriptures.
As Sengya said: "Now, when I hear the words of the sutras, every sentence resonates with my own mind. Moreover, Shi Fachong, upon hearing from Hui Min—
When the Dharma Master preaches the Dharma, he attains it within his own mind; it becomes vast and free from all burdens. Even when perceiving all objective realms, it is likewise so.
If one does not contemplate the mind, one will entirely follow along with external objects. Therefore, the *Mahāyāna-avatāra-mārga-citta-vyavasthāna-śāstra* says:
"If one takes 'existence' as being correct, then there is something that is not correct. If one takes 'non-existence' as being correct, then..."

There is nothing that is not so. This single gate of wisdom enters into hundreds of thousands of gates of wisdom. When seeing a pillar, one understands it as a pillar and grasps the characteristic of a pillar;
yet, if one does not form the conceptualization of it being a pillar, but contemplates the mind itself as the dharma of the pillar, there is no characteristic of a pillar.
Therefore, upon seeing the pillar, one immediately attains the dharma of the pillar. All forms and colors are likewise so. Thus, a verse in the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The world..."
Regarding all phenomena, the mind alone is sovereign. Following one's own interpretations, one grasps at manifold characteristics; thus, one is inverted and does not accord with reality as it is.
How magnificent is this perfect expression! How marvelous is this true path!

The Perfect Teaching of the Tathāgata correctly expounds the single mind. A sutra states: "The phenomena of the three realms, from the highest to the lowest, have their meaning solely within the mind.
This explains the mind in terms of the worldly environment and its support (*niśraya-vipāka*). It further states:

"Suchness, the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm, as well as the various mind-born bodies—I declare these to be the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*). This is explained according to the supramundane essence of phenomena.

The mind ultimately reaches the reality and arrives completely at this source. Following its conditions, it yields fruit; returning to the fundamental, it realizes the definitive meaning. Thus, a sutra says:
"The Way is not separate from the mind, and the mind is not separate from the Way.

As for the "Gate of Perfect Accomplishment through the Revolving of Mind" among the Ten Mysterious Gates, all such gates are established by the pure true mind of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature. If one is skillful...
If it is evil, it revolves according to the mind; therefore, it is said that by turning it back, it is perfected as good. Since there is no object external to the mind, it is called "mind-only.
If it follows the natural course, it is named *nirvāṇa*; as the sutra says, "The mind creates all Tathāgatas.
If it turns contrary to the flow, it is birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*); as the sutra says, "The three realms are illusory, all produced by the one mind. Thus, both birth-and-death and *nirvāṇa*...
[The Buddhas] all do not depart from the mind.

Though one possesses the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), how could they change it? Though one possesses the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*), there is nothing that can be spoken [of it].
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. This is because of the minds of sentient beings.
It is wondrous in its transcendence of all dependence, for there is no dharma with which it can be compared. It cannot be conceived by the mind, nor can it be debated by the mouth.
This is why Bodhidharma came from the West to silently transmit the essence of the mind; such was his purpose.
By grasping the branches one reaches the root; by following the water one exhausts the source.
The mind is the fundamental basis of all phenomena; thus, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says: "The Bodhisattva knows that all dharmas are the very nature of the mind;
he accomplishes the body of wisdom without depending on another for enlightenment. If one seeks dharmas outside of the mind, one is merely following others.
To seek [the Way] in this manner is like merely tracing the branches and tributaries, thereby losing sight of the root source. Therefore, the *Yongjia ji* states:
"One who takes the very mind as the Way may be said to have found the source by tracing the current."
The transmission was passed on until it reached Caoxi in its entirety; having received the records, all have together realized the state of Mahāgama.

Mount Caoxi in Shaozhou is the dwelling place of the Sixth Patriarch, Master Huineng. Addressing the assembly, he said: "Do not contemplate good or evil at all; naturally you will enter the essence of the mind.
It is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet its wondrous functions are as vast as the sands of the Ganges. Therefore—
The former masters said: "Not grasping a single dharma is called 'transmitting the mind. When Śākyamuni attained enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha, the Sūtra states:
'A Bodhisattva does not practice seeing dharmas; he does not practice hearing dharmas,' and so forth.

Because all Buddhas swiftly bestow upon him the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), the verse in the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* says: 'That which is grasped cannot be grasped; that which is seen cannot be seen; that which is heard...'"
It cannot be heard. It is the inconceivable single mind. When one simply and directly realizes one's own mind, there is absolutely nothing to be found outside of that mind;
this is precisely the moment of receiving the prediction of enlightenment.
This may be called the main thoroughfare for treading the Way and the true secret for awakening to the fundamental source.
This gateway of the one mind can encompass all things; thus it is said: "Within the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the Single Vehicle Dharma.
Therefore, the *Zhao Lun* states: "Heaven attains the One and becomes clear; Earth attains the One and becomes tranquil; the sovereign attains the One..."
One is used to govern the world; sentient beings attain One to accomplish the Way. One is the Way. Heaven has the Way and is light and clear;
Earth has the Way and is tranquil and still; the valleys have the Way and are full; plants and trees have the Way and grow;
ghosts and spirits have the Way and are numinous and sagely; and sovereigns have the Way and hold dominion over the world. Therefore—
One must know that this cannot be abandoned for even a moment. The Way is precisely the numinous mind.
*Commentary on the Heart Rhapsody*, Scroll Four (End).
Phonetic Glossary.
The sound "yue" (粤) refers to a particle used for discourse. "Zhi" (治) is pronounced with the initial *ch* (as in "direct");
"huai" (恢) is pronounced with the initials *k* and *h* (as in "ku-hui"). "Jian" (鍵) is pronounced with the initials *q* and *y* (as in "qu-yuan"), meaning a door bolt.
"Zhao" (爝) is pronounced with the initial *c* (as in "que"), referring to a torch or firebrand. "Dou" (逗) is pronounced with the initials *d* and *t* (as in "du-hou"), meaning to stay or to stop.
Zhào (zhào) is pronounced as jiāo (jiāo); qì (qì) is pronounced as xǔ (xǔ), meaning "to reach" or "to arrive";
dài (dài) is pronounced as tú (tú), meaning "near. Shùn (shùn) is pronounced as shū (shū), meaning "the movement of the eyes.
Luán (luán) is pronounced as kǔ (kǔ), meaning "bird's egg. Qíng (qíng) has the sound of jīn (jīn); it refers to "bone."
*Jiāo*: (pronounced with the *qǐáo* rhyme) arrogance and fury. *Jīng*: (pronounced *zǐyíng*) a military banner.
*Lǎn*: (pronounced *lújiǎn*) to grasp. *Mìu*: (pronounced *mǐyòu*) error or deception.
*Zhì*: (pronounced *zhīshí*) to roast. *Chù*: (pronounced *chūliù*) a dense crowd.
Tǐng (徒逞反) means to emerge. Gāi (古來反) means completeness;
it also means to irrigate (溉, 古代反). Yā (烏甲反) means to suppress or to descend.
Zhè (音者) means *zhě*. Bīn (疋賓反) means profuse or variegated.
Pián (píán bù tián fǎn): A cluster. Piè (piē piān miè fǎn):
To glance. Chū (chú cháng zhū fǎn): The root; the foundation. Jìn (jìn jù rèn fǎn): Famine; hunger.
Tiào (tiào tú liáo fǎn): To leap; to bound. Láo (láo yīn láo): Turbid wine.
*Biè* (pronounced with the initial *yù* and the final *liè*) means "to bend" or "to twist. *Shì* (pronounced with the initial *shì* and the final *yī*) means "to rely upon.

*Cí* (pronounced with the initial *jí* and the final *zhī*)— *Hé* (pronounced with the initial *xī* and the final *hū*, or alternatively *hú* and *jí*)— *Sì* (pronounced with the initial *shū* and the final *shì*) means "swift" or "fast. *Là* (pronounced with the initial *lú* and the final *dá*) means "deviant" or "crooked."
*Kāi* (揩) is pronounced with the *kǔ* and *guǎn* finals; it means to rub or wipe. *Bǐ* (鄙) is pronounced with the *bāng* and *měi* finals; it means lowly or vulgar.
*Tüè* (餮) is pronounced with the *tā* and *jié* finals;
it means greed for food. *Jī* (姬) is pronounced with the *yǔ* and *zhī* finals; it is another name for the wife of a king, and is also pronounced with the *jū* and *yí* finals.
Sì (sī): the pronunciation is sì. Piáo (piáo):
the phonetic reversal is pí xiāo. Bì (bì): the pronunciation is bì. Jù (jù): the phonetic reversal is qí jù; it means urgent and rapid. Tà (tà):
the phonetic reversal is tā dá; it means to strike. Nù (nù): the phonetic reversal is nǎi gù; it means to be angry.
*Wǎn* (烏板反): to tie; *gāo* (餻): pronounced *gāo*; *zhàng* (脹):
pronounced *zhàng*, meaning the belly is full; *tàn* (啗): pronounced *tú làn*, meaning to eat or consume;
*qiān* (籤): pronounced *qī lián*; *cǎn* (黲): pronounced *cāng gǎn*.
*Yi* (揖) means to yield or defer; *yī* (衣) is pronounced with the rhyme *fǎn* (反). *Biao* (褾) is pronounced with the rhyme *xiǎo* (小); it refers to the end of a sleeve.
*Zhù* (鬻) has the sound *yù* (育); it means to sell. *Sào* (噪) is pronounced with the rhyme *sī háo* (思號); it means to shout or clamor.
*Xiòu* (齅) is pronounced with the rhyme *xǔ jiù* (許救); it means to take in air through the nose. *Rèn* (仞) is pronounced with the rhyme *ér zhèn* (而振); seven feet is called one *rèn*.
Jiā (pronounced as in "gǔ" in gǔshāng) means merchant. Gé (pronounced as in "bó" in gébǎn) means manner or style.
Shēn (pronounced as in "shēn") means a sash or belt.
Pēng (pronounced as in "pū" in pūgēng) and duàn (pronounced as in "dù" in dùhuàn) mean to smelt or refine. Yì (pronounced as in "yú" in yújì) means to capture or to take.
"Shéng" (繩) means a rope or cord. "Jì" (悸), with the phonetic component "lí" (李), refers to a racing heart or palpitation.

"Wù" (杌), with the phonetic component "wú" (吳) and "hú" (鶻), refers to a wooden stool or stand. "Mó" (模), with the phonetic component "mò" (莫) and "hú" (胡), means a compass or a model. "Zhé" (謫), with the phonetic component "zhí" (陟) and "gé" (革), means to punish or banish.
"Shí" (蝕), with the phonetic component "shí" (食), refers to the waning of the sun or moon.
Chū (蒱): Pronounced *chū*; "corner" (*yú*) and "to respond" (*fǎn*).
Jué (訣): Pronounced *jué*; means "to decide" (*bié*). Bó (勃): Pronounced *bó*; a name for a star.
Suì (彗): Pronounced *suì*; a name for a star. Tóng (詷): Pronounced *tóng*; means "to slander. Shī (弑): Pronounced *shī*; when a minister kills his ruler, it is called *shī*.
*Jī* (譏) is pronounced as *jū-yī-fǎn-pái*; it means to revile. *Wú* (誣) is pronounced as *wú-yīn-wǎng*;
it means to wrong or falsely accuse. *Jiàn* (僭) is pronounced as *zǐ-niàn-fǎn*; "the mandate of Heaven is not *jiàn*" means it is not excessive or usurped. *Shì* (沵) is pronounced as *láng-jì-fǎn*;
it refers to the skin of a *yāo* (妖)—*fū* being pronounced as *fǔ-wú-fǎn*. *Bì* (閉) is pronounced as *bì-yīn-bì*; it means to shut or obstruct.
Xiǎn (險) and jiǎn (儉) rhyme with cān (嵾); they mean precipice. Pài (派) is pronounced with the *pī* and *mài* rhymes; it means to divide.
Hóng (泓) is pronounced with the *wū* and *héng* rhymes; it means deep water. Tǎn (坦) is pronounced with the *tā* and *dàn* rhymes;
it means level. Pì (闢) is pronounced with the *pí* and *yì* rhymes; it means to open. Bì (蔽) is pronounced with the *bì* and *miè* rhymes; it means to cover.
Dìng (錠): The sound of concentration; it belongs to the *xí* (錫) rhyme group. Chī (媸): The opposite of yán (妍);
it refers to ugliness. Gǎo (杲): The rising of the sun; it signifies bright clarity. Máng (芒):
The tips of grass or the awns of grain. Lí (釐): Principle or order. Yì (溢): Fullness; it means overflowing.
*Luò* (read with the reverse of *lú*) means rubble and debris. *Xún* (read with the pinyin *xùnlín*) means the edge of water.
*Kāo* (read with the pinyin *kǔjiāo*) means to strike. *Huǎn* (read with the pinyin *húguǎn*) means to relax or expand.
*Xiān* (read with the pinyin *xīlián*) means sharp or keen. *Kǜ* (read as *kǔchòu*) means silent and still.
Xiāo (梟): pronounced as in gǔ yáo, the name of a bird. Jìng (獍): pronounced as in jūn mìng, the name of a beast. Tī (剔):
pronounced as in tāng lì, to disarticulate the bones. Zhé (摘): pronounced as in zhé gé, to take with the hand. Dì (蔕):
pronounced as in dì, the root of plants and trees. Yì (抑): pronounced as in yú jí, to bend; to press down.
*Shī* (pronounced with the *shī* of *shīshǐ*) means moistened by water.
*Xia* (pronounced with the *hu* of *hújiǎ*) means a fungus; [the character is] *jùn* (pronounced *qūyǔn* or *qiúmiǎn*).
*Zhou* (pronounced *zhíyòu*) refers to armor (*jièzhòu*); *mao* (pronounced *móu*) refers to the spear (*gémáo*). *Ju* (pronounced *jūyú*) means arrogant.
Tàn (彖): read as tōng guàn fǎn; xuàn (衒): read as xián, meaning to advertise oneself;
chǎn (諂): read as chǔ yǎn fǎn, meaning flattery; chǎn (諂) also means to wound; shū (倏):
read as shū, meaning to run swiftly; làn (爛): read as lú dàn fǎn; tà (獺): read as tā dá fǎn, the name of an aquatic animal.
*He* (涸): read as *yi* (移) and *ge* (各); it means the water is exhausted. *Juan* (罥): read as *gu* (姑) and *xuan* (泫); it means to hang or entangle. *Ying* (蠅):
read as *yu* (余) and *ling* (凌); it refers to the green fly. *Pu* (捕): read as *pi* (皮) and *bu* (布). *Kao* (槁):
read as *ku* (枯) and *lao* (老); it means withered. *Niao* (橈): read as *nu* (奴) and *qiao* (巧); it means to disturb or confuse.
*Bǐng* (炳) is pronounced *yǒng* (永); it means brilliance and clarity.
*Niè* (嚙) is pronounced *liè* (列); it means sudden and violent. *Yí* (彝) is pronounced *zhī* (脂); it means constant and law.
*Jiá* (戞) is pronounced *jiá* (轄). *Yuān* (淵) is pronounced *xuán* (玄); it means deep.
*Yǒng* (swimming) is pronounced *mìngfǎn*; it means moving secretly beneath the water. *Kān* (leaping) has the phonetic *qiān*;
*jù* (詎) has the phonetic *jù*, meaning "how could" or "is it that. *Shuò* (flashing) is pronounced *zhòulèfǎn*; it means brilliant or dazzling.
*Bín* (frowning) has the phonetic *púzhēnfǎn*; it means to smile. *Shēn* (groaning) has the phonetic *shēn*; it means moaning or groaning.

*Xi* (隙) is pronounced *qū* (祛) with a retroflex initial; it refers to a crack or crevice in a wall. *An* (諳) is pronounced *yú* (於) with an aspirated nasal initial; *bó* (渤) is pronounced *pú* (蒲) with a guttural initial. *Shāng* (觴) is pronounced *shì* (式) with a palatal initial and *yáng* (羊) as the final;
*móu* (侔) has the sound *móu* (牟); it means "equal" or "uniform. *Nái* (荄) has the sound *jiē* (皆); it refers to the roots of grass.
Qū (pronounced kuāng yú fǎn): To drive away and rectify. Tiǎn (pronounced tú yǎn fǎn): To exterminate; it means "to destroy.
Jié (pronounced cí yè fǎn): Warp; it refers to the warp threads of a loom. Yī (pronounced yú lí fǎn): Long;
it also means "to lean against" or "to rely on. Huán (pronounced hú duān fǎn).
*Kǎn* (pronounced *gǎn*): to call out; to invoke. *Chà* (pronounced *suǒjiǎ*): to pinch; to press; to constrain. *Líàng*:
(phonetic transcription for *liáng*); to leap; to skip. *Diān* (pronounced *dōulián*):
epilepsy; madness. *Jué* (pronounced *jūyuè*): to stumble; to lose one's footing; also, to run.
Huì (潰) means to disperse or to be in disorder. Niè (躡) means to tread upon.
Yòu (牖) means a window. Bī (鎞) means a hairpin.
Jīng (晶) means light. Gài (槩) means to level out measures such as bushels and pecks.
*Shu* (pronounced as in "six" reversed): to contract; to withdraw.
*Chu* (pronounced as in "li" reversed): a type of tree. *Xǐ* (pronounced as in "si" with the *shì* tone):
a royal seal is called *xǐ*. *Jiān* (pronounced as in "ju" with the *yán* tone, or as in "cè" with the *lín* tone).

*Wei* (萎) [pronounced as *wei* with the initial *w* reversed] means to be withered; it is also used for being earnest. *Yi* (怡) [pronounced as *yi* with the initial *zhi* reversed] means harmony and joy.

*Fei* (懮) [pronounced as *fei* with the initial *fu* reversed] means water overflowing. *Yan* (偃) [pronounced as *yan* with the initial *yu* reversed] means to lie prostrate or to recline. *Fu* (鳧) [pronounced as *fu* with the initial *y*] refers to a wild duck.
*Xun* (循) [pronounced as *xun* with the initial *yin*] means to follow or to go around.
Tú (with the second tone, reversed from tú) means to ward off; yù (with the third tone, reversed from yǔ) means to prohibit.
Huǎng (with the third tone, reversed from huǎng) and hú (with the first tone, cut by hū and gǔ) mean indistinctness.
Zhí (with the second tone, reversed from zhì) means to be still. Pǐn (with the third tone, reversed from fú and lǚ, or alternatively pí and rěn) means female.
Jìn (cut by the rhyme-rank Ren): *hàn* (rhyme Han) means to ward off with the hand;
*zī* (the reverse of *zǐ*) is the name of a river. *què* (rhyme Kǒu Jiao): firm and solid. *pǔ*:
(rhyme Bù) a garden or orchard. *tài*: (rhyme Tài) [a type of insect].
The character 蟲*未 (chóng-wèi) has the pronunciation *wèi*. The character 齧 (niè) is pronounced niè;

it is a variant of 齧 (niè). The character 鏃 (zú) is pronounced zú; it refers to the tip of an arrow. The character 繢 (huì) is pronounced huì; it means painting or decorative coloring. The character 淳 (chún) is pronounced chún, and also lún;
it means pure or clear. The character 沃 (wù) is pronounced wù; it means to pour or to moisten. The character 清 (qīng) is pronounced qīng; it means clear or pure.
Dòu (dǒu, with the *dù* rhyme): to contend, to compete. Jìn (jí, with the *rèn* rhyme): the wick of a candle.
Miǎo (máng, with the *zhǎo* rhyme): to reach; the sound is *dài*.
Ào (wū, with the *dào* rhyme): deep; to store. Zhù (zhāng, with the *shù* rhyme): to lift up; to fly.
Yào (pronounced like yào): a lock. Mào (pronounced like mòuhòu): to trade or sell in the market.
Hào (pronounced like hào): great. Cǎo (pronounced like qīdào): to hold; intention.
Cuó (pronounced like zuóhé): short in stature. Yǎng (pronounced like yǎng): itching of the skin.
*Bǎ* (pronounced like *bà*) refers to the grip of a bow. *Yì* (at the end of the phrase *yú jì fǎn*) means "shady" or "darkness.
*Lèi* (at the end of the phrase *láng duì fǎn*) refers to coarse silk. *Pǒu* (at the end of the phrase *pǔ hòu fǎn*) means "to divide" or "to split.
*Bàng* (at the end of the phrase *bǎng fǎn*) refers to a clam or oyster. *Kuì* (at the end of the phrase *qiú wèi fǎn*) refers to a basket for carrying earth.
Tàn (pronounced *tàn* with the second tone; meaning "to take") Tàn (pronounced *dàn* with the fourth tone; a sandbank or mound in the water) Sǒu (pronounced *sǒu* with the fourth tone;
a marsh or thicket) Jiǎo (pronounced *jiǎo* with the third tone) Màn (pronounced *màn* with the fourth tone) Mài (pronounced *mò* with the second tone)
Fàn (pinyin: fán; note: *fú* jiǎn fǎn): To leap; to stride. Chào (pinyin: chāo; note: *chì* jué fǎn): To go far away. Zàn (pinyin: zàn; note:
*cái* dàn fǎn, also *cái* kǒu fǎn): A jade cup or ladle. Juǎng (pinyin: juǎng; note: *dǎ* guā fǎn): The bolt of a door. Chù (pinyin: chù; note:
*chū* liù fǎn): A crowd; to throng. Yù (pinyin: yù; note: *yī* jù fǎn): Congestion; blood congestion.
"Yù" (彚) is pronounced as "wèi"; it means "category. "Gān" (柑) is pronounced as "gān"; it is the name of a tree.

"Fàn" (汎) is pronounced as "fán" (with the rhyme category *fu* and the final *xiàn*). "Yōu" (攸) is pronounced as "yóu. "Gǎo" (藁) is pronounced as "hāo" (with the rhyme category *hū* and the final *láo*). "Jué" (厥) is pronounced as "jué" (with the rhyme category *jū*); it means "his" or "its."
Tuan (with the phonetic "duan" as a rhyme): the rushing of water. Chan (pronounced like "chi-wo," with the phonetic "wu-huo" as a rhyme):
a type of insect. Yun (with the phonetic "yu-run" as a rhyme): anger.
Zhi (with the phonetic "zhi-li" as a rhyme): a foundation for standing upon.
Chù (initially *chū*, also the reverse of *chì*): the appearance of being straight.
Bèng (*lǐ*, reversed): to scatter. Zàn (pronounced *zàn*): to splash water.
Shǐ (*shì*, reversed): excrement. Niào (*náo*, reversed): urine.
*Zhen*: reversed sound of *cè*. *Zhí*: reversed sound of *zǔ*; it means to gather and to stop.
*Jí*: sound of *jiē*; refers to the oars of a boat. *Xī*: reversed sound of *xū*. *Shěng*:
reversed sound of *shì xǐng*. *Chī*: reversed sound of *chǒu zhī*.
Ní (with the "lǐ" rhyme) Máng (with the "wǎng" rhyme) Zhuó (with the "zhè" rhyme) Lì (with the "jī" rhyme); small stones are called lì.
Zhù (with the "lǚ" rhyme); *zhú* (pronounced *jué*) is the name of a bamboo species.
Wā (rhymes with wǎ): a frog. Zuàn (rhymes with suàn): a drill or awl. Zī (rhymes with sī):
a weight, one hundredth of an ounce. Zhū (pronounced zhū): a fraction, one-tenth of a zī.
Háo (rhymes with láo): to cry out. Yǔn (rhymes with zhuǎn): to perish.
Xiè (pronounced with the *si* and *lie* finals reversed) means "to leak.

Wū (pronounced as in "wu") means "to prick" (*zhēn* with the *zhī* and *lín* finals reversed); it means "to rule" or "a ridgepole. Shàn (pronounced with the *shí* and *xiàn* finals reversed) means "to carve.
Wān (pronounced as in "wu" and "wán") means "to gouge. Wěn (pronounced as in "wu" and "fěn") means "to cut the throat."
Mén (pronounced mén): to feel with the hand; qí (pronounced jì or qí) and lǐ (pronounced lǐ):
*qí* is the opposite of *lǐ*; sòu (pronounced sòu or shì hòu): to rinse the mouth;
huán (pronounced huán): circular; yuán (pronounced yuán): to surround; xùn (pronounced luàn or rùn): to go around.
Yīn (湮) means to fall into silence; it means to sink. Xù (緒): the initial radical is "mouth" (口), with the phonetic "lǚ" (呂); the reading is xū (徐).
